Households from the hills settle the bay at Ros bheag, the first of them on the west coast. They build in the hill manner, round and turf-roofed, a little back from the beach, and they fish from the shore rather than from boats.
8 an Gearran 6295 BDE Seann Skell
Amber from the Hawk bay
Lumps of amber gathered from the wrack on the strands of the Hawk bay are found drilled for stringing in the middens below Seann Skell. A bead of the same amber lies in the oldest ground of the ford gathering, carried there the length of the island.
3 an t-Sultain 6254 BDE Cathair dhomhain
The first houses at Cathair dhomhain
A cluster of round houses goes up by the harbour where Cathair dhomhain now stands, near enough the Red Hill to pay it salt. The Red Hill list counts it among the holder's households.
25 am Màrt 6222 BDE Cnoc ghorm
Cattle in the north-west
Cattle bones appear in the hearths of Cnoc ghorm in the north-west for the first time. Until now the settlements there lived on seal, fish and deer. The herds must have been walked up the flint road.
24 an Gearran 6185 BDE Cathair gheal
The long-house at Cathair gheal
A long-house forty paces long is built on the rise at Cathair gheal, with byre and hall under one roof. It is the largest single building of this age in the north-west, and it burns and is rebuilt on the same footing twice.
21 an t-Iuchar 6149 BDE Toll-dubh
A youth let down into Toll-dubh
The tellings of the south-east keep the story of a youth let down on a rope of plaited hide into the eastern Toll-dubh, to the rope's end. He was drawn up alive, and he never said what was at the bottom. After him no one went down again in this age.
19 an Lùnastal 6112 BDE Marbh-bheò Doire uaine
A fire lit in the Doire uaine hills
A herding family, new to the hills, lights an open fire at Doire uaine against the custom. The telling says the hut was found empty and the fire still burning. The custom of the covered hearth is kept stricter after.
24 an Cèitean 6076 BDE Loch chrom
The lake dwellings burn
The platforms on Loch chrom burn to the waterline, and the charred piles are left standing in the shallows. No one rebuilds on the lake in this age.
22 an t-Ògmhios 6039 BDE Caol leathan
Seal-oil lamps at Caol leathan
Stone lamps with a hollow for seal oil and a moss wick are in use at Caol leathan. They are the first light on Rodos that is not a hearth, and they make no smoke to speak of.
27 am Màrt 6003 BDE Caol fhiadhaich
The fish-traps of Caol fhiadhaich
Wattle fences are staked across the river-mouth at Caol fhiadhaich to trap salmon on the ebb. The same line of stake-holes is used and re-used through the rest of the age.
25 an Giblean 5973 BDE Muileann leathan
The upright looms of Muileann leathan
Loom-weights of fired clay, lying in rows where they fell from the warp, are found in the houses at Muileann leathan in the north. Cloth is being woven there on standing frames, not twined by hand.
28 am Faoilleach 5930 BDE
The first tide-count
Someone begins marking the high-water line against a fixed rock, for reasons never recorded, in intervals later scholars recognize as suspiciously regular for a purely practical fisherman's habit.
26 an Gearran 5893 BDE Ros dhomhain
A second tide-rock at Ros dhomhain
The high-water marking is copied at Ros dhomhain on a boulder in the harbour mouth. The marks there are cut at the same intervals as on the first rock, which means someone carried the practice, and the interval with it.
10 am Màrt 5854 BDE Ros dhomhain
The lake is higher
The marks on the Ros dhomhain rock creep upward from keeper to keeper. By the end of this age Loch chrom stands a hand higher on the rock than it did at the first cut. The keepers kept cutting.
8 an Giblean 5820 BDE Cnoc àrsaidh
The flint of Cnoc àrsaidh
A pit is worked for flint on the hill of Cnoc àrsaidh in the north-west, the only good flint on Rodos. Grey flakes from it are found in hearths from one end of the island to the other.
11 am Faoilleach 5784 BDE Àth leathan
The flint road
A track worn by people carrying flint runs from Cnoc àrsaidh south and east toward the ford gathering. Stretches of it near Àth leathan are sunk a yard deep by feet.
13 an Dùbhlachd 5748 BDE Àth mhòr
The hawk lintel at Àth mhòr
A lintel stone over a house door at Àth mhòr in the north is carved with a hawk, wings closed, head turned. It is the oldest hawk carving on the island and the oldest carving of any bird.
10 am Màrt 5711 BDE Tobar fhiadhaich
Wolves at Tobar fhiadhaich
The bones of wolves are found buried whole and with care at Tobar fhiadhaich, laid on their sides like people. No other beast is buried that way in this age.
9 an Gearran 5674 BDE Dùn ìseal
Sìleas Bhàn and the hungry years
Sìleas Bhàn, eighth of the Stone Kings, holds Dùn ìseal through years of failed grazing. The telling gives her no deed but survival: she held, and the list goes on after her.
7 an Cèitean 5635 BDE Gorta Baile chrom
The hunger at Baile chrom
The hearths of the settlement on the site of the north-western Baile chrom are found with their pots full of boiled bark and seaweed, and the grave-rows beside them doubled. It is the oldest hunger on Rodos with a place to it.
8 an Giblean 5595 BDE Tiormachd Achadh shean
The drought at Achadh shean
The springs of Achadh shean in the east run dry for long enough that the field banks are abandoned and grown over. When people come back they cut new fields on a different line.
4 an t-Iuchar 5554 BDE
The naming of the wind directions
The eight-point wind system every later Ròdaich sailor still uses is fixed in this period, with names that translate awkwardly and have simply never been replaced.
5 an t-Ògmhios 5517 BDE Ceann leathan
The wind-stones of Ceann leathan
Eight tall stones are set in a ring on the point at Ceann leathan, one for each of the named winds. Sailors of every later age touch the stone of the wind they want before they go out.
24 an Cèitean 5477 BDE Eilean fhada
The wind-names carried to the islands
The eight wind-names are in use on Eilean fhada as well as the main island: stone markers on its high point carry eight cut notches, one facing each way.
25 an Giblean 5438 BDE Dùn ìseal
Tormod Liath
Tormod Liath, ninth of the Stone Kings, is remembered as old: the list says he outlived three heirs. In his time Dùn ìseal gets its second bank, doubling the enclosed ground.
4 an t-Iuchar 5400 BDE
The Ròdaich name
Somewhere in this age the hill-folk begin to call themselves Ròdaich and the island Ròdos. No one records the first use. The oldest tellings already assume both names, and the doctrine goes with them: they did not come; they were here.
2 an Lùnastal 5378 BDE
The first forbidden marriage
A union between two lineages is refused for reasons no surviving text explains — the earliest evidence that Rodian society organized itself by bloodline before it had any obsidian-caste reason to.
31 an Lùnastal 5354 BDE Fèill Muileann òg
Lines recited at the ford
At the ford gathering, households begin reciting their lines aloud before any marriage is agreed, seven names back on each side. The recitations are the first genealogies on Rodos. None of them survives complete.
29 an t-Sultain 5334 BDE Cnoc dhubh
The first seeking of another vein
Diggers from Dùn ìseal open a trench on a hill near Cnoc dhubh in the east, looking for black rock like the vein's. They give it up unfinished when two of them are crushed by a fall. The trench is left open, and no one says what it would have found.
10 am Màrt 5312 BDE
The stone that would not break
A second attempt to open a new vein elsewhere on the island fails entirely — ordinary rock, nothing beneath it. The first confirmation that the vein under the mountain is not a rule, but an exception.
8 an Giblean 5289 BDE
The prospecting ends
After the failed second opening, no one in this age tries a third. The Ròdaich take it as a sign that the vein chooses where it lies, and that the choosing is not theirs to test.
7 an Cèitean 5273 BDE
The first shared meal law
An unwritten custom, later formalized, requiring any household with surplus food to share it before a storm season — the earliest form of the communal obligation later ages will lean on more heavily than they admit.
5 an t-Ògmhios 5245 BDE Dùn ìseal
Surplus shared at Dùn ìseal
At Dùn ìseal the sharing before the storm season is done in the open: every household brings its surplus to the space inside the bank and it is divided by count of mouths. The bank is the first place the custom is known to have a place.
14 an t-Samhain 5223 BDE Àth shean
A household turned out at Àth shean
A household at Àth shean hides its surplus grain in a pit under the floor and brings nothing to the sharing. When the pit is found the household is put out of the settlement with what it can carry. It is the first known punishment under the custom.
13 an Dùbhlachd 5201 BDE Dùn ìseal
Eilidh Ghlas
Eilidh Ghlas, tenth of the Stone Kings, sends her younger son to the Red Hill to be fostered. It is the first fosterage in either list. The son's name is not kept; only that he went, and that the peace of the ford held while he was there.
25 an Dùbhlachd 5200 BDE Cathair dhearg
Lachlann Ruadh takes the fosterling
Lachlann Ruadh, holder of the Red Hill, takes Eilidh Ghlas's son into his house. The Red Hill list gives him a byname for it, Lachlann an Altraim, 'Lachlann of the fostering', and uses it more often than his own.
26 an t-Samhain 5198 BDE Tobar dhìreach
Oighrig, first keeper by lot
The families who watch the slab over the crack agree to choose one keeper at a time by lot instead of taking turns by household. The first lot falls to a woman the tellings call Oighrig nic Dhòmhnaill. She keeps the slab for the rest of her life.
28 an Dàmhair 5197 BDE Tobar dhìreach
The keepers' house
A house is built beside the slab at Tobar dhìreach for whoever holds the lot, with a door facing the stone. It is rebuilt on the same footing many times. It is the first building on Rodos that exists only to be near the vein.
29 an t-Sultain 5196 BDE Tobar dhìreach
The stone cup
Oighrig nic Dhòmhnaill has a cup ground out of grey stone to the size of her own cupped hand, so that the handful of ore would be the same for every household. The cup is carried round the hill settlements. Whether it survived the age is not known.
31 an Lùnastal 5194 BDE Cnoc chaol
The stone cup copied
Copies of the keeper's cup are ground at Àth gharbh, Achadh dhìreach and Cnoc chaol, each checked against the first by filling it with water. The hill settlements now measure the ore with one measure.
28 an Dùbhlachd 5193 BDE Coinneachadh nan Cupan
The meeting of the cups
The keeper's cup and its three copies are carried to a spring on the moor between Àth gharbh and Tobar dhìreach, set side by side on a flat stone and filled from the spring in turn. The place is called Coinneachadh nan Cupan, the meeting of the cups, and the hill settlements come back to it whenever a cup is broken and a new one must be checked.
2 an Lùnastal 5192 BDE Eilean chrom
Gilleasbuig Beag takes ore
A keeper by lot named Gilleasbuig Beag is found with a basket of broken ore in his own house. The households of the hills sit in judgement at the slab and row him out to Eilean chrom and leave him there without a boat. He is the first person on record exiled for the vein.
4 an t-Iuchar 5190 BDE Tobar dhìreach
The ore returned to the crack
The ore found in Gilleasbuig Beag's house is not burned and not kept. It is carried back to the slab and laid under it, piece by piece, by the keeper who followed him. The tellings make much of this: the ore went home.
4 an t-Iuchar 5189 BDE Dùn ìseal
Calum Ciar asks for the lot
Calum Ciar, eleventh of the Stone Kings, asks the households at the slab that the keeper's lot be drawn at Dùn ìseal in his sight. The households refuse. The list records the refusal, which is more than the list usually records of anything.
7 an Cèitean 5185 BDE Dùn ìseal
The kings and the keepers
After Calum Ciar's refusal the lot is still drawn at the slab, and the Stone Kings go on ruling the grazing and the gatherings but not the vein. The line between the two holds for the rest of this age. It is not yet written anywhere.
1 an Gearran 5184 BDE Cuan ruadh
A' Ghaoth Dhubh
A storm the tellings call A' Ghaoth Dhubh, the Black Wind, strips the thatch from every house on the east coast from Cuan ruadh to Ceann chiar. It is the oldest storm whose name is kept.
8 an Giblean 5184 BDE Ceann chiar
The sharing holds after the Black Wind
After the Black Wind, the settlements of the east coast feed the people of Cuan ruadh through a whole winter from their shared surplus. No one on that coast is recorded as dying of hunger that season.
2 am Màrt 5183 BDE Taigh-solais Baile ìseal
The beacon at Baile ìseal
A fire is built up on the eastern cape where Taigh-solais Baile ìseal now stands, kept by the households of the coast in turn. Its purpose, in the tellings, is to bring boats home in a storm, not to warn them off.
3 am Faoilleach 5182 BDE Taigh-solais Muileann bheag
The beacon at Muileann bheag
A second shore-fire is kept on the north coast, on the point where Taigh-solais Muileann bheag stands now. The ash under the modern tower goes down through three yards of fire-reddened soil.
5 an Dùbhlachd 5182 BDE Taigh-solais Àth dhearg
The beacon at Àth dhearg
Households of the north-east coast keep a fire on the cape where Taigh-solais Àth dhearg now stands, and cut steps up to it from the shore. The steps are narrower than those at Seann Bhral and less worn.
28 an Cèitean 5181 BDE Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg
The beacon at Tobar dhearg
On the southern cape where Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg stands a fire is kept for the boats of the south coast. With the fires at Baile chrom, Baile ìseal, Muileann bheag and Àth dhearg, the island's coasts are lit at five points.
31 am Màrt 5180 BDE Uilebheist na Mara
The Sea-Watcher seen from Seann Skell
Watchers on the north-western tower at Seann Skell report a back as long as three boats, rising and going under off the point. It is the first sighting of the Sea-Watcher that the tellings tie to a named place and a count of witnesses: four.
26 an t-Ògmhios 5180 BDE Spùinneadairean-mara
Wreckage in the western water
Planks of stitched boats, broken small, wash up for a season along the western shore below the waters where raiders are later seen. No bodies come with them. No settlement on that coast is missing a boat.
29 an Giblean 5179 BDE Fèill Muileann òg
Anndra Breac says 'we came'
At the ford gathering a teller from the western coast, Anndra Breac, recites a telling in which the people came to Rodos over the sea. The households of the hills shout him down and the gathering puts him out of the ford for the rest of his life. His telling is not kept, only the fact of it.
21 an t-Sultain 5178 BDE Calbh Cnoc ghorm
The doctrine said at the column
After Anndra Breac, the saying cut on the column at Cnoc ghorm is spoken aloud at the opening of the ford gathering: we did not come; we were here. It is the first time the doctrine is known to be said as a rule rather than a belief.
25 an t-Iuchar 5177 BDE Ros dhomhain
The keepers of the Ros dhomhain rock
The tide-rock at Ros dhomhain passes to a woman remembered as Seònaid Mhòr, who cuts her marks in pairs, one for the high water and one for the low. Her pairs are still readable. The keepers after her go back to single marks.
20 an Dàmhair 5177 BDE Inis thais
A third tide-rock at Inis thais
Households at Inis thais cut their own high-water marks on the harbour rock, at the same interval as Ros dhomhain. The three rocks now run side by side. None of them says why the interval is what it is.
26 an t-Ògmhios 5176 BDE Ros dhomhain
Ros dhomhain grows
The settlement at Ros dhomhain becomes the largest on the shores of Loch chrom, with some sixty houses round the tide-rock. Its people fish from boats now, not from the shore.
23 an Lùnastal 5175 BDE Cathair dhearg
The Red Hill's harbour
The Red Hill's households build a landing of laid stone on the river-mouth below the hill, where Cathair dhearg's harbour is now. It is the Red Hill's first way onto the water, and by the lake and the Abhainn gheal to the sea.
21 an t-Sultain 5175 BDE Cathair dhearg
Peigi Dhubh of the Red Hill
Peigi Dhubh holds the Red Hill after Lachlann an Altraim. She sends the fostered son of Dùn ìseal home grown, with gifts of salt, and the ford peace holds a generation more.
31 am Màrt 5174 BDE Dùn ìseal
The foster-son returns
The son of Eilidh Ghlas comes home from the Red Hill to Dùn ìseal. The Stone Kings' list gives him no name and no reign; he is remembered only as the one who went, and for bringing western salt-songs home with him.
2 am Màrt 5173 BDE Baile ghorm
The first songs kept
The salt-songs of the south and west, work-songs for raking the pans, are the oldest songs on Rodos whose words are said to survive. What survives is a refrain of four lines that no one can fully translate.
14 am Màrt 5173 BDE Cnoc àrsaidh
Bone pipes at Cnoc àrsaidh
Pipes of hollow bird-bone, bored with four holes, are found in a house at the southern Cnoc àrsaidh near the panther road. They are the oldest instruments on the island.
29 an Giblean 5173 BDE Imrich nam Pantar
The panthers turn back
In one season the great cats come down the panther road near Imrich nam Pantar and turn back at the foothills instead of crossing. The hill-folk take it as a sign of a hard winter and store double. The winter is hard.
28 an Cèitean 5173 BDE Muileann bhàn
The cattle lost in the passes
Herders from Muileann bhàn drive cattle up into the passes out of season, against the custom of the crossing. The panthers take thirty head in a night. The herders come down with nothing.
15 am Faoilleach 5154 BDE Baile dhomhain
The panther season kept at Baile dhomhain
The households at Baile dhomhain in the south cut a sign on their gateposts at the start of the crossing season and scrape it off at the end. It is the island's first mark for a season.
13 an Gearran 5154 BDE Seann Chwen
The wind-stone at Seann Chwen
One of the eight wind-names is cut in the Ròdaich manner on a boulder at the central Seann Chwen, over an older mark of the Seann-Dhaoine. It is one of the few places where the marks of the two peoples touch.
14 an Gearran 5154 BDE Caol bheag
Boats named for the winds
Fishing households at Caol bheag, who fish the north coast from the mouth of the Abhainn ghorm, name their boats for the winds they fish in. A boat named for the wrong wind is thought unlucky, and one that sinks has its name never used again.
14 am Màrt 5154 BDE Tuam Cnoc dhìreach
The Tuam keepers
A family living by Tuam Cnoc dhìreach takes on the clearing of the thorn from the old graves. They bury no one of their own there. They only keep it.
12 an Giblean 5154 BDE Tuam Cnoc dhìreach
A grave at Tuam opened
Diggers laying a new row at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach break into an older grave than any they knew, lined with slabs cut in the Seann-Dhaoine way. They close it and move the row. No one opens that grave again.
11 an Cèitean 5152 BDE Coille Naomh Muileann chiar
Pilgrims at Coille Naomh Muileann chiar
People begin to walk to the edge of Coille Naomh Muileann chiar and sit a night at the line of the trees without entering. Hearths along the edge show the visits: small fires, a single night each.
9 an t-Ògmhios 5150 BDE Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag
A child lost in Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag
A child from Cnoc bheag's settlement goes past the line of stones into Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag and is not found. The search party stops at the stones. The telling does not blame them.
8 an t-Iuchar 5148 BDE Cnoc bheag
The first house at Cnoc bheag
Settlers from the Red Hill build at Cnoc bheag, near the forest's edge. They take their timber from the far side of the river, never from the unclaimed wood.
6 an Lùnastal 5146 BDE Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh
The spring at Muileann ruadh
Pilgrims come to the warm springs at Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh in numbers, and a ring of shelters is built. The oldest cure-telling on Rodos is set there: a herder who came lame and walked home.
28 an Cèitean 5144 BDE Marbh-bheò Doire uaine
The Hollow Man seen again
Two herders driving past the Doire uaine hills after dark say they saw a figure walk the ridge without breath showing in the cold. They had no fire lit, and the telling says that is why they lived.
26 an t-Ògmhios 5141 BDE Muileann chiar
The covered hearth spreads
The custom of the covered hearth, pit-dug and roofed, spreads from the Doire uaine hills to the settlements around Muileann chiar. The later rule that no open fire is lit on those slopes after dark starts here.
31 an Dùbhlachd 5139 BDE Caol mhòr
Settlers at Caol mhòr
Ròdaich households settle at Caol mhòr in the north-west, on the strait where the Seann-Dhaoine once hunted seal. They find the old middens and build on them.
2 an Dùbhlachd 5137 BDE Baile chrom
Settlers at Baile chrom in the north-west
The ground at Baile chrom that was emptied by the old hunger is settled again by households from Cnoc ghorm. They dig their pits for storage deeper than anyone else on the coast.
3 an t-Samhain 5135 BDE Muileann àrsaidh
Muileann àrsaidh settled
A cluster of houses goes up on the stream at Muileann àrsaidh in the north-west. Their flint is from Cnoc àrsaidh and their salt from the south, carried the length of the island.
5 an Dàmhair 5133 BDE Muileann àrsaidh
The salt road to the north-west
A salt road runs from the pans of Baile ghorm through the ford gathering to the north-west. The salt reaches Muileann àrsaidh at three times its price at the pans, paid in flint and seal-skins.
26 an Giblean 5131 BDE Doire ghlas
Doire ghlas settled
Households move in under the oaks at Doire ghlas in the north. The settlement grows in rings, each ring of houses built outside the last as the wood is cleared back.
28 am Màrt 5128 BDE Dùn thais
The east settled at Dùn thais
The hill-folk push east and build a banked enclosure at Dùn thais, on a hill above good grazing. It is the first defended place built by the Ròdaich away from Dùn ìseal and the Red Hill.
27 an Gearran 5126 BDE Achadh chaol
Achadh chaol cleared
Fields are cleared by fire and stone-picking at Achadh chaol in the east. The picked stones are laid in banks round each field, and the banks are still the field boundaries.
29 am Faoilleach 5124 BDE Cuan ruadh
Cuan ruadh rebuilt
Cuan ruadh, stripped by the Black Wind, is rebuilt in stone to the height of the eaves. It is the first settlement on the east coast to build its walls against wind rather than cold.
13 an Cèitean 5078 BDE Cathair fhada
Cathair fhada on the south coast
A settlement is founded at Cathair fhada on the south coast, between the old Seann Dunn and Seann Chwen. It takes its water from a well the Seann-Dhaoine dug and never mentions where the well came from.
14 an Giblean 5031 BDE Caol ruadh
Caol ruadh on the southern strait
Fishing households settle Caol ruadh on the south coast and take the strait's cod on long lines. Their middens are the first on the south coast with more fish than shell in them.
13 an t-Sultain 4985 BDE Baile Mòr mhòr
Baile Mòr mhòr in the north
Houses are built at Baile Mòr mhòr, on the northern plain, around a spring that never freezes. The settlement is large for the age: some eighty houses at its height.
15 an Lùnastal 4939 BDE Baile gharbh
Baile gharbh in the north-east
Households settle the rough ground at Baile gharbh and live by sheep, not cattle. Their wool goes south along the coast to the ford gathering.
17 an t-Iuchar 4892 BDE Baile fhiadhaich
Baile fhiadhaich on the west coast
Settlers at Baile fhiadhaich build on the western coast where boars run in the thickets. Boar tusks are hung over their doors, and boar is their main meat for the rest of the age.
18 an t-Ògmhios 4846 BDE Cuan shean
Cuan shean settled
Ròdaich households take up the harbour at Cuan shean on the west coast, next to an old landing whose builders are not known. The landing is reused without repair.
7 am Faoilleach 4800 BDE Dùn chrom
Dùn chrom raised
A banked hill-fort is raised at Dùn chrom in the centre of the island, between the Red Hill and the hills of the vein. Its bank faces both ways.
9 an Dùbhlachd 4754 BDE Cathair mhòr
Cathair mhòr below the old outpost
Households settle on the ground below Làrach an Dùin-fhaire, where Cathair mhòr now stands. They take no stone from the ruin above them, though it would have been the nearest quarry.
10 an t-Samhain 4707 BDE Cnoc naomh
Cnoc naomh
A hill called Cnoc naomh, the holy hill, is settled by households who come there for its spring. Why the hill was already called holy when they came is not known.
12 an Dàmhair 4654 BDE Tobar dhearg
Tobar dhearg on the southern cape
The households that keep the beacon at Tobar dhearg build their settlement on the cape itself, round a well whose water runs reddish from the rock. It becomes the largest place on the south coast.
24 am Faoilleach 4615 BDE Muileann naomh
Muileann naomh founded
A settlement is founded at Muileann naomh near the south coast, between the beacon at Tobar dhearg and the old Seann Skell. Its first houses are built on stilts over a marsh and later moved to firm ground.
26 an Dùbhlachd 4573 BDE Ceann mhin
Ceann mhin on the south-eastern shore
The south-eastern Ceann mhin is settled near Làrach an Dùin. Its people are the first to live in sight of the fortress ruin, and they will not go up to it.
23 am Màrt 4522 BDE Seann Skell
Seann Skell of the south
Ròdaich households take up the old harbour at the southern Seann Skell, keeping its old name. Within a few generations it is the busiest landing on the south coast.
21 an Giblean 4476 BDE Achadh shean
Achadh shean resettled
After the drought, households come back to Achadh shean and cut new fields on the higher ground. They sink a deep well first and plant after, and the well does not fail again in this age.
20 an Cèitean 4429 BDE Inis mhin
Inis mhin settled
A few households settle at Inis mhin on the eastern coast. They live by eggs and birds from the cliffs, and trade feathers inland.
18 an t-Ògmhios 4383 BDE Muileann chaol
Muileann chaol on its hill
Households settle on the hill at Muileann chaol, above the upper reaches of the rivers. The ground where the library stands now is a cattle-fold in this age.
17 an t-Iuchar 4337 BDE Leabharlann Muileann chaol
Cairns on the hill at Muileann chaol
The households of Muileann chaol raise a cairn for each head of a household at his or her death, on the slope above the fold. Some forty cairns stand there by the end of the age.
15 an Lùnastal 4290 BDE Baile Mòr ruadh
Baile Mòr ruadh in the east
A settlement grows up at Baile Mòr ruadh near the eastern Seann Dunn, on land its people call empty. The Seann Dunn middens lie a morning's walk away. The settlers do not dig into them.
13 an t-Sultain 4244 BDE Làrach an Teampaill
The temple ruin avoided
The Ròdaich of the eastern hills pass Làrach an Teampaill on their paths without stopping and without taking stone from it. A path is worn round it at a distance.
12 an Dàmhair 4198 BDE Còmhrag Ceann leathan
Ceann leathan's contests
At Ceann leathan the gathering by the wind-stones is ended with wrestling and stone-lifting. The heaviest lifting-stone, a black boulder, is still on the point, and few have raised it.
3 an Lùnastal 4151 BDE Fèill Muileann òg
The ford gathering grows
The ford gathering at Muileann òg now draws households from every coast. Its ground is divided into places by custom: the salt people downstream, the hill people upstream, the flint people on the far bank.
1 an t-Sultain 4105 BDE Àth àrsaidh
Stone axes from the north
Axes of polished green stone from a quarry near Àth àrsaidh in the north-west turn up across the island. They are too fine for work, and most are found unused, in graves or under house floors.
13 an Giblean 4054 BDE Àth àrsaidh
The quarry at Àth àrsaidh
The green-stone quarry at Àth àrsaidh is worked by a few households who trade nothing else. The chips around it are knee-deep. The quarry is abandoned before the age ends, and the axes stop.
19 an t-Sultain 4013 BDE Doire ghlas
The moor takes the north
The pollen in the bog under Doire ghlas shows the oak falling back. Heather, birch and bog-moss spread over the northern lowlands, and the groves that give the north its many Doire names shrink to the sheltered valleys, where they still stand. The tellings of the north remember it as the time the winters lengthened.
15 am Màrt 3973 BDE Abhainn fhionn
The river crossings of Abhainn fhionn
Stepping-stones are laid across Abhainn fhionn at its shallows, the first made crossing of any river on the island. They are older than the first bridges and in places lie under them.
10 an t-Ògmhios 3921 BDE Abhainn chaol
A drowning at the fords of Abhainn chaol
A spate on Abhainn chaol takes a party of twelve crossing with salt at its fords. After it the crossing is not made in the wet season.
12 an Cèitean 3875 BDE Ceann chiar
The Black Wind remembered at Ceann chiar
The people of Ceann chiar, rebuilding after the Black Wind, set a stone in the middle of their settlement and cut on it one mark for every house lost: twenty-two.
7 an Lùnastal 3830 BDE Muileann bhàn
A dry year on the eastern plain
The rivers of the eastern plain run low for a whole summer, and the households of Dùn ìseal and Muileann bhàn drive their cattle to the warm springs for water. The shared surplus holds; the tellings count no deaths.
9 an t-Iuchar 3784 BDE Tonn Mhòr Cnoc chaol
A second wave on the south coast
The sea comes in again over the low ground at Cnoc chaol, less far than the first time. The new houses were built higher up the slope, and none is lost.
4 an Dàmhair 3738 BDE Scàineadh Cill ghlas
The ground shakes at Cill ghlas again
The old crack at Cill ghlas moves again and the spring shifts back uphill. The line of white stones is found broken in two places and relaid.
5 an t-Sultain 3693 BDE Cnoc bheag
Cnoc bheag under the Carragh
Households settle on the bank of the Abhainn ìseal at Cnoc bheag, a short walk from Carragh Cnoc bheag. They set their houses so that none has its door toward the stone.
1 an Dùbhlachd 3646 BDE Inis bhàn
The seal rocks of Inis bhàn
The households of Inis bhàn on the lower Abhainn ìseal take seals from the skerries off the river mouth by agreement, one household to a rock. A rock taken out of turn is the commonest quarrel in their tellings.
2 an t-Samhain 3601 BDE Achadh mhòr
Fields at Achadh mhòr
The wide field at Achadh mhòr, near the warm springs, is cleared and banked, the largest single field of the age. Its bank is laid with the stones of an older wall no one claims.
7 an Cèitean 3554 BDE Baile ghlas
The harbour at Baile ghlas
Boats of the Red Hill households are drawn up at Baile ghlas, along the lake shore from the hill, in sheds of stone and turf. It becomes the Red Hill's fishing harbour.
5 an t-Ògmhios 3510 BDE Achadh naomh
Achadh naomh's spring-fields
Settlers at Achadh naomh in the north water their fields from a spring they will not build over, and carry the water in channels round it. The spring is fenced before any house is.
10 am Màrt 3473 BDE Caol gharbh
Caol gharbh on the rough strait
Households settle at Caol gharbh on the north-east coast and fish the strait in skin boats. Their graves hold paddles laid beside the dead.
8 an Giblean 3418 BDE Doire chiar
Doire chiar
A settlement grows up under the dark oaks at Doire chiar in the north. Its people pen pigs in the wood and drive them out to the acorns in the fall of the year.
11 am Faoilleach 3373 BDE Caol shean
The river landing at Caol shean
Caol shean, on the Abhainn ìseal east of the vein, becomes the river landing for the hill households east of the vein. Salt, fish and seal-skins come up the river to it from the coast, and on from it to the keepers' country.
9 an Gearran 3327 BDE Dùn dhearg
Dùn dhearg raised
A hill-fort with a double bank is raised at Dùn dhearg, east of the vein, by households who owe nothing to Dùn ìseal. The Stone Kings' list does not name its holders; it only says Dùn dhearg did not come to the gatherings.
14 an t-Samhain 3280 BDE Fèill Muileann òg
Dùn dhearg comes to the ford
The households of Dùn dhearg come to the ford gathering for the first time in Catrìona Mhòr's time, bringing seal-skins and asking for salt. They are given their own ground on the far bank.
13 an Dùbhlachd 3276 BDE Àth fhiadhaich
Settlers at Àth fhiadhaich
Households settle at Àth fhiadhaich in the south-eastern hills, by a ford where wild cattle cross. They catch the calves and raise them, and their herds are later the best in those hills.
17 an t-Sultain 3273 BDE Ceann àrsaidh
Ceann àrsaidh
The point at Ceann àrsaidh on the Abhainn fhionn is settled by households from the Red Hill. They find an old river landing there and name the place for it: the ancient headland.
19 an t-Sultain 3273 BDE Cnoc thais
Cnoc thais in the north-west
Households settle on the damp hill at Cnoc thais in the north-west and drain it with ditches. The ditches still carry water.
16 an Dàmhair 3273 BDE Inis mhòr
Inis mhòr
Households settle Inis mhòr on the Abhainn ghorm in the north-east, and live by the fish of its sheltered river pools. Their houses are built in two rows facing each other, the oldest street on Rodos.
27 an Giblean 3254 BDE Baile gheal
Baile gheal in the south-west
Baile gheal, on the south-western plain, is founded around a house with white-limed walls. The lime is burned from shells from the old middens along the coast.
26 an Cèitean 3254 BDE Àth bheag
Àth bheag on the eastern coast
Households settle the small ford at Àth bheag on the far eastern coast, the easternmost settlement of the age on the main island. Their boats go out to the geese on the islands.
26 an Cèitean 3254 BDE Dùn ìseal
Catrìona Mhòr
Catrìona Mhòr, twelfth of the Stone Kings and the last name the oral list gives, holds Dùn ìseal. Her telling says she knew every household of the hills by its line back seven names.
23 an t-Iuchar 3254 BDE Cathair dhearg
Seumas Òg of the Red Hill
Seumas Òg holds the Red Hill. He is the last name in the Red Hill's oral list; the list stops with him, and in the next age what the reciters kept of it is written down and no longer only spoken.
23 an t-Iuchar 3254 BDE Fèill Muileann òg
The two lists recited together
At the ford gathering in Catrìona Mhòr's time, the Stone Kings' list and the Red Hill list are recited one after the other, from first name to last. It takes from dusk to dawn. It is the first time anyone hears both whole.
29 am Màrt 3251 BDE Tobar dhìreach
Lots drawn for the slab
The lot for the keeper of the slab is now drawn among households from every part of the hills, not only those near the crack. The keeper's house at Tobar dhìreach becomes a place people walk to.
28 an Gearran 3248 BDE Tobar dhìreach
The keepers number nine
The keepers of the slab are nine at a time, one drawn by lot for each of nine districts of the hills. They meet at the slab when a keeper dies, and not otherwise.
9 an Cèitean 3246 BDE
Ore in every hearth by the handful
Every household of the hills burns its handful of ore on one night in the dark of the year, the night later kept as Samhain, measured in a copy of the stone cup. The burning is done at once in every house, by agreement, so the colour shows on every hillside the same night.
10 an Giblean 3243 BDE Cnoc dhubh
A handful refused at Cnoc dhubh
The household of the Cnoc dhubh trench, the one that crushed two diggers, refuses its handful of ore for as long as anyone remembers. It is the first household on record to choose not to burn at all.
4 an Dàmhair 3240 BDE Dùn ìseal
Counting the households
Catrìona Mhòr's people count the households of the hills by knots on a cord, a knot to a hearth. The cord from Dùn ìseal is said to have had some nine hundred knots. It is the largest count made on Rodos in this age.
2 an t-Samhain 3237 BDE Calbh Cnoc ghorm
The saying on the column recut
The words on the column at Cnoc ghorm, worn shallow, are recut along their old grooves by a hand from the Stone Kings' hill. Some later readers say the recutting changed a letter; no one can prove which.
1 an Dùbhlachd 3234 BDE Seann Dunn
The last Seann-Dhaoine midden disturbed
Households at the eastern Seann Dunn cut into the old midden there for a house-floor and find the tally stones. They put them back in the order they found them and build elsewhere.
30 an Dùbhlachd 3231 BDE Eilean ìseal
Eilean ìseal given to the dead
The households of the south-east coast begin to row their dead to Eilean ìseal, in the old Seann-Dhaoine manner. Whether they learned it from the Seann Vell graves on Eilean dhearg, or from nothing, no telling says.
10 an t-Ògmhios 3228 BDE Eilean chrom
Gilleasbuig Beag's island
Eilean chrom, where Gilleasbuig Beag was sent, is left empty and is not fished. The tellings say his fire was seen on it for three nights and then not at all.
9 an t-Iuchar 3225 BDE Fèill Muileann òg
The keepers ask to be named
The nine keepers of the slab ask Catrìona Mhòr that their charge be declared before the whole ford gathering, so that no king after her can draw the lot at Dùn ìseal. She does not refuse and does not agree. The matter is carried forward.
7 an Lùnastal 3051 BDE
The eve of the Binding
At the close of this age the handful custom is everywhere in the hills, the keepers are nine, the sharing before the storms is kept on every coast, and the doctrine is said at every gathering. None of it is yet declared, and no god is yet named over the vein. The next age begins when it is.

Age II · An Aois Naomh the Holy Age

23 an t-Sultain 2998 BDE
The Binding of the First Flame
A formal custodianship is declared over the vein, and the first flame is bound at Dùn ìseal: Brìde's undying flame, kept over the stone of Crom Cruaich. Its keeping, Òrd Bhrìde, is the first Rodian institution recognizable as a religious-political order, centuries before anything like a king.
28 an t-Ògmhios 2995 BDE Dùn ìseal
Beathag Bhàn keeps the first flame
At Dùn ìseal, under the central mountains, the keepers of the slab and the households who swore the Binding choose Beathag Bhàn to hold the first flame for Brìde and answer to Crom for what is taken from the vein. The Keepers' recited roll begins with her name. Nothing is remembered of her before it.
27 an t-Iuchar 2989 BDE Dùn ìseal
The nine hearths
Nine households round the mountain's foot, one for each district of the old keepers of the slab, take the flame's tending in turn, each sending a son or a daughter to sit with it through a season. The later houses of custody all claimed descent from one or another of the nine; not all of the claims can be true.
19 an Dùbhlachd 2984 BDE Dùn ìseal
Talla na Lasrach raised
A long hall of dry stone and turf is raised over the flame at Dùn ìseal, with one door facing the vein and none facing the sea. It is rebuilt many times on the same footings, and the footings are all that anyone can now swear to.
17 am Faoilleach 2978 BDE
Seann Spioradan nan Ròdach established
The island's oldest continuous folk tradition takes shape at the hearths: reverence for ancestors, for the vein, for the weather that decides the mining season, and for the sìth of the hills and mounds. It keeps no priests.
22 an Dàmhair 2972 BDE Cnoc ghlas
The weather-cairns of Cnoc ghlas
Watchers build cairns on the ridge above Cnoc ghlas and read the cloud on the high passes from them, to tell the Hall when the galleries may be opened for the season. A wrong reading there costs the whole mountain its season, and the watchers are chosen with more care than the Keeper.
20 an t-Samhain 2966 BDE Marbh-bheò Doire uaine
The ban on fires in sight of Doire uaine
The Keepers forbid any fire, of wood or of ore, to be lit where the Doire uaine hills can see it, in obedience to the old inscriptions there. Herders who winter on those slopes eat cold for the season. The ban is never repealed, and nobody in the record admits to breaking it.
5 am Faoilleach 2965 BDE Làrach an Teampaill
Làrach an Teampaill left unentered
Beathag Bhàn walks to Làrach an Teampaill, finds its altar already turned toward the mountain, and declares the place not the Hall's to keep. The Keepers set no foot inside it for the rest of the age. Whose it was, they did not say, and it seems they did not know.
3 an Gearran 2955 BDE Dùn ìseal
Death of Beathag Bhàn
Beathag Bhàn dies at Dùn ìseal and is laid on the slope facing the vein, not the sea. The nine hearths choose Muireach Liath, her sister's son, to keep the flame after her.
15 an Gearran 2951 BDE Dùn ìseal
Ore by the basket
Muireach Liath fixes the first common measure for ore carried down from the galleries: a lidded basket of plaited heather, one to a household, filled once a season. Baskets of that weave are still made at Dùn ìseal for no purpose but the making.
17 am Faoilleach 2946 BDE Allt an Àigh
Allt an Àigh named
A stream said to grant fortune to anyone who drinks from it during a particular phase of the moon becomes a site of pilgrimage that has never fully stopped.
14 an Giblean 2942 BDE Caol shean
The pilgrims' path from Caol shean
A path is worn from the river landing at Caol shean up the valley to Allt an Àigh, walked by night so that pilgrims reach the water in the right quarter of the moon. Fishermen who walk it are said to lose fewer boats; the record keeps no count either way.
16 am Màrt 2940 BDE Allt an Àigh
The Hall declines the stream
Muireach Liath rules that Allt an Àigh belongs to the ancestors and the weather, not to the vein, and that the Hall will not keep it. The ruling is the first visible parting between the Keepers' rite and the older folk reverence, and both sides later cite it as proof they were right.
22 an Dàmhair 2933 BDE Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh
The sick carried to Muileann ruadh
The warm springs below Muileann ruadh are first used for the sick, who are carried up in litters and bathed at dawn. The Keepers allow it because the water's heat comes from the mountain without anyone breaking the stone.
23 an t-Sultain 2928 BDE Muileann chiar — baile mèinne airgid
Muileann chiar founded
A silver seam is found near, but distinct from, the great vein — the island's first confirmed resource that isn't obsidian.
20 an t-Samhain 2925 BDE Muileann chiar
Fearchar Airgeadach works the silver
Fearchar Airgeadach, a basket-carrier of the nine hearths, is the first on record to smelt the silver of Muileann chiar and hammer it into rings. His furnace is fed with wood and peat. It is the first fire in the island's record that answers to no one in the Hall.
19 an Dùbhlachd 2925 BDE Muileann chiar
Silver is not holy
Asked whether the new seam falls under the flame, Muireach Liath answers that silver does not bleed and so is not the mountain's. The ruling leaves Muileann chiar free to dig as deep as it likes, and it digs. Every later quarrel over the silver begins from this sentence.
28 an t-Ògmhios 2915 BDE Ros fhionn
Silver for salt at Ros fhionn
Carriers take Muileann chiar rings down to the river quays at Ros fhionn and trade them for salt fish and sealskin. It is the first trade in the record carried on in something other than food, and the first in which a price is remembered: one ring for a boatload.
30 an Cèitean 2910 BDE Dùn ìseal
Death of Muireach Liath
Muireach Liath dies at Dùn ìseal, keeping the flame. The nine hearths pass over three candidates of other lines and choose his daughter Gormshuil nic Mhuirich, and from her election the Keeper's office stays in the house of Muireach for many generations.
11 an t-Sultain 2903 BDE Dùn ìseal
Sliochd Mhuirich named
Gormshuil nic Mhuirich's kin at Dùn ìseal begin to be called Sliochd Mhuirich, the house of Muireach: the first custodian house in the record known by a name rather than by a hearth. The other eight hearths do not object in any account that survives.
10 an Dàmhair 2896 BDE
The first school of the druids founded
The first of the Scoiltean nan Draoidhean, the druid schools, forms around the question of why the vein answers some hands and not others — the first attempt within the Old Faith to reason about the obsidian rather than simply revere it.
8 an t-Samhain 2889 BDE Coille Naomh Muileann chiar
Sìleas nic Coinnich in the wood
Sìleas nic Coinnich, a cutter from Muileann chiar in the far east, begins teaching in Coille Naomh Muileann chiar. She had noticed at the galleries that the ore bleeds colour freely under some cutters' picks and sullenly under others, and she will not leave the question alone.
7 an Dùbhlachd 2881 BDE Muileann chiar
The stag in the grove
Sìleas nic Coinnich's hearers at Muileann chiar are named for a stag that is said to have stood in the grove through a whole lesson. They call themselves the stag's people. The school's later name, the stag's name Camaran, and the telling that it was the white stag of Flidais, lady of the deer, are first found in texts much younger than these events.
18 an Cèitean 2874 BDE Dùn ìseal
The Hall shuts the galleries to the stag's people
Gormshuil nic Mhuirich forbids Sìleas's hearers to cut in the galleries of Dùn ìseal, on the ground that a question asked of the vein is a demand made of it. The stag's people keep their school in the east and send no cutters to the mountain for a long time after.
16 an t-Ògmhios 2867 BDE Cnoc dhubh
The smoke at Cnoc dhubh
A hard winter drives a household at Cnoc dhubh to burn its ore by the basketful rather than by the handful. The smoke settles in the valley; three of the household and two neighbours die of it. The Keepers are sent for, and the case is argued at Dùn ìseal for the rest of the season.
15 an t-Iuchar 2860 BDE Dùn ìseal
Fionnlagh Dall and the stone cup
Fionnlagh Dall, Keeper after Gormshuil, has the old keepers' stone cup re-cut in grey stone to hold exactly what a cupped pair of hands will hold, and sets it on the threshold of Talla na Lasrach at Dùn ìseal as the measure. A blind man, he fills it by touch before the council, and nobody afterward can say he favoured anyone's hands.
13 an Lùnastal 2857 BDE
The Small-Burning Law
A custom hardens into formal rule: no household may burn more than a measured handful of the ore in a season. It becomes the sacred law of the Keepers of Brìde's flame and Crom's stone, and it holds for centuries.
1 an Cèitean 2854 BDE Seann Tarr
The first sentence under the Law
A household at Seann Tarr is found to have burned twice its measure in a season and loses its right to the ore for the season after. It is the first sentence under the Small-Burning Law in the record. The household's name is kept on the roll and its offence beside it, and its descendants petitioned for many centuries to have the offence struck out.
30 an Cèitean 2851 BDE Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg
No ore on the beacons
The Keepers rule that no ore may feed a beacon, since a beacon burns for strangers. The fire on the headland at Tobar dhearg is kept with driftwood and seal fat, and so are all the island's sea-lights after it.
4 am Màrt 2848 BDE Ceann chaol
The carriers' path to Ceann chaol
A carriers' path is cut from the mountain down to the harbour of Ceann chaol, with steps hewn at the steep places. Along it the Hall's baskets go to the southern households and the south's dried fish comes back up.
3 an Gearran 2845 BDE Abhainn dhomhain
The carriers drowned on the Abhainn dhomhain
Eleven carriers and their baskets are lost at a ford of the Abhainn dhomhain when the river rises in the night. The Hall mourns the ore as well as the carriers, and Fionnlagh Dall asks the council for a way across that the river cannot take.
5 am Faoilleach 2842 BDE Drochaid Cathair dhearg
The first bridges
Stone crossings begin linking the interior mining paths to the coast — ancestors of what will later be Drochaid Cathair dhearg and Drochaid Ros fhionn.
7 an Dùbhlachd 2839 BDE Drochaid Ros fhionn
Ailean Clachair's crossing at Ros fhionn
Ailean Clachair and forty masons of the nine hearths bridge the river above Ros fhionn with a single span of fitted stone, the ancestor of Drochaid Ros fhionn. Ailean sets a hearth-sign in the keystone. Every bridge the masons build after this carries one, and a bridge without one is not trusted.
8 an t-Samhain 2836 BDE Ros dhomhain
The masons' custom
The bridge-masons form a fellowship with its own oath, sworn on the stone cup at Dùn ìseal: no span to be closed in the dark, none to be paid for in ore. Its lodge is kept near the western crossing in the country of Ros dhomhain.
10 an Dàmhair 2833 BDE Am Buabhall Fortanach
The tavern roads begin
The first waypoint houses appear along the mining roads — ancestors of Am Buabhall Fortanach, An Taigh-òsta Grianach, and the rest of the circuit.
11 an t-Sultain 2830 BDE Am Buabhall Fortanach
Mòr nic Dhùghaill's house
The first keeper of the waypoint house that will become Am Buabhall Fortanach is Mòr nic Dhùghaill, a widow of Doire shean. She serves carriers jugged buffalo from her own herd, a dish the house has never stopped serving.
13 an Lùnastal 2827 BDE An Taigh-seinnse Mòr
The house at the middle of the road
A second waypoint house is built where the carriers' road from the mountain meets the road to the western harbours, on the site of An Taigh-seinnse Mòr. It is a turf longhouse with a hearth at each end, one for carriers going up and one for carriers coming down.
22 an Dàmhair 2824 BDE An Sligeanach Fad' às
The road-peace
The keepers of the waypoint houses agree that no feud may be pursued under an inn roof or within a spear's throw of its door. The custom is first recorded at the house on the site of An Sligeanach Fad' às. It is the oldest law on the island that no Keeper made.
23 an t-Sultain 2821 BDE Seann Mhorn
Seann Mhorn resettled
Fishers of the nine hearths settle the harbour at Seann Mhorn and keep the name they found there, which is not in their own tongue. They say the old name came with the stones. It is the first such name the record shows being taken over rather than replaced.
20 an Dàmhair 2818 BDE Seann Warr
Seann Warr resettled
On the western shore of Loch chrom, the harbour called Seann Warr is resettled in the same way, by families walking the new road from the mountain. They find house-footings there already and build on them, as the carriers' song has it, without asking whose.
23 an Lùnastal 2815 BDE Dùn ìseal
Death of Fionnlagh Dall
Fionnlagh Dall dies at Dùn ìseal. By his own asking he is not laid on the slope with the Keepers before him but carried south to the old graves near Cnoc dhìreach, which no living people had yet claimed.
18 an t-Samhain 2815 BDE Tuam Cnoc dhìreach
Fionnlagh Dall carried to the old graves
The bearers take eleven days over the road with Fionnlagh Dall's body and lay it among graves older than any name at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach. The Keepers who follow him cannot agree why he asked it, and the record gives two answers without choosing.
21 an t-Sultain 2810 BDE
The mausoleum consecrated
Tuam Cnoc dhìreach, already ancient, receives its first formally recorded burial — an unclaimed necropolis becoming a claimed one.
26 an t-Ògmhios 2805 BDE Cnoc dhìreach
The grave-keepers of Cnoc dhìreach
A few families settle at Cnoc dhìreach to tend Tuam Cnoc dhìreach after the Keeper's burial there. They are paid in ore by the Hall, one handful each a season, the only payment in ore the Law ever allowed.
25 an t-Iuchar 2618 BDE Dùn ìseal
Eilidh nic Ìomhair keeps the flame
For the first time the nine hearths choose a Keeper outside the house of Muireach: Eilidh nic Ìomhair, of Dùn dhearg. Sliochd Mhuirich accepts it at Dùn ìseal after a season of refusal, on condition that the stone cup never leaves Talla na Lasrach.
29 an Giblean 2614 BDE Dùn ìseal
The Four Houses sworn
Under Eilidh nic Ìomhair the Keepers' office is bound to four custodian houses: Sliochd Mhuirich of Dùn ìseal, Sliochd Ìomhair of Dùn dhearg, Sliochd Thormoid of Seann Dunn and Sliochd Raghnaill of Seann Tarr. The other hearths keep their seats on the council but not their claim to the flame. Most of the island's later nobility descends, or says it does, from one of the four.
28 an Cèitean 2610 BDE Seann Dunn
The house of Tormod at Seann Dunn
Sliochd Thormoid raises a hall and a shrine at Seann Dunn, facing the mountain across the river. The shrine keeps a lamp of ore burning at the Law's measure, and the other houses complain that Seann Dunn's measure is always fullest.
2 am Màrt 2606 BDE Seann Tarr
The house of Raghnall at Seann Tarr
Sliochd Raghnaill takes Seann Tarr on the north-eastern coast for its seat, the same town whose household was the first sentenced under the Law. The house keeps boats rather than galleries and grows rich on the fishing.
31 am Màrt 2602 BDE Eilean dhubh
Round Eilean dhubh
Boats of Sliochd Raghnaill sail round Eilean dhubh and come home, the first voyage in the record undertaken to see a coast rather than to fish it. The steersman is named in the house's songs as Tormod Ruadh. He brings back no report beyond rock, birds and the fact of having gone.
26 an t-Sultain 2598 BDE Spùinneadairean-mara
The outlaws of the north-west waters
Households stripped of their right under the Law for a third offence begin to take to boats and live off the north-western waters, raiding the fishing strands. They are called spùinneadairean, plunderers, and the name stays with those waters after them.
28 an Lùnastal 2594 BDE Uilebheist na Mara
The boat lost off the north-west
A fishing boat out of Baile chrom is lost in calm water off the north-western coast, and the two men who swam home say something rose under it. The boat's village keeps a wake for it each year thereafter. Nothing further is recorded of the thing they saw.
23 an t-Samhain 2590 BDE Taigh-solais Baile chrom
The fire at Baile chrom relit
The fishers of Baile chrom relight the old beacon on the point after the loss, fed with driftwood as the Law requires. It is the ancestor of Taigh-solais Baile chrom.
25 an Dàmhair 2586 BDE Seann Bhrenn
Seann Bhrenn resettled
On the northern coast the harbour of Seann Bhrenn is resettled by fishers from the mountain's north side, who keep its old name as the western settlers had kept Seann Warr's. They find a stone quay under the silt and use it.
20 am Faoilleach 2582 BDE Cathair naomh
The ancestor-cairn at Cathair naomh
The people of Cathair naomh in the north raise a cairn for their dead on the hill above the town and bring it a stone at every burial. It is the largest ancestor-cairn in the north, and it is still growing.
22 an Dùbhlachd 2578 BDE Imrich nam Pantar
The panthers let pass
The great cats' crossing of the mountains is found to run straight over the carriers' southern road. Eilidh nic Ìomhair rules that no panther may be killed on the road in its season, and the carriers wait in the waypoint houses until the crossing is done. The rule is kept because it costs the carriers only time.
19 am Màrt 2565 BDE Dùn dhearg
The granaries of Dùn dhearg
Sliochd Ìomhair builds stone granaries at Dùn dhearg and fills them from the lowland fields, holding grain against the storm season as the old unwritten custom of sharing asks. The granaries give the house the thing the Hall never had: people who owe it food.
18 an Gearran 2551 BDE Baile Mòr dhomhain
Baile Mòr dhomhain at the foot of the pass
Carriers who take the Hall's baskets north over the high pass settle at its southern foot, where Baile Mòr dhomhain now stands, to rest their beasts before the climb. The town lives by the pass and by little else.
16 an Cèitean 2538 BDE
The reverent centuries
Generation after generation mines the same modest quantity, burns the same modest quantity, and nothing about the population changes. This is the last age in which that remains true.
17 an Giblean 2524 BDE Seann Dunn
Coinneach Mòr mac Tormoid keeps the flame
The first Keeper of Sliochd Thormoid is Coinneach Mòr mac Tormoid of Seann Dunn. He is remembered for keeping the flame longer than any Keeper before him and changing nothing while he did.
5 an t-Sultain 2511 BDE Achadh chaol
The shepherds of Achadh chaol
Shepherds settle the upland fields at Achadh chaol in the north-east and send their wool down to the harbours. Their headman sits on the council at Dùn ìseal for a single season, is found to hold no hearth-right, and goes home.
4 an Dàmhair 2497 BDE Làrach an Dùin-fhaire
The Keepers' count of the old places
Coinneach Mòr sends walkers to list the ruins of the old people, and they return with Làrach an Dùin-fhaire, Làrach an Dùin, Làrach an Teampaill and the standing stones. The list says who does not own each place. It does not say who built them, and the Keepers ruled that it should not guess.
2 an t-Samhain 2484 BDE Carragh Cnoc bheag
The fence round Carragh Cnoc bheag
The people of Cnoc bheag set a ring of stakes round the old obelisk above their town so that cattle will not rub against it. The ring is renewed by every generation afterward; the stone is never moved.
1 an Dùbhlachd 2470 BDE Muileann ruadh
The bath-house at Muileann ruadh
A roofed bath-house is built over the warm springs below Muileann ruadh, with sleeping-places for the sick and their carriers. The Hall appoints a keeper of the springs, the first office it creates that has nothing to do with the ore. The keeper tends the springs in the name of Dian Cècht, the healer.
30 an Dùbhlachd 2457 BDE Muileann chiar
The silver weights of Muileann chiar
The silversmiths of Muileann chiar cast a set of weights, the smallest the weight of a barley-corn and the largest of a newborn lamb, and every trader on the carriers' roads comes to use them. For the rest of the age a thing weighed at Muileann chiar is said to be weighed fairly.
10 an Dùbhlachd 2443 BDE Dùn ìseal
The market under the Hall
A market is held under the walls of the Hall at Dùn ìseal on the four quarter days, Samhain, Là Fhèill Brìde, Bealltainn and Lùnastal, when the households of the eastern hills come up with their dues. Hides, venison, charcoal, honey and the silver of Muileann chiar change hands there, weighed on the new weights. The Keepers allow no ore to be sold on their ground, and none is.
28 am Faoilleach 2434 BDE Cnoc bhàn
The stag's people at Cnoc bhàn
A house of the stag's people is founded at Cnoc bhàn, north of the mountain, and takes cutters again after the long exclusion. Its teachers keep Sìleas nic Coinnich's question in the form she left it: why does the ore bleed for one hand and not another.
26 an Gearran 2425 BDE Dùn ìseal
Seonaid Chiar reopens the galleries to the stag's people
Seonaid Chiar, Keeper of the house of Muireach, lets cutters trained by the stag's people back into the galleries at Dùn ìseal, on oath to ask nothing of the vein aloud. The Hall's record calls it a reconciliation. The school's own memory calls it a truce.
27 am Màrt 2420 BDE Cathair mhòr
Cathair mhòr walled
The people of Cathair mhòr on the southern coast build a wall of fitted stone around their headland town, the first town wall in the record. Nobody in the record says what they feared.
16 am Faoilleach 2415 BDE Ceann leathan
Ceann leathan's fish-market
Ceann leathan becomes the market for the southern fishing, trading dried fish inland along the carriers' paths. Its harbour-master keeps tallies on notched sticks, and several sticks survive in the collection at Muileann chaol, the oldest counted objects there.
14 an Gearran 2410 BDE Inis thais
The shrine at Inis thais
A shrine is raised at Inis thais on the western coast to the ancestors lost at sea. Its keepers burn their season's handful of ore on the shore rather than indoors, so that the drowned, gone west over the sea, can see it.
29 an Giblean 2405 BDE Cuan shean
Cuan shean's salt-pans
The people of Cuan shean on the western coast dig salt-pans on the flats below the town and boil sea-water over peat. Their salt goes inland along the western road and preserves the fish of half the island.
31 am Màrt 2400 BDE Baile fhiadhaich
Baile fhiadhaich on the western heath
Baile fhiadhaich is founded on the western heath by salt-carriers from Cuan shean, on a stream that runs all summer. The heath round it is not worth ploughing, and its people keep goats.
2 am Màrt 2395 BDE An Taigh-òsta Grianach
The sunny house
A waypoint house is built on the eastern road where carriers from Cnoc leathan meet the southern coast path, on the site of An Taigh-òsta Grianach. It faces south and is known from the first for its warmth, which is the only thing its name has ever meant.
1 an Gearran 2390 BDE Cnoc leathan
Cnoc leathan's market
Cnoc leathan, at the eastern end of the road past the sunny house, becomes the market town of the south-eastern hills. Its carriers' guild holds the right to carry for the Hall on the stretch down to the coast.
23 an Lùnastal 2385 BDE Dùn ìseal
The fall in the high gallery
A roof falls in the highest gallery at Dùn ìseal and kills four cutters. The gallery is walled up and left. Seonaid Chiar orders props of oak in every gallery afterward, the first time the Hall spends timber on the mountain.
25 an t-Iuchar 2365 BDE Cathair dhomhain
Cathair dhomhain founded
Carriers who had settled at the mouth of the western road raise a town on the rise above the harbour and call it Cathair dhomhain. Its shrine keeps the Law's measure strictly and its people are proud of it.
26 an t-Ògmhios 2345 BDE Cathair dhearg
A fishing town at Cathair dhearg
The Red Hill's old settlement, shrunk to a small fishing town, grows again at the western bridge-foot on the Abhainn dhomhain, a little above its meeting with the Abhainn gheal below Loch chrom, on the ground later called Cathair dhearg. Its red stone gives it its name. At this time it is a place carriers pass through on their way to somewhere else.
28 an Cèitean 2325 BDE Dùn dhearg
Goraidh mac Ìomhair called rìgh
At Dùn dhearg the lowland households who eat from the granaries of Sliochd Ìomhair begin to call its head, Goraidh mac Ìomhair, their rìgh, their king. He is the first person in any record so called. Goraidh claims nothing over the vein and is careful to say so to the Hall.
9 an t-Sultain 2305 BDE Dùn ìseal
The division of keeping
The council at Dùn ìseal and Goraidh mac Ìomhair agree on a division: the Keeper keeps the flame and the galleries, and the rìgh keeps the roads, the granaries and the peace of the lowlands. The rìgh may not enter the galleries; the Keeper may not raise spears. The division is the frame of Rodian government for the rest of the age.
11 an Lùnastal 2285 BDE Dùn dhearg
Goraidh Mòr's hall
Goraidh mac Ìomhair, called Goraidh Mòr, builds a timber hall on the hill at Dùn dhearg with a granary at each corner. Its post-holes were still visible when the Library's surveyors walked the hill, and were measured and drawn then.
22 an t-Sultain 2280 BDE An Taigh-seinnse Mòr
The first road-toll
Goraidh Mòr sets a toll on the carriers' roads, one fish in twenty or its worth, to pay for the road-guards and the upkeep of the bridges. The keepers of the waypoint houses collect it. They also keep a share of it, and the record says so.
21 an Dàmhair 2245 BDE Dùn dhearg
Mòrag of the Roads
Goraidh Mòr's daughter Mòrag nic Ghoraidh takes the hall at Dùn dhearg after him. She is remembered as Mòrag nan Rathad, Mòrag of the Roads, for walking every carriers' road on the island in her first years and ordering the bad stretches remade.
26 an t-Iuchar 2218 BDE An Taigh-seinnse Òir
The golden house
Mòrag nan Rathad has a waypoint house built on the road north of Seann Dunn, on the site of An Taigh-seinnse Òir, to shorten the carriers' stage from the coast to the mountain. It is the first waypoint house raised by a ruler rather than a family.
24 an Lùnastal 2205 BDE Drochaid Cathair dhearg
The bridge-foot rebuilt
The western crossing of the Abhainn dhomhain is rebuilt in wider stone at Mòrag nan Rathad's order, so that two laden carriers can pass on it. The hearth-sign in its keystone is Ailean Clachair's, recut. From this rebuilding the town at the bridge-foot begins to grow.
16 am Faoilleach 2165 BDE Dùn dhearg
Dòmhnall Crùbach
Dòmhnall Crùbach, Dòmhnall the Lame, follows his mother Mòrag at Dùn dhearg. He cannot walk the roads as she did, and he governs through the keepers of the waypoint houses, who grow powerful in his reign.
14 an Gearran 2136 BDE Ceann mhin
The waypoint-keepers of Ceann mhin
The keepers of the waypoint houses round the harbour town of Ceann mhin take the collection of the road-toll into their own hands in Dòmhnall Crùbach's reign and pay the rìgh what they judge fair. Their judgment is generous to themselves, and the rolls record the sums.
19 an t-Samhain 2120 BDE Baile àrsaidh
Baile àrsaidh on the western heath
Settlers from Cathair dhomhain take the wet heath of the west coast and found Baile àrsaidh there, where the soil is thin and the yellow scorpions are thick. They swear their oaths on a scorpion's sting kept in a box, and neighbours find the custom strange.
18 an Dùbhlachd 2120 BDE Seann Chwen
The storm at Seann Chwen
A storm drives the sea over the harbour at Seann Chwen and takes the boats and a third of the houses. The Keeper sends the Hall's grain from Dùn ìseal, and Dòmhnall Crùbach sends his from Dùn dhearg. The survivors remember that the Hall's came first.
15 am Màrt 2085 BDE Muileann chiar
The stag-letters
At Muileann chiar in the far east, the teachers of the stag's people turn the cutters' tally-notches into signs for sounds, so that a teaching can be kept without a teacher. These are the first letters on Rodos in use by the Ròdaich: the ogham, which the druids call the gift of Ogma. Nearly every later hand on the island descends from them.
12 an Cèitean 2085 BDE Carragh Cnoc bheag
The letters set against the obelisk
Stag-scholars carry their new letters to Carragh Cnoc bheag and compare them with the marks on the obelisk. They match nothing. The scholars write down that the stone's writers were not their teachers, the first thing the Ròdaich ever put in writing about the old people.
10 an t-Ògmhios 2085 BDE Dùn dhearg
Sìleas Dhonn
Sìleas Dhonn, Dòmhnall Crùbach's niece, holds Dùn dhearg after him. In her reign the keepers of the waypoint houses are made to render account of the tolls at her hall once a year, and several of them do.
14 an Gearran 2008 BDE Caol leathan
The lords of Caol leathan
The harbour town of Caol leathan in the south-west grows rich on the western fishing and the southern end of the carriers' road. Its leading family, headed by Lachlann Ciar, begins to take the road-toll for itself and send none of it to Dùn dhearg.
12 an Cèitean 2005 BDE Dùn dhearg
Iain Garbh
Iain Garbh, Iain the Rough, son of Sìleas Dhonn, takes the hall at Dùn dhearg and demands the western tolls from Caol leathan. Lachlann Ciar sends back a basket of fish-bones.
13 an Giblean 2000 BDE Muileann òg
The War of the Roads begins at Muileann òg
Iain Garbh marches west with the road-guards and the lowland levies, and his men burn the toll-house at Muileann òg that Lachlann Ciar's people had taken. It is the first war in the record between Ròdaich and Ròdaich. The Hall refuses to bless either side.
19 an t-Samhain 1999 BDE Dùn ìseal
Uisdean mac Ruairidh's refusal
The Keeper Uisdean mac Ruairidh refuses Iain Garbh's messengers at Dùn ìseal the Hall's handful for the warband's hearths, saying the flame does not warm men who are going to kill. The warband winters on peat. Iain Garbh never forgives the Hall, and never enters it.
21 an Dàmhair 1998 BDE Àth fhiadhaich
The fight at Àth fhiadhaich
The men of Caol leathan meet Iain Garbh's levies at the ford of Àth fhiadhaich and hold it for a day before giving way. Forty are dead on both sides. The ford is called by the carriers for a long time afterward the ford of the forty.
16 am Faoilleach 1997 BDE Baile ghlas
Baile ghlas burned
Retreating toward Caol leathan, Lachlann Ciar's men burn Baile ghlas so that Iain Garbh's levies will find no grain. The town's people walk to Cathair dhomhain and many never return.
18 an Dùbhlachd 1996 BDE Baile chiar
Baile chiar holds
Baile chiar, south of the western bridge-foot, shuts its gate against both armies in the War of the Roads and feeds the burned-out people of Baile ghlas through the winter. Neither side forgives it, and neither side attacks it.
2 an t-Samhain 1994 BDE Caol leathan
The siege of Caol leathan
Iain Garbh closes Caol leathan from the land for a season, but its boats bring in fish from the sea and he cannot close the harbour. His levies begin to go home for the harvest. The siege ends without an assault.
4 an Dàmhair 1993 BDE Am Buabhall Fortanach
The peace at Mòr nic Dhùghaill's house
Iain Garbh and Lachlann Ciar meet under the roof of the waypoint house that will become Am Buabhall Fortanach, where by the road-peace neither may draw. Caol leathan keeps half its tolls and sends half to Dùn dhearg, and Lachlann Ciar swears to the Law before the Keeper's witness. The War of the Roads ends in a house built to feed carriers.
12 am Faoilleach 1990 BDE Caol leathan
The wolf-sworn of Caol leathan
Men who fought for Caol leathan become its road-guards and swear their watch on a white stone carved as a wolf, which they keep at the town gate. They call themselves the wolf-sworn. Later ages will read more into the stone than they did, and call it Lia Fàil.
14 an Dùbhlachd 1963 BDE Caol fhiadhaich
Caol fhiadhaich rebuilt
Caol fhiadhaich, on the south-western shore, which had sent its boats to feed Caol leathan through the siege, is given a share of the western tolls by Lachlann Ciar in thanks. The town builds a harbour wall with it.
15 an t-Samhain 1955 BDE Dùn dhearg
Death of Iain Garbh
Iain Garbh dies at Dùn dhearg. His daughter Catrìona has him buried in the hall's floor and not on the slope at Dùn ìseal, and the Hall does not ask for him.
17 an Dàmhair 1953 BDE Dùn dhearg
Catrìona Ghlic
Catrìona Ghlic, Catrìona the Wise, rules from Dùn dhearg and sends her own son to sit with the flame for a season, the first child of the royal house to do so since the division of keeping. The Hall and the hall are on speaking terms again by the end of her reign.
8 an Cèitean 1918 BDE An Leòmhann Buidhe
The house on the northern road
Catrìona Ghlic has a waypoint house built on the northern road above Inis mhòr, on the site of An Leòmhann Buidhe. It serves the carriers who take the Hall's baskets to the northern households and bring back wool.
9 an Giblean 1914 BDE An Taigh-seinnse Reòta
The house on the cold road
A stone house is built on the open moor on the road between Baile Mòr dhomhain and the northern coast, on the site of An Taigh-seinnse Reòta, for carriers caught by snow. Its keepers are paid by the Hall in grain and by the crown in cloth, and complain of both.
11 am Màrt 1910 BDE Inis mhòr
Inis mhòr grows
The river port at Inis mhòr in the north becomes the gathering place of the northern wool trade and outgrows every other northern town. Its people petition Catrìona Ghlic for a road-guard of their own, and are given one.
22 an t-Samhain 1877 BDE Baile Mòr dhomhain
The market at the fords of Baile Mòr dhomhain
The lords of the deep river set a market at Baile Mòr dhomhain, where the carriers' road from the south meets the paths down from the hill pastures. Cattle, sheep, horses, hides and the white stone of the hills are sold at the fords on the day after each new moon, and the lords take one fleece in forty from the sellers.
10 an Gearran 1833 BDE Muileann shean
Muileann shean on the northern road
A mill is built at Muileann shean, on the northern road, to grind the grain the carriers bring over the pass, and a town grows round it. The miller is paid by the Hall in grain, and pays the rìgh's toll in flour.
1 an t-Sultain 1788 BDE Dùn dhearg
The unrecorded rulers
Between Catrìona Ghlic and Ealasaid Chiar, the later king-list sets eleven names at Dùn dhearg, of which nothing is known but the names and the order. The Keepers' roll for the same years gives five Keepers, and their names also are all it gives.
3 an Lùnastal 1744 BDE Muileann chiar
Tormod Scrìobhaiche learns the letters
Tormod mac Iain, a younger son of the house of Tormod, is sent east to Muileann chiar to learn the stag-letters. He is the first of the royal kin to read, and is called Tormod Scrìobhaiche, Tormod the Writer, for the rest of his life.
22 an t-Iuchar 1700 BDE Dùn dhearg
Ealasaid Chiar
Ealasaid Chiar takes the hall at Dùn dhearg and brings Tormod Scrìobhaiche there as her clerk. She orders him to set down the names of every ruler of the hall that the reciters can give him, in order.
20 an Lùnastal 1700 BDE
The first written king-list
Rulers begin to be recorded by name rather than remembered by story — a shift the later succession records will inherit directly.
18 an t-Sultain 1699 BDE Dùn dhearg
The contents of Tormod's roll
Tormod Scrìobhaiche's roll, kept in the hall at Dùn dhearg, begins with Goraidh Mòr and runs to Ealasaid Chiar. Its earliest names come from the reciters and the later ones from living memory, and he marks which are which. The roll disagrees with the Keepers' recited roll in three places, and Tormod writes down both readings without choosing.
17 an Dàmhair 1679 BDE Dùn ìseal
The Keepers' roll written down
Shamed, in the Hall's own words, by the rìgh's clerk, the Keepers have their recited roll set down in stag-letters at Dùn ìseal. Its first name is Beathag Bhàn, and it is longer than Tormod's by several centuries.
15 an t-Samhain 1430 BDE Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag
The watchers of the dark wood
A small company settles on the edge of Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag, the wood nobody had ever cleared, and keeps watch there for a black horned beast they say walks in it. The people of Cathair dhearg call them the wood-watchers. None of the watchers' own accounts are older than Òrd Mhacha, the order of Macha that later claims them and takes the beast for a sign of Dubh Sainglenn, the black horse.
14 an Dùbhlachd 1423 BDE Coille Naomh Muileann chiar
The wood-watchers in the stag's grove
Wood-watchers come east and cut a black-barked tree in Coille Naomh Muileann chiar, saying the beast had shown it to them. The stag's people call it theft from a teaching-place. Both sides send to Dùn dhearg and to Dùn ìseal.
12 am Faoilleach 1418 BDE Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag
The stag's people claim the dark wood
In answer, the stag's people send teachers west to hold their lessons in Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag, saying the first stag had come from there. Each side now claims both woods, and in each wood the two companies meet and do not speak.
10 an Gearran 1410 BDE
The holy-wood dispute
The first recorded conflict between rival religious claims to Coille Naomh Muileann chiar and Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag — settled by dividing custody rather than choosing a winner.
11 am Màrt 1404 BDE Dùn dhearg
The boundary stones of the woods
The division of the woods is made at Dùn dhearg before Fearchar Òg, rìgh after Ealasaid Chiar, and the Keeper Calum Liath: the stag's people keep the eastern wood and the wood-watchers the western, and each may walk in the other's wood unarmed and without cutting. Boundary stones are set at both woods' edges with the terms cut on them in stag-letters. Two of the eastern stones survive.
9 an Giblean 1397 BDE Dùn ìseal
Calum Liath's surveyors
The Keeper Calum Liath sends cutters with knotted cords and lamps into every gallery at Dùn ìseal to follow the vein as far as it can be followed and mark how it thickens and thins. The work takes the cutters out of the ore-season for three seasons, and the households go short to pay for it.
27 an t-Samhain 1392 BDE
The measuring of the vein
The first attempt to estimate how much obsidian the mountain holds. The estimate will prove wildly optimistic.
26 an Dùbhlachd 1392 BDE Dùn ìseal
The reckoning of the cords
Calum Liath's reckoning, cut on a slab in the Hall at Dùn ìseal, holds that the mountain can give every household its handful for more generations than there are grains in the granaries of Dùn dhearg. It was read out at the council and received in silence, which the Hall took for assent.
22 an Gearran 1378 BDE Dùn ìseal
The deaths in the lower gallery
Two youths of the nine hearths, sent into the lower gallery at Dùn ìseal without a Keeper's cutter to guide them, break the wrong face and are crushed. They had been in the galleries less than a season. Their families ask the council what the Hall owes them, and the council has no answer.
24 am Faoilleach 1371 BDE
The apprentice-binding custom
Young Rodians are first formally bound to a master custodian of the vein for seven years before being trusted near the ore themselves — the origin of every later mining guild's structure.
21 an Giblean 1365 BDE Dùn ìseal
Oighrig Bhàn's first bound
Oighrig Bhàn, Keeper after Calum Liath, binds the first twelve apprentices under the new custom at Dùn ìseal, each to a master cutter by name. They swear on the stone cup to serve seven years before touching the vein. Four of the twelve are later Keepers, which is the custom's best argument for itself.
23 am Màrt 1358 BDE Cnoc bhàn
The stag's people take apprentices
The house of the stag's people at Cnoc bhàn adopts the seven years for its own cutters and adds a teaching to it: an apprentice keeps a written account of every strike, and the account is read. These strike-books are the school's chief record for the rest of the age.
18 an t-Ògmhios 1352 BDE Dùn dhearg
The long reign of Fearchar Òg
Fearchar Òg, who made the division of the woods, rules long at Dùn dhearg and is remembered for nothing so much as for dying old. The list gives him a byname, Òg, the young, from his accession as a boy, and it stuck.
20 an Cèitean 1345 BDE Muileann chiar
The silver tokens
Fearchar Òg's clerks begin paying the road-guards in small silver rings of Muileann chiar weight, stamped with the hall's mark. It is the first time a ruler on Rodos pays in metal. The rings travel further than the guards do.
8 an Cèitean 1338 BDE Àth ghlas
The toll-house at Àth ghlas
A toll-house is built on the ford at Àth ghlas, where the southern road crosses the river toward Ceann leathan, and the road-guards are paid there in the new silver rings. It is the first toll-house on the island with a keeper sent from the rìgh's hall rather than chosen locally.
9 an Giblean 1334 BDE Còmhrag Ceann leathan
The road-guards' games at Ceann leathan
The road-guards of the south begin meeting at Ceann leathan each year to fight with blunted staves for a silver ring. The meeting outlives its purpose; the field it used is the one where Còmhrag Ceann leathan is later fought. The first winner the record names is a woman, Mòrag Dhubh of Cnoc mhòr.
5 an t-Iuchar 1334 BDE Fèill Muileann òg
The fair at Muileann òg
Muileann òg, burned in the War of the Roads, is rebuilt as a market town, and a fair is held there each harvest at Lùnastal for the western and southern roads to trade. The fair is the ancestor of Fèill Muileann òg.
3 an Lùnastal 1334 BDE Cidhe Beag
The landing on the Abhainn uaine
A landing for river-boats is built on the Abhainn uaine at the place since called Cidhe Beag, so that grain from the lowlands can go upriver in boats rather than on carriers' backs. The carriers of the eastern road protest to Fearchar Òg and lose.
11 am Màrt 1314 BDE Abhainn uaine
The river-boats
Flat river-boats of hide over withy begin to carry grain and salt fish up the Abhainn uaine from the landing at Cidhe Beag. Boatmen become a fellowship of their own, with an oath sworn on a paddle, and they compete with the carriers for the Hall's baskets.
8 an Cèitean 1314 BDE Muileann chrom
The boatmen of Muileann chrom
Muileann chrom, up the valley from the landing at Cidhe Beag, becomes the home of the river-boatmen and their fellowship. Its boatyards build the flat hide boats for every river on the island.
6 an t-Ògmhios 1314 BDE Dùn dhearg
Beathag Mhòr
