Beathag Mhòr, great-granddaughter of Fearchar Òg, takes the hall at Dùn dhearg. She is the first ruler the list calls banrìgh, queen, rather than rìgh with a woman's name after it, and the change of word is the list's own.
12 am Faoilleach 1300 BDE Baile Mòr fhionn
The fleece-measure of Baile Mòr fhionn
The lords of the western plain hold a market at Baile Mòr fhionn and make the fleece of a grown ewe its measure. Grain, wine, cattle and the horses of the plain are all priced in fleeces. The silver rings of Muileann chiar are taken there too, but reckoned in wool.
10 an Gearran 1300 BDE Cathair dhearg
The hall moves to Cathair dhearg
Beathag Mhòr moves her hall from Dùn dhearg to the town at the western bridge-foot, Cathair dhearg, so as to sit where the roads, the river and the western harbours meet. Dùn dhearg keeps the old granaries and the house of Ìomhar's graves. Cathair dhearg is the seat of rule on Rodos from this reign onward, whatever else changes.
22 an Gearran 1300 BDE Dùn dhearg
Dùn dhearg after the move
Dùn dhearg, left behind, keeps its granaries and its pride. Its people go on calling it the rìgh's hill, and for many generations its reeves refuse to send their accounts to Cathair dhearg in any hand but their own.
23 am Màrt 1300 BDE Cathair dhearg
The red hall
Beathag Mhòr's hall at Cathair dhearg is built of the red stone that gives the town its name, on the rise above the harbour. Its foundations lie under the later citadel. The masons cut the hearth-sign into its lintel as if it were a bridge.
9 an Giblean 1300 BDE Cathair dhomhain
Cathair dhomhain against Cathair dhearg
The harbour of Cathair dhomhain, older and larger, resents the new seat on its doorstep and refuses the queen's toll on its boats. Beathag Mhòr grants it a charter of its own tolls, and the two towns, a few miles apart, are rivals for the rest of the age.
22 an t-Iuchar 1300 BDE Dùn ìseal
Disputed hands
The council at Dùn ìseal is asked to judge more disputes over which households hold a right to the handful than over anything else: new households, divided households, households that claim descent from one of the nine hearths without proof. Oighrig Bhàn's successor as Keeper, Dùghall mac Raghnaill, asks the queen for a counting.
11 am Faoilleach 1264 BDE Cathair dhearg
Beathag Mhòr orders the count
Beathag Mhòr and Dùghall mac Raghnaill agree that every household on the island claiming the handful shall be counted, its right proved or refused, and its name written. The clerks at Cathair dhearg are to write; the Keepers are to judge.
9 an Gearran 1264 BDE An Taigh-seinnse Mòr
The waypoint houses as counting-houses
The census-takers use the waypoint houses as their stations, since every household on the island is within a day of one. The keepers of the houses feed the counters at the queen's cost. The census is later remembered in the houses as a good year.
22 an t-Ògmhios 1264 BDE
The census of hands
The first attempt to count, island-wide, how many households hold a customary right to burn obsidian at all — proof the reverent tradition was already being formally rationed, not simply assumed.
21 an t-Iuchar 1264 BDE Cathair dhearg
The count of hands
The census rolls kept at Cathair dhearg give eleven thousand four hundred households holding the right, and some two thousand whose claims were refused. The refused households are written on a separate roll, and it is the separate roll that later generations went looking for when they wished to prove an ancestor's standing.
19 an Lùnastal 1264 BDE Seann Tarr
The refused of Seann Tarr
Most of the refused households on the north-eastern coast are fisher-families around Seann Tarr who had never burned ore at all and now found they had no right to begin. Sliochd Raghnaill takes up their cause at the council and loses it. The fisher-families burn peat and say it is warmer.
17 an t-Sultain 1264 BDE Taigh-solais Baile ìseal
The light at Baile ìseal
The old beacon on the eastern point at Baile ìseal is rebuilt, kept with driftwood and seal fat as the Law requires, to bring the fishing boats of the eastern coast home in the dark. It is the ancestor of Taigh-solais Baile ìseal.
16 an Dàmhair 1264 BDE Taigh-solais Muileann bheag
The light at Muileann bheag
The old beacon on the northern headland at Muileann bheag is rebuilt, the ancestor of Taigh-solais Muileann bheag. Its keepers are fisher-families of the north-west who pay no toll to Cathair dhearg in return for keeping it.
14 an t-Samhain 1264 BDE Taigh-solais Àth dhearg
The light at Àth dhearg
The old beacon on the north-eastern cape at Àth dhearg is rebuilt by Sliochd Raghnaill, to mark the passage in toward Seann Tarr. It is the ancestor of Taigh-solais Àth dhearg.
13 an Dùbhlachd 1264 BDE Dùn dhearg
Death of Beathag Mhòr
Beathag Mhòr dies at Cathair dhearg and, by her own order, is carried back to Dùn dhearg to be buried among the house of Ìomhar. The procession between the two is the longest royal journey in the record to this point.
24 an Cèitean 1263 BDE Cathair dhearg
Ruairidh Liath
Ruairidh Liath, Beathag Mhòr's son, rules from Cathair dhearg. He is already grey when he takes the hall, and his byname is the list's joke, the only one it makes.
19 an Lùnastal 1254 BDE Muileann chiar
The Silver Feud begins
Ruairidh Liath demands one ring in five of the silver taken at Muileann chiar, saying the tokens that pay his guards should cost him nothing. Sliochd Fhearchair, the silversmiths' house, answers that silver is not holy and so not the crown's either, citing Muireach Liath's ruling. They close the workings rather than pay.
17 an t-Sultain 1253 BDE Muileann chiar
The closing of the silver
For three seasons no silver leaves Muileann chiar. The road-guards go unpaid, the fair at Muileann òg trades in grain again, and the carriers' tolls go uncollected on the eastern road. The record calls it the Silver Feud, though no one is killed in it.
16 an Dàmhair 1250 BDE Dùn ìseal
The Keeper's judgment on the silver
Asked by both parties, the Keeper Dùghall mac Raghnaill rules at Dùn ìseal that Muireach Liath's words stand: silver is not the mountain's. But he rules too that the crown keeps the roads the silver travels on. Ruairidh Liath takes one ring in ten, Sliochd Fhearchair reopens the workings, and both call it a victory.
14 an t-Samhain 1249 BDE Muileann chiar
The Muileann chiar weight made law
As part of the settlement, the silver weights of Muileann chiar are declared the only lawful weights on the island's roads. Copies in bronze are sent to every waypoint house, and the house of Fearchar is paid for each.
25 an Giblean 1218 BDE Muileann dhearg
The bronze-casters of Muileann dhearg
The bronze copies of the Muileann chiar weights are cast at Muileann dhearg, where a family of casters learned the work from the silversmiths. They go on casting bells, pins and lamp-bowls, and their lamp-bowls hold exactly the Law's measure.
24 an Cèitean 1218 BDE Cathair dhearg
Seonag Chrom
Seonag Chrom, Ruairidh Liath's granddaughter, rules at Cathair dhearg. She has the clerks' office there given a room of its own in the red hall and a stipend in silver, and from her reign the king-list is kept year by year rather than reign by reign.
22 an t-Ògmhios 1145 BDE Inis bheag
Inis bheag's school of letters
At Inis bheag on the Abhainn bheag in the north a teacher of the stag's people begins teaching letters to fishers' children who will never cut ore. It is the first teaching of letters for their own sake. The Hall's roll records it with the remark that fish do not need reading.
21 an t-Iuchar 1073 BDE Cathair dhearg
Peigi nic Tormoid, clerk of the hall
Peigi nic Tormoid, a descendant of Tormod Scrìobhaiche, is the first clerk of the hall at Cathair dhearg whose own hand can be told apart from the others in the surviving copies. Her entries are short and she never gives a reason when a fact will do. Much of what is known of the middle of the age is in her hand or copied from it.
30 an Dùbhlachd 1000 BDE Seann Skell
The hawk-keepers of Seann Skell
At Seann Skell on the northern coast, fowler families keep a hawk in each household and feed it before the household eats. They burn their season's handful at dawn with the hawk on the wrist, saying that the flame is a hunger and should be fed the way a hunger is fed. They call the hawk Mòd, and say it is the Hawk of Acaill, the grey hawk of time, as old as Fionntan mac Bòchra, the oldest of men, who lived through the ages as a salmon, an eagle and a hawk; between them the two remember everything. Òrd an t-Seabhaig counts its beginning from them.
28 am Faoilleach 927 BDE Inis ìseal
The hawk-rite spreads up the Abhainn ìseal
The dawn burning with the hawk spreads from Seann Skell on the northern shore up the Abhainn ìseal to Inis ìseal and Cnoc bheag. The Keeper at Dùn ìseal writes that the rite keeps the measure exactly and is therefore no concern of the Hall's. It is the last time the Hall says so about any rite.
1 am Faoilleach 854 BDE Ros bheag
The sting-oath at Ros bheag
The custom of swearing on a scorpion's sting spreads from Baile àrsaidh up the western coast to Ros bheag, where the harbour court adopts it for every oath of trade. A merchant who will not swear on the sting is not trusted in the western harbours for the rest of the age.
3 an Dùbhlachd 782 BDE Inis thais
The wolf-stone at Inis thais
The wolf-sworn road-guards of Caol leathan set a second wolf-stone at the shrine of Inis thais, and the shrine's keepers begin to pray before it as well as to the drowned. The stone is white quartz and was carried from the mountain on a sledge, which cost more than the shrine.
28 an Gearran 709 BDE Cnoc bhàn
The strike-books compared
A teacher of the stag's people at Cnoc bhàn, Donnchadh mac Iain, reads through generations of apprentices' strike-books and finds that the ore bleeds brighter for cutters in their later years than in their first, whatever house they come from. He argues from it that the vein answers practice. The house's elders answer that the vein answers what a cutter was born with, and that practice only shows it.
30 am Faoilleach 699 BDE Muileann chaol
Donnchadh mac Iain leaves Cnoc bhàn
Donnchadh mac Iain and twenty-two of his hearers leave the house at Cnoc bhàn and settle at Muileann chaol, taking copies of the strike-books with them. The elders of Cnoc bhàn call it theft of the books. Donnchadh calls it a copying, which it was.
7 an t-Sultain 682 BDE
The founding of the rival druid school
A breakaway school of druids argues the vein answers effort, not birth — a quiet, centuries-early rehearsal of the argument the Long War will eventually be fought over in a very different form.
9 an Lùnastal 669 BDE Muileann chaol
The school at Muileann chaol
Donnchadh mac Iain's school at Muileann chaol keeps its own strike-books and adds a rule the elder school never had: a cutter's parentage is not written in the book at all. The two schools of the stag argue by letter for the rest of the age, and the letters are kept by both.
4 an t-Samhain 633 BDE Dùn ìseal
The Hall hears the two schools
The Keeper Raonaid Dhubh hears both schools of the stag at Dùn ìseal and gives no ruling, saying the vein has not asked the Hall to decide. The Hall's roll notes the hearing and the refusal. It was the most-cited refusal in the Hall's history.
6 an Dàmhair 623 BDE Calbh Cnoc ghorm
What the people of Cnoc ghorm say of their stone
Stag-scholars from Muileann chaol visit Calbh Cnoc ghorm and find they cannot read it. The people of Cnoc ghorm tell them that the stone says: we did not come; we were here. The scholars write that the people say so. Neither the stone nor the saying is explained in any later hand.
21 an Lùnastal 613 BDE Làrach an Dùin
The digging at Làrach an Dùin
Men of Baile ghorm dig under the fallen walls of Làrach an Dùin for the riches the ruin was said to hold. They find ash and nothing else. The Keeper has them sentenced as if they had broken the Law, though no law covered it, and the sentence stands as the rule for all the old places after.
23 an t-Iuchar 608 BDE Baile ghorm
Baile ghorm's penance
The families of the diggers at Baile ghorm pay their penance by keeping the road from their town to Tuam Cnoc dhìreach in repair. The road is still called the diggers' road in the southern hills.
16 am Faoilleach 593 BDE Cathair dhearg
Lachlann Bàn
Lachlann Bàn takes the red hall at Cathair dhearg. He is remembered for his granaries, which he builds in every province seat that will take one, and for a law about them.
14 an Gearran 588 BDE Cathair dhearg
The shared-meal law written
Lachlann Bàn and the Keeper Raonaid Dhubh set the old unwritten custom down as law at Cathair dhearg: any household with grain above its winter's need gives the surplus to the common granary of its district before the storm season, and the granary feeds any household of the district that runs short. Peigi nic Tormoid's successors wrote it into the rolls in full. It is the first law in the record made by rìgh and Keeper together.
19 an t-Samhain 574 BDE Cnoc mhòr
The granary of Cnoc mhòr
Cnoc mhòr builds its common granary under the new law before any other district, and sends word of it to Cathair dhearg. Lachlann Bàn sends back a silver ring for the reeve.
18 an Dùbhlachd 564 BDE Muileann chiar
The common granaries of the mountain
Common granaries are raised under the new law in the mountain districts round Muileann chiar, where the households live by cutting and carrying and grow little of their own. The lowland districts grumble at filling them.
12 an Cèitean 554 BDE Cathair mhòr
The granary at Cathair mhòr
A common granary is built inside the old wall at Cathair mhòr, the first put behind a town wall. The southern fishing towns send dried fish to it as their share, since they have no grain to send.
10 an t-Ògmhios 544 BDE Spùinneadairean-mara
Raiders in the eastern waters
Boats of outlaws begin raiding the eastern fishing strands from the islets offshore, taking dried fish and nets. Sliochd Raghnaill arms its boats at Seann Tarr and burns two of the raiders' boats. The rest are not caught.
15 am Màrt 538 BDE Cathair dhearg
Oighrig nic Lachlainn
Oighrig nic Lachlainn, Lachlann Bàn's daughter, takes the hall at Cathair dhearg. She has no children. The houses begin to count their claims before her reign is half done.
13 an Giblean 527 BDE Cnoc ghlas
The late snow on the high passes
The weather-watchers on the cairns above Cnoc ghlas report snow lying on the high passes long past the time the galleries should open. The Hall keeps the galleries shut for the cutters' safety. The mountain households wait.
5 an t-Sultain 527 BDE Muileann chiar
The poor season in the mountain
The galleries open late and close early, and the ore carried down is a third of a common season's. The mountain households of Muileann gheal, Doire uaine and Àth dhìreach, who trade their carrying for grain, have nothing to trade. By the end of the season they are eating their seed.
4 an Dàmhair 526 BDE
The first recorded famine averted
A poor mining season nearly starves three settlements before the shared-meal custom, formalized a generation earlier, holds and prevents it — the tradition's first real test.
15 an Dùbhlachd 526 BDE Muileann gheal
The granaries opened
Under the shared-meal law the common granaries of the mountain districts are opened at Muileann gheal, and when they run low the granaries of Dùn dhearg and the southern coast send grain up the carriers' roads without being asked twice. The carriers carry it for no fee. No one in the three settlements is recorded as having died of hunger that winter.
18 an Dàmhair 525 BDE Àth dhìreach
Àth dhìreach after the poor season
At Àth dhìreach, one of the three settlements the granaries fed, the carriers who brought the grain up are given the right to rest in any house of the town without payment for as long as they live. The last of them died old, and the right with him.
16 an t-Samhain 525 BDE Dùn dhearg
The reeves of Dùn dhearg send the grain
The reeves of Dùn dhearg, who had refused Cathair dhearg their accounts for generations, open the old granaries of the house of Ìomhar to the mountain without waiting for an order. Oighrig nic Lachlainn writes that she would have given the order had they waited. Peigi nic Tormoid's successor notes that they did not.
19 an t-Sultain 488 BDE Cathair dhearg
Death of Oighrig nic Lachlainn
Oighrig nic Lachlainn dies at Cathair dhearg without an heir of her body, and the line of Goraidh Mòr, as the list reckons it, ends with her. The red hall is shut and its clerks keep it.
10 an Giblean 486 BDE Dùn ìseal
The four houses meet
The Four Houses of custody meet at Dùn ìseal to choose a ruler, since no custom covers a hall without an heir. Sliochd Ìomhair claims it by blood, Sliochd Thormoid by the clerks, Sliochd Raghnaill by its boats. Sliochd Mhuirich, holding the Keeper's office, will not claim at all.
12 am Màrt 483 BDE Seann Dunn
The election of Gilleasbuig Mòr
The houses choose Gilleasbuig Mòr mac Tormoid of Seann Dunn, a grandson of the clerks' line, to hold the red hall. The Keeper sets the stone cup in his hands before the council, the first time a ruler is made at Dùn ìseal. Sliochd Ìomhair accepts on condition that its graves at Dùn dhearg remain the kings' burying-place.
11 an Gearran 482 BDE Cathair dhearg
Gilleasbuig Mòr at Cathair dhearg
Gilleasbuig Mòr takes the red hall. He keeps the clerks' office in his own house's hands and has the king-list recopied from the beginning, with a line drawn under Oighrig nic Lachlainn. The line is in every later copy.
13 am Faoilleach 462 BDE Seann Dunn
The shrine at Seann Dunn enlarged
Gilleasbuig Mòr enlarges his house's shrine at Seann Dunn into a temple with a court for pilgrims. Its ore-lamp is still said by the other houses to burn fuller than the measure, and a Keeper's cutter is sent to check it every season.
27 an Giblean 458 BDE Dùn dhearg
Death of Gilleasbuig Mòr
Gilleasbuig Mòr dies at Cathair dhearg and is buried among the house of Ìomhar at Dùn dhearg, as agreed. His son Tormod Òg succeeds him without a meeting of the houses, and nobody asks for one.
29 am Màrt 441 BDE Cathair dhearg
The gap in the list
Between Tormod Òg and Anna Ruadh the king-list kept at Cathair dhearg gives the names of nine rulers of the house of Tormod with their years and little else. Peigi nic Tormoid's successors were diligent and brief; in these reigns the rolls record mostly harvests, tolls and repairs to bridges.
24 an t-Ògmhios 428 BDE Drochaid Cathair dhearg
The bridge at Cathair dhearg widened
The bridge at Cathair dhearg is rebuilt a third time, wide enough now for a cart, since carts have come onto the lowland roads. The hearth-sign is recut again in the keystone. The span stands on the same piers as Mòrag nan Rathad's.
24 an Giblean 416 BDE Dùn dhearg
Riders on the lowland roads
The road-guards of Dùn dhearg begin to ride the lowland roads on the small horses of the southern grass country. A guard can now reach a waypoint house before a quarrel there has cooled. They are the first riders the record names, and for a long time the only ones.
23 an t-Iuchar 401 BDE Drochaid Ros fhionn
The crossing at Ros fhionn repaired
Ailean Clachair's span above Ros fhionn is repaired after a flood takes its eastern approach. The masons find their founder's hearth-sign still sharp in the keystone and leave it untouched.
21 an Lùnastal 386 BDE Dùn chrom
The bridge at Dùn chrom
The masons' fellowship bridges the river below Dùn chrom, joining the southern road to the western one without the long way round by Cathair dhearg. The toll is set at half the road-toll, and Cathair dhearg complains.
19 an t-Sultain 371 BDE Ceann àrsaidh
The bridge at Ceann àrsaidh
A bridge is built at the river town of Ceann àrsaidh, the fourth stone crossing in the lowlands. The masons' roll lists the names of the forty who built it, all of them of Sliochd Raghnaill's fisher-kin, who had learned the trade because the boats were idle.
18 an Dàmhair 356 BDE Doire mhin
The bridge at Doire mhin
The masons' fellowship builds a small bridge at Doire mhin to carry the southern road over a stream that floods each spring. The keystone carries the hearth-sign and, beside it, the first mason's mark in the record: the name of Beathag Clachair, who cut it.
16 an t-Samhain 341 BDE An Sligeanach Fad' às
The far-off house
The waypoint house on the site of An Sligeanach Fad' às, the oldest house under the road-peace, is rebuilt in stone. It has become so far from any town that carriers say one is never nearer to it than halfway, and the name comes from the saying.
15 an Dùbhlachd 327 BDE An Leòmhann Buidhe
Fire-water on the northern road
The house on the northern road on the site of An Leòmhann Buidhe begins serving a spirit distilled from barley that the carriers call fire-water. The Keepers rule it is not a burning and not their concern. The house's trade doubles.
13 am Faoilleach 312 BDE Caol mhòr
Caol mhòr in the north-west
Fisher-families of the north-west gather at Caol mhòr under a headman of their own and send tolls to Cathair dhearg only in the years the road-guard comes to collect them. The record for the north-west in this age is thin, and most of it is complaints about that.
4 an t-Samhain 297 BDE Ceann mhòr
Seal-oil from Ceann mhòr
Ceann mhòr on the north-west coast begins trading seal-oil down the western coast to Ros bheag for silver rings, and its beacons burn it. The seal-oil lamps of the western harbours are the brightest light on Rodos for many generations.
3 an Dùbhlachd 282 BDE Muileann leathan
The high pastures of Muileann leathan
Herding families take the high pastures above Muileann leathan in the north and keep sheep there for the wool of Inis mhòr. They hold no right to the handful, have never held one, and are not counted in the census of hands.
30 am Faoilleach 267 BDE Inis mhin
Inis mhin on the northern shore
Inis mhin, a fishing harbour on the northern shore, is recorded in the rolls for the first time, when its headman comes to Inis mhòr's wool-fair to complain about the road-guard's toll. The complaint is written down in full, and is the town's whole record for the age.
28 an Gearran 252 BDE Spùinneadairean-mara
The raid on the western strands
Raiders from the north-western waters take a season's dried fish from the strands of the north-western coast. The sting-sworn merchants of Ros bheag pay for two armed boats to watch the strands, and the raiders move north.
29 am Màrt 238 BDE Uilebheist na Mara
The second sighting
Two boats from Baile chrom report something vast moving under them in the north-western water, the second sighting in the record. One boat does not come home. The wake kept in Baile chrom for the first loss is kept for both.
27 an Giblean 223 BDE Seann Tarr
Round the islands
Boats of Sliochd Raghnaill sail from Seann Tarr and make the round of the offshore islands, Eilean ruadh, Eilean dhearg and Eilean fhada among them, and come home in one season. No crew of the age goes further from the coast than the islands, and none is recorded as wanting to.
26 an Cèitean 208 BDE Eilean ruadh
Summer herders on Eilean ruadh
Families from the coast begin taking sheep over to Eilean ruadh for the summer grazing and bringing them back before the storms. They build turf shelters there, which later herders reuse.
24 an t-Ògmhios 193 BDE Cathair dhearg
Anna Ruadh
Anna Ruadh of the house of Tormod takes the red hall at Cathair dhearg. She is the first ruler since Mòrag nan Rathad to walk the whole road circuit, and she does it twice.
23 an t-Iuchar 190 BDE Am Buabhall Fortanach
Anna Ruadh at Am Buabhall Fortanach
On her first circuit Anna Ruadh stops at the house on the site of Am Buabhall Fortanach where the War of the Roads was ended, and eats the jugged buffalo like a carrier. The house's keepers still tell it.
21 an Lùnastal 186 BDE An Taigh-òsta Grianach
Anna Ruadh at the sunny house
On the eastern road Anna Ruadh stays at the house on the site of An Taigh-òsta Grianach, and grants its keepers the right to a toll of their own for the upkeep of the road to Cnoc leathan, Slighe Cnoc leathan. It is the only waypoint house on the island with a royal charter.
12 an t-Ògmhios 183 BDE Ceann mhin
Anna Ruadh at Ceann mhin
At Ceann mhin on the south-eastern coast Anna Ruadh hears the fishers' dispute with the carriers over who may carry dried fish up to the mountain, and rules that both may. The ruling doubles the fish going inland and halves its price at Dùn ìseal.
11 an t-Iuchar 180 BDE Ceann leathan
The contest at Ceann leathan in stone
Anna Ruadh gives the road-guards' contest at Ceann leathan a stone-walled field and a silver ring from the red hall as its prize. The contest draws fighters from across the south, and the losers are fed at the crown's cost.
23 an t-Iuchar 177 BDE Cathair dhearg
A wood-watcher in the red hall
Anna Ruadh keeps a wood-watcher from Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag in her household at Cathair dhearg to read the omens of the hall. It is the first sign in the capital of the wood-watchers' rite, the rite of Macha, goddess of sovereignty and of horses. The Keeper sends a protest from Dùn ìseal and receives no answer that the rolls record.
24 an t-Ògmhios 173 BDE Cathair dhomhain
Cathair dhomhain and the wood-watchers
The shrine at Cathair dhomhain, proud of keeping the Law strictly, refuses to take a wood-watcher, and its people say the capital has given its omens to people who sit in trees. The rivalry of the two towns takes a religious turn it never loses.
26 an Cèitean 170 BDE Cathair dhearg
Death of Anna Ruadh
Anna Ruadh dies at Cathair dhearg and is buried at Dùn dhearg with the house of Ìomhar and her own house's kings. Her son Coinneach Bàn takes the hall.
27 an Giblean 167 BDE Cathair dhearg
Coinneach Bàn
Coinneach Bàn rules long and quietly from Cathair dhearg. In his reign the clerks of the hall begin copying the rolls for the provinces, so that each province seat has its own copy of the laws, and several of those copies survive where the originals do not.
16 an t-Samhain 164 BDE Dùn ìseal
Seumas Bàn keeps the flame
Seumas Bàn of Sliochd Mhuirich is chosen Keeper. He finds, on reading the Hall's roll at Dùn ìseal, that more than half the Keepers of the age have been of his own house, and has the fact struck from the preface. The unstruck copy survived.
18 an Dàmhair 161 BDE Dùn ìseal
The rites counted at Dùn ìseal
Seumas Bàn has the Hall's clerks list every rite on the island that burns the handful and every one that claims the vein, so the council can know what it is keeping. The list holds the Hall's own rite, the ancestor-keeping of the old folk, the dawn-hawk of the north coast, the wood-watchers of the west, the wolf-sworn, the sting-oath, and both schools of the stag. The clerks note that the list would not have been needed a thousand years before.
19 an t-Sultain 159 BDE Seann Skell
The hawk-keepers refuse the Hall's cutter
The hawk-keepers of Seann Skell refuse the Hall's cutter who comes to check their measure, saying their measure is the hawk's and the hawk is not the Keeper's. The cutter goes home with the refusal in writing. It is the first rite to refuse the Hall's measure-check outright.
21 an Lùnastal 156 BDE Caol leathan
The wolf-sworn build a hall
The wolf-sworn of Caol leathan build a hall of their own around the white wolf-stone at the town gate and take oaths there that are no longer road-guards' oaths. They say the stone watches the whole island as the guard watches the road, and will cry out under the rightful king. From this hall comes Òrd na Cloiche, the order of the Stone, and the wolf-sworn begin to be called the Fianna.
3 an Dùbhlachd 153 BDE Seann Skell
The sting-oath at Seann Skell
At Seann Skell in the west the harbour court's sting-oath becomes a creed: its keepers say that one power stings the liar wherever he is, Manannan mac Lir, lord of the sea, and that the scorpion is only his sign. The Hall's roll records it as a new teaching. It is the first on the island to call itself the only true one. The oath is sworn from now on over a cup marked with the scorpion, called Manannan's Cup of Truth, which is said to break in three at three lies spoken over it and to be made whole by three truths. Òrd Mhanannain dates itself from this court.
4 an t-Samhain 150 BDE Seann Vell
Seann Vell swears on the sting
Seann Vell, on the western coast below Cuan shean, takes up the sting-oath of its neighbours. Its shrine keeps a scorpion carved in yellow stone, the first image of the creature made for worship rather than for swearing on.
13 am Faoilleach 147 BDE Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag
The dark wood keeps its own rite
The wood-watchers of Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag stop sending to the Hall for judgment of their disputes and judge them under the trees. They hold that the black beast has two natures, one that keeps and one that devours, and that the vein has the same. The order of Macha later tells the saying of the two horses that drew one chariot, the black Dubh Sainglenn and the grey Liath Macha: two horses, one yoke.
11 an Gearran 144 BDE
The common root of the orders
A single unified folk practice begins visibly splitting into the distinct threads later ages will separately name, the orders of An Creideamh Sean, the Old Faith, and the hearth-keeping of Na Seann Spioradan, the Old Spirits — the moment 'Rodian belief' stops being one thing.
16 an t-Samhain 141 BDE Dùn ìseal
The council divided by rite
The council at Dùn ìseal, which had sat by hearth and by house, begins to sit in companies by rite. Seumas Bàn complains that he now keeps the flame for eight peoples who each think they are its only keepers. The seating is kept for the rest of the age.
15 an Dùbhlachd 139 BDE Allt an Àigh
Allt an Àigh keeps its pilgrims
Whatever their rite, pilgrims go on walking to Allt an Àigh in the right quarter of the moon, the one custom on the island that the Hall's list sets under no company. The path from Caol shean is repaved by pilgrims of four different rites in the same season.
19 an t-Sultain 136 BDE Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh
The springs at Muileann ruadh common to all
The keeper of the springs at Muileann ruadh rules that the sick of every rite shall be bathed without asking which. Her ruling is copied into the provincial rolls. It is the last ruling of the age on which every company of the council agrees.
18 an Dàmhair 133 BDE Cnoc dhìreach
Cnoc dhìreach's weavers
The town of Cnoc dhìreach in the east, the one on the carriers' road south of the springs and not the grave-keepers' village by the old tombs, becomes known for a heavy undyed cloth the carriers wear on the high passes. The two Cnoc dhìreachs are told apart in the rolls by that cloth.
23 an t-Iuchar 130 BDE Muileann bhàn
The dyers of Muileann bhàn
The dyers of Muileann bhàn in the eastern hills learn to fix a pale blue from a hill plant, and the carriers' cloth of the whole mountain country begins to be dyed there. The Keepers wear it undyed, and say so.
21 an Lùnastal 127 BDE Muileann dhomhain
Muileann dhomhain's mill
A water-mill is built at Muileann dhomhain in the eastern hills to grind the grain of the mountain districts' common granaries. The miller keeps one measure in sixteen, which the rolls record as fair.
26 an Cèitean 124 BDE Àth chiar
The flood at Àth chiar
Rain on the eastern hills brings the river over the ford at Àth chiar and carries off the carriers' shelter and six of the townsfolk. The common granary of the district, built on a rise, is untouched and feeds the town through the winter.
24 an t-Ògmhios 121 BDE Seann Bhral
The oyster-beds of Seann Bhral
The people of Seann Bhral on the south-eastern coast begin laying oyster-beds in the shallows, a practice they say came with the name of their town. The Library's copy of the provincial roll records the claim and marks it doubtful.
20 an Gearran 119 BDE Seann Vell
Seann Vell's harbour
Seann Vell on the south-eastern coast grows into a city on the trade of the southern fishing and the Muileann chiar silver brought down the eastern road. Its harbour is the first on the island with a stone quay.
22 am Faoilleach 116 BDE Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg
The light at Tobar dhearg rebuilt
The old beacon at Tobar dhearg on the southern cape is rebuilt as a stone tower with the fire on its top, the first sea-light raised above the ground. It burns seal-oil from the north-west carried the whole length of the island.
19 an Giblean 113 BDE Muileann naomh
Muileann naomh's mill-shrine
At Muileann naomh on the southern coast a mill and a shrine share one roof, the miller keeping the shrine's handful beside his millstones. The Keeper's cutter who inspects it finds the measure kept and the flour good.
21 am Màrt 110 BDE Dùn thais
Dùn thais walled
Dùn thais in the eastern hills is walled and a temple of the stag's people is raised in it, the first built in stone rather than kept in a grove. The elder school at Cnoc bhàn sends it teachers.
16 an t-Ògmhios 107 BDE Inis mhòr
The wool-fair of Inis mhòr
Inis mhòr holds a wool-fair each shearing that draws buyers from the whole northern coast and some from Cathair dhearg. Its silver is weighed on the Muileann chiar weights sent to the northern road.
18 an Cèitean 104 BDE Baile Mòr mhòr
Baile Mòr mhòr on the northern coast
Baile Mòr mhòr, on the northern coast west of Seann Toll, grows large enough on the fishing to send its own member to the council at Dùn ìseal. The Four Houses do not like it, and seat its member at the foot of the hall.
13 an Lùnastal 101 BDE Seann Toll
The northern boats at Seann Toll
The harbour at Seann Toll becomes the home of the northern fishing fleet. Its boatbuilders make the longest craft on the island, meant for a day's run along the coast and never for open water.
15 an t-Iuchar 99 BDE Achadh shean
Drought at Achadh shean
A dry summer burns the pastures round Achadh shean in the east, and the district's common granary is emptied by spring. Grain is sent from Baile chaol and Cuan ruadh under the shared-meal law, and the district repays it over the following harvests.
10 an Dàmhair 96 BDE Baile chaol
Baile chaol's repayment
The rolls at Baile chaol record Achadh shean's repayment of the drought grain, measure by measure, down to the last. The clerk adds that it is the first such debt in the rolls repaid in full.
11 an t-Sultain 93 BDE Imrich nam Pantar
The panthers late
The great cats' crossing of the southern road comes late and fewer than the carriers remember. The weather-watchers call it a sign of a hard winter and are right. The Keepers note it without comment.
13 an Lùnastal 90 BDE Baile ruadh
The watch-tower at Baile ruadh
A timber watch-tower is raised at Baile ruadh on the north-eastern coast to look out for raiders from the islands. It is manned by Sliochd Raghnaill's fisher-kin by turns, and it is the only tower of war the age built.
11 an t-Sultain 87 BDE Cuan ruadh
Cuan ruadh's boats
The fishers of Cuan ruadh on the eastern coast give boats and men to the watch against the island raiders. In return Sliochd Raghnaill gives the town a place on the council at Dùn ìseal beside its own seat.
10 an Dàmhair 84 BDE Inis chrom
The drowned-feast at Inis chrom
At Inis chrom on the western coast the families of the drowned hold a feast on the shore each year and set an empty place for each of the lost. The custom spreads to the harbours north as far as Seann Warr.
8 an t-Samhain 81 BDE Baile ghorm
The potters of Baile ghorm
Potters at Baile ghorm on the south-western coast begin firing a hard red ware from the local clay, and their jars carry the oil and grain of the western road. Sherds of it are found on every waypoint-house site the Library's surveyors have walked.
19 an Giblean 79 BDE Cnoc àrsaidh
Cnoc àrsaidh's kilns
Potters of Baile ghorm set up new kilns at Cnoc àrsaidh in the south-west, where the clay is better and the wood nearer. The red ware of the western road is made there for the rest of the age.
18 an Cèitean 76 BDE Cathair fhada
Cathair fhada founded
Cathair fhada is raised on the southern coast by families moving out of the crowded harbours round Cathair dhearg. Its founders bring a wood-watcher with them, and a copy of the laws.
16 an t-Ògmhios 73 BDE Cnoc naomh
Cnoc naomh's ancestor-shrine
The people of Cnoc naomh keep a shrine to the ancestors and to the sìth of the hill in the old folk way, with no hawk, wolf, sting or stag in it. The Hall's list of rites names them among the keepers of the old reverence, which by now is a company of its own.
15 an t-Iuchar 70 BDE Cathair dhearg
Mòr nic Coinnich crowned
Mòr nic Coinnich, granddaughter of Coinneach Bàn, takes the red hall at Cathair dhearg. The Keeper Catrìona nic Mhuirich sets the stone cup in her hands at Dùn ìseal as the houses had done for Gilleasbuig Mòr. Her name is the last written in the king-list of the Holy Age.
2 an Giblean 60 BDE Dùn ìseal
The Hall's roll at the close of the age
At the close of the age the Keepers' roll holds the names of one hundred and forty Keepers from Beathag Bhàn to Catrìona nic Mhuirich, and the king-list the names of more than ninety rulers from Goraidh Mòr to Mòr nic Coinnich. The Small-Burning Law has not been changed in a word since Fionnlagh Dall's stone cup. The cup is still on the threshold of Talla na Lasrach at Dùn ìseal.
1 an Cèitean 50 BDE
The last age of even population
Chroniclers later look back and note, with some unease, that this is the final stretch of Rodian history in which no single family held meaningfully more years of life than any other.

Age III · An Aois Scaraidh the Age of Sundering

6 am Faoilleach 39 BDE
Land is found
Word returns of a land across open water, unpeopled by anyone resembling the Ròdaich. No record survives of who found it first.
9 an t-Samhain 39 BDE Cathair dhearg
The report heard at Cathair dhearg
The report of the far land is repeated at Cathair dhearg in the hall of Queen Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill, daughter of Mòr nic Coinnich, by three separate crews from the western harbours, none of whom claims to have been first. The queen's scribe takes down all three accounts and notes that they agree on the coast and on nothing else.
8 an Dùbhlachd 39 BDE
The Choosing
A vote — or something the later chronicles call a vote — decides who will go. Volunteers only. No lots are drawn, no conscription recorded.
12 an t-Sultain 38 BDE Seann Skell
The roll of the willing
At Seann Skell the harbour scribes open a roll for those who mean to go, entered by household rather than by name. The roll is kept on boards in the harbour-house, and a later hand notes that entries were struck out as often as they were added.
11 an Dàmhair 38 BDE Cathair dhearg
The queen neither commands nor forbids
Queen Beathag declares that the crown will neither send anyone across the water nor keep anyone back. Her younger sister, Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill, enters her own household on the roll at Seann Skell within the season.
14 an Lùnastal 37 BDE Muileann dhearg
The custodians count the cost
The vein-house above Muileann dhearg, keeper of Crom's stone and heir to the Keepers' Hall at Dùn ìseal where Brìde's flame was first bound, reckons which of the households holding the customary right to burn the ore have entered the roll. The custody-book puts it at nearly one household in five, and adds that the reckoning was made twice because the first figure was not believed.
16 an t-Iuchar 35 BDE
The ships are built
The island's shipwrights, used to modest coastal craft, build vessels meant to survive open water for the first time in Rodian memory.
14 an Lùnastal 35 BDE Seann Skell
Alasdair Saor lays the first keel
On the river strand below Seann Skell, the shipwright Alasdair mac Iain, called Alasdair Saor, lays down the first deep-keeled hull ever built on Rodos. The island's craft until then were sewn-plank coasters that never slept out of sight of land.
26 an Lùnastal 35 BDE Doire fhionn
The oaks of Doire fhionn
The oak grove that gave Doire fhionn its name is felled for the fleet's keels and carried down to the coast by ox-sled. The grove never regrew, and the village kept a name it no longer had a reason for.
24 an t-Sultain 35 BDE Seann Skell
The shipwrights' fellowship bound
Alasdair Saor takes the wrights of the Seann Skell strand into a single fellowship, binding each apprentice for seven years in the manner of the vein custodians. The custody-book calls it Comann nan Saor-luinge, the fellowship of the ship-wrights.
12 an t-Sultain 34 BDE Inis àrsaidh
The trial hull lost off Inis àrsaidh's harbour
The first finished hull is taken down the Abhainn naomh and sailed out past Ros àrsaidh, where the ships of Inis àrsaidh put to sea, to be tried in open water, and founders in a following sea. Eleven are drowned. Alasdair Saor changes the setting of the keel, and every later hull of the fleet is built to the changed pattern.
11 an Dàmhair 32 BDE Cuan shean
The rope-walks of Cuan shean
Cuan shean lays out long rope-walks along its harbour front and turns its hemp fields over entirely to cordage for the fleet. The town's rope trade outlasts the Sundering by some centuries.
9 an t-Samhain 31 BDE Baile àrsaidh
The sail-cloth levy
Every weaving household in Siorrachd Baile àrsaidh is asked for a set length of close-woven cloth for sails, reckoned on tally-sticks at the shire seat. The tallies survive; how many households paid does not.
20 an Giblean 27 BDE Cuan ruadh
The star-lore taught at Cuan ruadh
Old steersmen of Cuan ruadh on the eastern coast, the only sailors on the island who had ever kept a course by night, teach the fleet's pilots to hold a heading by the stars. Their lore was written down only in part, and that part has not survived.
19 an Cèitean 22 BDE Seann Skell
The volunteers name their leaders
The households on the roll meet at Seann Skell and choose their own leaders: Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill, the queen's sister, and Fearchar mac Ruairidh, a custodian of the vein. The custody-book records the choice and nothing of how it was made.
17 an t-Ògmhios 15 BDE Muileann dhearg
The handful for the new hearth
The vein-house rules on whether departing custodians may carry the ore. Each ship may take one sealed measure, no more than a single household may burn in a season under the Small-Burning Law. The ruling is the only text in the custody-book addressed to people who were leaving.
16 an t-Iuchar 10 BDE Seann Skell
The west quay lengthened
The west quay at Seann Skell is lengthened with dressed stone so that the deep hulls can lie alongside it at low water. Masons are brought from the capital to do the work, and the new stones are the ones the later rite would be held on.
20 an Gearran 2 BDE
The provisioning debate
A dispute over how much of the island's stored grain the departing ships may take nearly cancels the whole expedition. It is resolved, unrecorded how, within a season.
21 am Màrt 2 BDE Àth shean
Àth shean shuts its granaries
During the dispute over the fleet's grain, the reeve of the granaries at Àth shean, Tormod mac Coinnich, bars the store-houses and sets a watch on them. The watch is kept until the matter is settled, and Tormod is not recorded as holding office afterward.
3 an Giblean 2 BDE Abhainn dhomhain
Grain down Abhainn dhomhain
Once the dispute is settled, grain barges are sent down Abhainn dhomhain to the capital and on by coast to Ros àrsaidh and up the Abhainn naomh to Seann Skell. A tally-keeper at Drochaid Cathair dhearg counts the barges passing and makes the count forty-one.
2 an Cèitean 2 BDE Seann Skell
The fleet assembled
The fleet lies at Seann Skell complete. The custody-book gives it as nineteen hulls; a later hand in the margin corrects this to twenty-one, and no one since has been able to settle which is right.
18 an Giblean 1 DE Seann Skell
The night of lamps
On the last night before the sailing, every house along the Seann Skell waterfront sets a lamp on its sill and keeps it burning until morning. It is the first custom of the Sundering recorded as a custom, and the town kept it long after the reason was a story.
19 an Giblean 1 DE
The Setting-Out
The volunteers depart west. The island's chronicles simply stop describing them the moment the ships clear the harbor; the Ròdaich tell that the fleet sailed into Manannan's mist, toward the Otherworld.
19 an Giblean 1 DE Seann Skell
The sunwise turn
Before going down the Abhainn naomh to open water the fleet goes once round the river pool of Seann Skell sunwise, diosal, for luck, and the watchers on the quay count the hulls as they pass. The harbour scribe's account of them ends at the foot of the pool.
22 am Faoilleach 5 DE Muileann dhearg
The years counted from the turn
Donnchadh mac Thormoid, scribe of the vein-house, begins to number the years from the sunwise turn at Seann Skell, and calls them the years of the Diosal. The count is his; the crown's scribes adopt it only a generation later.
27 an Dàmhair 5 DE Seann Skell
A report reaches Seann Skell
A report of the fleet reaches Seann Skell. The custody-book does not say how or by whom it came, only that the harbour scribe copied it in a hand that shook. The copy came down to later keepers stained by water and missing its end.
24 an Dùbhlachd 5 DE
Two landfalls
What fragmentary report ever returns describes two separate coasts reached, not one — the seed, in this telling, of two later peoples rather than one.
1 an Lùnastal 7 DE Cathair dhearg
Mòrag's line struck
Queen Beathag removes her sister Mòrag and Mòrag's children from the order of succession, as persons no longer on Rodos. The act is entered without comment between a grain ruling and the repair of a bridge.
3 an t-Iuchar 14 DE
The thinning
Cut off from the vein, whatever strength the crossing required fades across the departed's own children. By the third generation abroad, nothing remains that Rodos would recognize.
28 an t-Sultain 14 DE Muileann dhearg
The custodians' second reckoning
The vein-house counts again the households that hold the right to the ore. The loss is set down as one hand in five, and beside it Donnchadh mac Thormoid writes that the vein itself answers no differently for those who stayed.
1 an Lùnastal 15 DE
The Mourning Custom
Rodos formalizes a mourning rite for the departed that is not quite grief and not quite celebration — reused, uneasily, for a very different departure in a much later age.
27 an Dàmhair 15 DE Cathair dhearg
The white sorrow first kept at court
Queen Beathag keeps the new mourning for her sister in undyed wool, with one place set empty at a meal that is neither feast nor fast. The court calls it an Tùrsa Geal, the white sorrow, and by the next generation it is kept in every harbour town on the island.
7 am Faoilleach 16 DE
Population correction
With a portion of the obsidian-bonded population gone, Rodian society reorganizes around a smaller, more concentrated custodian class — the shape every later aristocracy inherits.
4 an t-Iuchar 16 DE Muileann dhearg
The seven houses of custody
The remaining custodian households are regrouped into seven houses, each answerable to the vein-house for its share of the ore and of the measured burning: Clann Mhuirich, Clann Fhearchair, Clann Ìomhair, Clann Raghnaill, Clann Thormoid, Clann Choinnich and Clann Lachlainn. The division is the first in the record to treat the right to the ore as something inherited by house rather than earned by apprenticeship.
28 an t-Iuchar 16 DE Cathair dhearg
Death of Queen Beathag
Queen Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill dies at Cathair dhearg, the last ruler of Rodos to have seen the fleet. Her son Raghnall mac Uilleim is crowned in the same hall.
25 an t-Samhain 22 DE
The empty harbor rite
A ceremony develops around the specific dock the ships departed from, still observed in reduced form on an anniversary no one can precisely date anymore.
24 an Dùbhlachd 25 DE Seann Skell
The harbour at half trade
Seann Skell's harbour-master records his berths at half their former use. The fishing households that had crewed the fleet are simply gone, and the rope-walks at Cuan shean lay off hands for the first time.
8 an Gearran 26 DE
The second silence
A rumor of a second, smaller crossing — fewer ships, no surviving record of a destination — is neither confirmed nor denied by anything that survives.
5 am Màrt 28 DE Ceann mhòr
The watch at Ceann mhòr
Fishing families at Ceann mhòr on the north-west coast keep a watch from the headland for returning sails, taking turns by household. The watch lapses within a generation, and no sail is recorded.
13 am Màrt 28 DE
The renaming of the west quay
The dock the ships departed from is given a new name specifically so ordinary trade could resume using the old one without the association — an early, quiet act of managed forgetting.
15 an Lùnastal 28 DE Seann Skell
Cidhe an Diosail
In the harbour rolls of Seann Skell the departure berth is entered as Cidhe an Diosail, the quay of the sunwise turn. The name Cidhe an Iar passes to the new fish-wharf at the north end of the strand, and within a few years the fishers use it without a thought.
21 an Lùnastal 28 DE
Roghnaich takes its narrow sense
In the custody-book the verb roghnaich, to choose, begins to appear with no object at all, meaning to have chosen the crossing. Scribes of the next century use it this way without explaining it, which is the surest sign it had become ordinary speech.
31 an Lùnastal 28 DE
The first generation to never see the sea empty
Children born just after the Setting-Out grow up never having known the harbour with those particular ships in it. For them the departure is already history.
8 an t-Sultain 28 DE Seann Skell
Death of Alasdair Saor
Alasdair Saor, who laid the first deep keel, dies at Seann Skell. His last work was a coasting trader of the old sewn-plank kind, built for a fish merchant of Inis àrsaidh.
27 an t-Ògmhios 45 DE
The closing of the shipwrights' guild
With no more ocean-crossing vessels needed, the guild that built the Sundering fleet quietly dissolves — its techniques half-forgotten by the time anyone thinks to need them again.
29 an Cèitean 46 DE Seann Skell
The keel-moulds burned
The patterns and moulds of the dissolved fellowship, kept in a shed on the strand at Seann Skell, are broken up and burned as firewood during a hard season. The harbour-master notes the loss of the shed, not of what was in it.
30 an Giblean 70 DE Muileann dhearg
The mountain divided among the houses
The seven houses draw lots at the vein-house for the galleries each will keep, and the vein-house confirms the Small-Burning measure for each of them. The lot-stones were kept in a bag at Muileann dhearg and shown to visitors for centuries after.
14 an t-Iuchar 70 DE Doire fhionn
The coppice law of Doire fhionn
With the great oaks gone to the fleet, the shire of Doire fhionn forbids the felling of any living oak without the reeve's mark and begins to cut its woods by coppice. The law spreads to every shire with a Doire in its name.
12 an Lùnastal 70 DE Seann Skell
The lamps kept at Seann Skell
The waterfront of Seann Skell keeps the night of lamps each year on the eve of the empty-harbour rite. Children are told the lamps are for ships coming home, which the priests do not correct.
9 an Dàmhair 70 DE Muileann dhearg
Death of Donnchadh mac Thormoid
Donnchadh mac Thormoid, the vein-house scribe who began the count of years, dies at Muileann dhearg. His last entry is a list of the ore burned that season, household by household, in the same hand as his first.
7 an t-Samhain 86 DE Cathair dhearg
Raghnall dies; Ìomhar crowned
King Raghnall mac Uilleim dies at Cathair dhearg after a long and uneventful reign, and his son Ìomhar mac Raghnaill is crowned. The custody-book gives Raghnall's reign a single line.
6 an Dùbhlachd 110 DE Muileann chiar — baile mèinne airgid
The silversmiths of Muileann chiar
The silver of the seam at Muileann chiar, mined since the Holy Age, is worked into neck-rings for the heads of the seven houses. The smiths' fellowship of the seam, heir to Sliochd Fhearchair, closes its methods within four families.
4 am Faoilleach 115 DE Inis mhòr
Inis mhòr's grain fleet
Inis mhòr in the north builds a fleet of barges to carry grain down the Abhainn ghorm to Caol bheag and, from Ros chiar at the river mouth, west along the coast to Cnoc bheag. They are sewn-plank boats of the old kind, and none sleeps out of sight of land.
2 an Gearran 117 DE Caol fhiadhaich
The coughing sickness at Caol fhiadhaich
A coughing sickness runs through Caol fhiadhaich on the south-west coast and kills some two hundred before it burns out. The shared-meal custom is kept throughout, and the town's reeve credits it with the survival of the rest.
3 am Màrt 125 DE Am Buabhall Fortanach
Am Buabhall Fortanach rebuilt in stone
The old road-house of Am Buabhall Fortanach burns to its footings and is rebuilt in stone by its keeper, Eilidh nic Chaluim. The account of her rebuilding mentions the jugged buffalo it was already known for.
7 an Dàmhair 140 DE Dùn ìseal
The spirit-house at Dùn ìseal
The keepers of the Old Spirits, the faith of the hearths, raise a house for the ancestors at Dùn ìseal, where the names of the dead of the eastern shires are cut on wooden posts. The posts are recut every generation as the old ones rot.
30 an Giblean 141 DE Cathair dhearg
Ìomhar dies without an heir
King Ìomhar mac Raghnaill dies at Cathair dhearg with no living child, and the line of Beathag ends with him. The heads of the seven houses are summoned to the capital to name a successor.
19 an Gearran 143 DE Cathair dhearg
Fearchar mac Lachlainn chosen
The heads of the houses choose Fearchar mac Lachlainn of Baile Mòr dhomhain, of Clann Fhearchair, and he is crowned at Cathair dhearg. It is the first crowning in the record decided by the custodian houses rather than by descent.
20 am Màrt 155 DE Baile Mòr dhomhain
A court at Baile Mòr dhomhain
King Fearchar keeps his court for part of each year at Baile Mòr dhomhain, near the mountain, so that the vein-house may be consulted without a journey. The custom of the double court lasts as long as his house.
21 an Gearran 170 DE Àth fhiadhaich
The fishers of Àth fhiadhaich
The fishing families of Àth fhiadhaich form a single fellowship to share boats and nets after a season of losses. It is the first fishers' fellowship on the east coast.
21 an t-Ògmhios 172 DE Cathair dhearg
Fearchar Donn crowned
Fearchar mac Lachlainn dies and his son, called Fearchar Donn, is crowned at Cathair dhearg without dispute.
20 an Giblean 190 DE Cnoc bheag
Gormshuil of the Hawk
At Cnoc bheag, where the dawn-hawk rite of the Holy Age is still kept, the priestess Gormshuil nic Artair teaches that the hawk of the rite is Mòd, the Hawk of Acaill, who is as old as Fionntan mac Bòchra, the oldest of men, and remembers everything with him, and that the vein is the Hungry Hawk, who must be fed the measured handful and no more, since a hawk overfed will not hunt and a hawk starved will turn on the hand. Her followers gather the old rite into the first house of Òrd an t-Seabhaig, the order of the Hawk of Acaill.
22 am Màrt 200 DE Ros gheal
The hawk-house at Ros gheal
A second house of the Hawk is founded at Ros gheal by Gormshuil's pupils. Its priests take charge of the measured burning for the whole country between Ros gheal on the coast and Cnoc bheag up the river.
17 an t-Ògmhios 205 DE Seann Vell
Flood at Seann Vell
The river at Seann Vell on the south-east coast breaks its banks in a wet spring and carries away the lower mills. The mill-wrights rebuild them on the higher bank.
5 an t-Ògmhios 212 DE Cnoc bheag
The sayings of Gormshuil written
After Gormshuil's death her sayings are written down at Cnoc bheag as Leabhar an t-Seabhaig, the Book of the Hawk. The copyist, Ùisdean mac Pàdraig, marks every saying he did not hear from her own mouth, and there are more of these than of the rest.
23 an t-Samhain 220 DE Seann Toll
The storm that took Seann Toll's boats
A northern storm, named in the harbour rolls Am Fuath Mòr, breaks the harbour wall of Seann Toll and sinks forty boats at their moorings. Eighteen fishers are drowned.
16 an t-Iuchar 222 DE Seann Toll
Seann Toll walls its harbour again
Seann Toll rebuilds its harbour wall higher and with a hooked end, to a plan the reeve had from the masons of the capital. The wall stands through every later storm in this age.
12 an t-Sultain 222 DE Dùn dhearg
The walls of Dùn dhearg
Dùn dhearg in the eastern hills is walled in stone by Clann Ìomhair, who hold the land around it. The walls are the first on the island built by a custodian house rather than the crown.
11 an Dàmhair 222 DE Cathair dhearg
Queen Sìleas's measures
Sìleas nic Fhearchair, crowned after her father Fearchar Donn, fixes a single measure for grain across the island, the firlot of Cathair dhearg, so that barter between shires need not begin with a quarrel over the size of a basket. Standard firlots of oak bound with iron are sent to every shire seat.
22 an t-Sultain 245 DE Cathair dhearg
Tally-houses in the royal granaries
Queen Sìleas sets a tally-house in each royal granary, where every exchange of grain for cloth, salt or labour is cut on paired sticks, one for each party. It is the first island-wide account of trade, and it runs entirely without coin.
17 an t-Samhain 248 DE Cathair fhada
The market charter of Cathair fhada
Queen Sìleas grants Cathair fhada a market each week on its ridge and a tally-house for the south, the first market right cut on paired sticks. The long city's merchants carry the honey, hemp, wax and pots of the south to the capital, and they begin to go to the harvest fair at Muileann òg as one company.
21 an Dàmhair 250 DE Drochaid Cathair dhearg
Drochaid Cathair dhearg widened
The old stone bridge over Abhainn dhomhain at Cathair dhearg is widened so that two carts can pass. Queen Sìleas's name is cut on the downstream parapet, where it can still be read.
26 an t-Iuchar 265 DE Imrich nam Pantar
The crossing days of the panthers
Herders in the southern hills near Imrich nam Pantar begin keeping the panther roads clear on the days the great cats cross, driving their flocks off the paths beforehand. The crossing days are the first thing the southern shires agree on in writing.
24 an Lùnastal 265 DE An Leòmhann Buidhe
An Leòmhann Buidhe on the north road
An Leòmhann Buidhe, a road-house on the northern mining road, is recorded as serving oatcakes fried in linseed oil, and fire water, to the ore-carters. Its keeper is fined for watering the fire water.
29 an Cèitean 275 DE Dùn thais
The house of disputation at Dùn thais
Coinneach mac Mhàrtainn, a druid of the schools of Flidais, lady of the deer, founds a house of disputation at Dùn thais where the schools' old question, Carson an làmh seo?, why the vein answers some hands and not others, is argued by rule. Pupils come from as far as Caol bheag.
1 an Giblean 285 DE Dùn thais
Coinneach's question
Coinneach mac Mhàrtainn asks in open disputation whether the hands that went with the fleet were the ones the vein answered best, and whether it now answers fewer. The seven houses forbid the question at their own tables, which the record notes is the first time they forbade a question rather than an act.
30 an Giblean 285 DE Baile Mòr mhòr
Baile Mòr mhòr grows
Baile Mòr mhòr on the northern plain takes in families from the upland farms after a run of poor seasons and doubles in size within a generation. Its reeve divides the common grazing anew.
27 an t-Ògmhios 285 DE Cathair dhearg
Death of Queen Sìleas
Queen Sìleas nic Fhearchair dies at Cathair dhearg after a reign of more than half a century. Her son Uisdean mac Dhùghaill is crowned.
2 an Gearran 305 DE Inis àrsaidh
The deep hull that would not float true
A merchant of Inis àrsaidh pays to have a deep-keeled hull built for the long coast run to the east. The wrights cannot remember how Alasdair Saor's keels were scarfed, and the hull lists so badly at launch that it is broken up for timber.
3 am Màrt 315 DE Ros fhionn
Salt pans at Ros fhionn
The river town of Ros fhionn in the north-east lays out salt pans at the brine springs on its river flats and begins to send salt inland over Drochaid Ros fhionn. Within a generation Ros fhionn salt is the common measure of value in the north-eastern shires.
18 an t-Sultain 322 DE Baile gharbh
The wool of Baile gharbh
The weavers of Baile gharbh make a heavy undyed cloth that sheds rain, and it becomes the common cloak of the north-east. It is also the cloth in which the white sorrow is kept.
20 an Lùnastal 330 DE Drochaid Ros fhionn
Salt over Drochaid Ros fhionn
Traffic over Drochaid Ros fhionn grows so heavy with salt carts that the bridge-keeper is given the right to take a handful from each load. The keeper's salt-box is recorded as holding more than some villages' granaries.
27 an Cèitean 340 DE Scàineadh Cill ghlas
The wells crack at Cill ghlas
An earth tremor in the hills around Cill ghlas cracks three wells and brings down a byre. The custodians of the vein-house note it and note also that the galleries were untouched.
26 an Giblean 355 DE Marbh-bheò Doire uaine
The Hollow Man spoken of again
Shepherds of the Doire uaine hills refuse to light fires on the high pastures, citing the old inscriptions of Marbh-bheò Doire uaine. A reeve sent from Muileann chiar to make them see sense does not stay the night.
25 an Cèitean 355 DE Cathair dhearg
Aonghas mac Uisdein crowned
Uisdean mac Dhùghaill dies and his son Aonghas mac Uisdein is crowned at Cathair dhearg. Aonghas is recorded as the first king to learn his letters as a child.
23 an t-Ògmhios 355 DE Àth fhiadhaich
Àth fhiadhaich salt fish
Àth fhiadhaich begins to salt its catch with Ros fhionn salt and send it inland to the mining towns. The mining shires eat salt fish in the lean season from this time on.
28 am Màrt 370 DE Inis thais
Clach first preached at Inis thais
Dòmhnall mac Ailein, a net-maker of Inis thais, where the wolf-sworn's stone Clach stands, preaches that the stone is Lia Fàil, the stone that cries out under the rightful king, and that its sworn guards are the Fianna, who keep the island as a wolf keeps its range. His hearers are the first congregation of Òrd na Cloiche, the order of the Stone.
16 an Dùbhlachd 380 DE Inis thais
The wolf-house at Inis thais
Dòmhnall mac Ailein's followers raise a temple at Inis thais, the first temple on the island raised to Lia Fàil by name. It is roofed with slate brought by sea from the north.
29 am Faoilleach 390 DE Caol leathan
Hawk and wolf at Caol leathan
Priests of the Hawk and the Fianna of the Stone both claim the harbour shrine at Caol leathan. The king's reeve divides its days between them, as the Holy Age had divided the sacred woods, and the arrangement holds.
28 an Dùbhlachd 396 DE Seann Skell
The market inside the new gate
Seann Skell on the Hawk bay is walled, and a market is chartered inside the new landward gate. Amber, whale-oil, honey and the sheep of the northern moors are sold there, and the amber-workers of the bay agree to sell no rough amber outside the walls.
31 an Dùbhlachd 402 DE Cathair dhearg
Macha at court
King Aonghas takes up the wood-watchers' rite of Macha, which keeps the two horses of one chariot, foaled on one night, Liath Macha, the grey, and Dubh Sainglenn, the black: two horses, one yoke; light and dark are two powers in balance, and the vein belongs to both. The court follows him, and Òrd Mhacha, the order of Macha, becomes the order of Cathair dhearg and the crown.
28 am Màrt 407 DE Tobar dhearg
Fire at Tobar dhearg
A fire in the thatch spreads through Tobar dhearg and burns most of the village. The villagers rebuild with slate from the quarries nearby, and the village is known for its slate roofs after.
14 am Faoilleach 432 DE Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag
Macha's priests in Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag
The share of custody over Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag, divided since the Holy Age, passes by royal grant to the priests of Macha. The other claimants withdraw from the wood without contest, and the record does not say why.
11 an t-Iuchar 440 DE Coille Naomh Muileann chiar
The druid schools keep Coille Naomh Muileann chiar
The druids of the schools take formal keeping of Coille Naomh Muileann chiar, the wood of Flidais's white stag, walking its bounds each year. The walk becomes the schools' one public observance.
29 am Faoilleach 445 DE Àth chiar
The drovers of Àth chiar
Drovers from Àth chiar begin driving cattle over the eastern hills to the mining towns each year. Their routes are the first on the island to be marked with cairns.
23 an t-Ògmhios 445 DE Doire chiar
Eilidh Dhubh's tracts
At Doire chiar, Eilidh nic Iain, called Eilidh Dhubh, revives the teaching of the Holy Age's rival school, that the vein answers effort and not birth, and writes it out in tracts copied by her pupils. The tracts are read aloud at harvest gatherings across the north-east.
2 an Dùbhlachd 445 DE Muileann dhearg
The tracts burned at Muileann dhearg
The vein-house orders every copy of Eilidh Dhubh's tracts brought to Muileann dhearg and burned. Some hundred copies are surrendered. Eilidh herself is not punished and dies at Doire chiar, still teaching.
31 an Dùbhlachd 445 DE Cathair dhearg
Death of King Aonghas
King Aonghas mac Uisdein dies at Cathair dhearg and is buried by the rite of Macha, the first king so buried. His son Iain mac Aonghais is crowned.
27 an Gearran 457 DE Cathair dhearg
Tormod Bàn crowned
Iain mac Aonghais dies after a short reign and his son Tormod mac Iain, called Tormod Bàn for his white hair, is crowned at Cathair dhearg. The houses swear to him without dispute.
8 an Lùnastal 470 DE An Taigh-seinnse Mòr
Winter at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr
An Taigh-seinnse Mòr, on the central mining road, becomes the house where the ox-teams of the mountain wait out the worst of the snow. Its keeper, Iain mac Mhurchaidh, builds a second byre for them and keeps a book of the teams that lodged.
6 an t-Sultain 475 DE Muileann naomh
The bell-founders of Muileann naomh
A family at Muileann naomh casts the first bronze bell on Rodos hung in a hawk-house. The bell cracks in its first frost, and the second holds.
5 am Màrt 480 DE Cuan dhearg
An Gàire Dubh
A storm named in the south-coast rolls An Gàire Dubh, the Black Laugh, drives the sea over the waterfront of Cuan dhearg and ruins the season's salt fish. The town is rebuilt a street further back from the shore.
13 an t-Sultain 487 DE Muileann naomh
The hawk-house at Muileann naomh
Muileann naomh in the south becomes the southernmost house of the Hawk, its bell rung at each measured burning. The Hawk's teaching holds there when it fades elsewhere in the south.
18 an t-Ògmhios 495 DE Abhainn fhionn
The king's sons drowned in Abhainn fhionn
Both sons of King Tormod Bàn are drowned when a ferry overturns crossing Abhainn fhionn in spate. The king has no other child.
8 an t-Sultain 508 DE Cathair dhearg
Death of Tormod Bàn
King Tormod Bàn dies at Cathair dhearg without naming an heir. Three claims are laid before the houses at once.
21 an Giblean 513 DE Cathair dhearg
The three claimants
The crown is claimed by Catrìona nic Aonghais of Inis thais, the late king's niece; by Dùghall Garbh of Baile Mòr dhomhain, his half-brother; and by Raghnall Ruadh, head of Clann Raghnaill and master of the vein-house. The seven houses split among them and the War of the Three Claimants begins.
20 an Cèitean 514 DE Seann Warr
Seann Warr shuts its gates
Seann Warr, the port nearest the capital on the west, closes its gates to all three claimants and declares for none. It is besieged twice in the war and taken by neither.
22 an Gearran 515 DE Àth shean
The ford at Àth shean
Dùghall Garbh's host meets Raghnall Ruadh's at the ford of Àth shean and breaks it. The custody-book counts some three hundred dead, most of them drowned in the ford.
24 an t-Sultain 516 DE Doire mhin
The burning of Doire mhin
Raghnall Ruadh's retreating men burn the village of Doire mhin and its granary to deny it to Dùghall. The villagers winter at Cathair mhòr on the charity of Macha's priests.
26 an Dùbhlachd 518 DE Cathair dhomhain
The siege of Cathair dhomhain
Catrìona nic Aonghais besieges Cathair dhomhain, which had declared for Dùghall, and takes it after forty days when its wells are poisoned by the dead of the siege lines. She lets the garrison go free on their oath.
24 am Faoilleach 519 DE Muileann dhearg
The hearths refused
Raghnall Ruadh, holding the vein-house, refuses the measured handful of ore to every hearth and temple in the shires that stand against him. Hearths that had been lit with the ore for generations go cold, and the act turns more people against him than any battle.
14 am Faoilleach 521 DE Muileann chrom
The battle of Muileann chrom
The hosts of Catrìona and Dùghall, joined for the purpose, meet Raghnall Ruadh below Muileann chrom. Raghnall is killed on the field and the vein-house is opened by his own custodians the next day.
16 an Dùbhlachd 522 DE Baile Mòr dhomhain
Death of Dùghall Garbh
Dùghall Garbh dies of his wounds from Muileann chrom at Baile Mòr dhomhain. His followers go over to Catrìona without a further fight.
13 am Màrt 523 DE Cathair dhearg
Catrìona Bhuadhach crowned
Catrìona nic Aonghais is crowned at Cathair dhearg and is known after as Catrìona Bhuadhach. The War of the Three Claimants ends with her crowning, having lasted about a decade.
12 an Gearran 526 DE Muileann dhearg
The ruling of the hearth
Catrìona Bhuadhach and the vein-house fix in law that no claimant, house or king may withhold the measured handful from any lawful hearth. It is the first law in the record written to bind the custodians themselves.
10 an Cèitean 545 DE Am Buabhall Fortanach
Catrìona's road south
Queen Catrìona has the road from the capital south by Baile shean and Am Buabhall Fortanach at Doire shean laid with stone, so that her own town of Inis thais may be reached in any weather. The road is known as Rathad na Banrighinn.
11 an Giblean 555 DE Seann Warr
Seann Warr's gates honoured
Queen Catrìona grants Seann Warr the right to keep its own gates and levy its own tolls, in memory of its standing aside in the war. The grant is cut over the landward gate.
7 an t-Iuchar 565 DE Cathair dhearg
Death of Catrìona Bhuadhach
Catrìona Bhuadhach dies at Cathair dhearg. Her son Lachlann mac Iain is crowned, and the houses swear to him in one day, which the record remarks on.
8 an t-Ògmhios 585 DE Cathair dhearg
The Book of the Three Claimants
A clerk of Queen Catrìona's household, Seònaid nic Coinnich, writes an account of the war from the custody-book and from the testimony of those who fought. It is the oldest surviving history on Rodos written as a single narrative rather than as entries.
3 an t-Sultain 585 DE Inis chrom
The sickness at Inis chrom
A spotted fever kills some three hundred at Inis chrom on the south-west coast. The Fianna of the Stone nurse the sick and many of them die of it, and the town becomes the Stone's for good.
5 an Lùnastal 595 DE Doire shean
The oyster beds of Doire shean
Doire shean, a village on the southern shore, lays out oyster beds in its shallow bay and sends oysters by cart to the capital. The trade makes the village rich enough to be a shire seat.
26 an Dàmhair 605 DE Seann Tarr
The feast-market at Seann Tarr
The crowds that come to the ancestor shrine at Seann Tarr for the great feasts begin to hold a market on the three feast days. Its chief goods are honey, beeswax for the shrine lights and the dyes of Baile fhiadhaich. The wax lights of Seann Tarr are soon burned at ancestor shrines along the whole north-eastern coast.
1 an t-Sultain 615 DE Seann Skell
Manannan preached at Seann Skell
At Seann Skell, where the sting-creed of the Holy Age first called itself the only true one, a preacher named Mànas mac Ruairidh proclaims its one power as Manannan mac Lir, lord of the sea, whose Cup of Truth bears the yellow scorpion, and teaches that Manannan shut the western sea behind the fleet with his mist, which hides Rodos from every ship beyond it, and that it must not be tried again. His hearers are the first congregation of Òrd Mhanannain, the order of Manannan.
30 an t-Sultain 615 DE Cathair dhearg
Death of Lachlann mac Iain
Lachlann mac Iain, son of Catrìona Bhuadhach, dies at Cathair dhearg, and his daughter Anna is crowned. The record calls his reign quiet and means it as praise.
29 an Dàmhair 635 DE Ros bheag
Manannan's order at Ros bheag and Cuan shean
The teaching of Manannan's order spreads down the west coast to Ros bheag and Cuan shean, carried by fishing families. At Cuan shean the rope-makers are among the first converts.
27 an t-Samhain 655 DE Ros bheag
Within sight of land
Manannan's priests at Ros bheag lay it down that no boat of the faithful may go beyond sight of the headlands. The rule is kept on the west coast for centuries, and the steering of boats by the stars, already half lost, is lost there entirely.
19 an t-Ògmhios 660 DE Àth shean
The granaries of Àth shean rebuilt
The royal granaries at Àth shean, old since before the Sundering, are pulled down and rebuilt in stone on raised floors against the rats. The tally-house is rebuilt with them.
24 am Faoilleach 675 DE Cuan shean
The rope-walks shortened
Cuan shean takes up half its rope-walks and puts the ground to barley. The rope trade had lived on the fleet and then on the fishing, and the fishing no longer needs rope of that length.
22 an Gearran 685 DE Cnoc chaol
Wave at Cnoc chaol
A great swell, with no storm behind it, runs up the beach at Cnoc chaol on the south coast and carries off the drying racks and two children. The village moves its racks further up the shore.
11 an t-Samhain 692 DE Baile Mòr dhìreach
The market of the eastern road
Baile Mòr dhìreach, the citadel on the eastern straight road, is given a market for the east coast. The fish and sail-cloth of the coast towns meet the furs, hides and dyes of the hills there, and the dyers of Baile Mòr ruadh sell their colours nowhere else.
23 am Màrt 700 DE Muileann dhearg
The two counts reconciled
The vein-house and the crown's scribes find that their counts of years since the Setting-Out differ, and settle the difference by agreement. The day of the empty-harbour rite, which each count had placed differently, is fixed by the same agreement, and later scribes stop pretending it was fixed by evidence.
12 am Faoilleach 730 DE Inis mhòr
The druid school at Inis mhòr
A house of disputation is founded at Inis mhòr by pupils of Dùn thais, and the question of the vein is argued in the north for the first time. Its first master, Fionnlagh mac Aonghais, is remembered for refusing every answer offered him.
10 an Gearran 730 DE Cathair dhearg
Queen Eilidh Bhàn crowned
Eilidh Bhàn, the fifth ruler of the house of Catrìona, is crowned at Cathair dhearg. The record of her long reign is almost entirely one of harvests.
22 an Gearran 730 DE Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh
The bath-house at the hot springs
Clann Choinnich rebuilds the old bath-house over the hot springs of Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh in dressed stone and admits the sick of any house on one day in seven. The house's physicians keep a book of cures that is later lost.
24 am Faoilleach 745 DE Spùinneadairean-mara
The sea-thieves of the north-west
Boats working out of the small islands off the north-west coast begin taking fish and grain from coasting traders. The sea-thieves are Ròdaich, men of the north-west shore, and the harbour rolls give some of their names.
26 an Dùbhlachd 750 DE Baile chrom
Baile chrom half empty
The reeve of Baile chrom on the north-west coast reports half the town's houses empty, their families gone east after the sea-thieves and the poor harvests. The crown remits the town's grain dues.
27 an t-Samhain 762 DE Eilean dhubh
The raid on Eilean dhubh
A force sent by Queen Eilidh Bhàn lands on Eilean dhubh and burns the sea-thieves' boats on the strand. Their leader, Uilleam Ruadh, is taken to Cathair dhearg and hanged.
19 an Giblean 780 DE Gorta Baile chrom
The dearth on the north-west shore
A run of failed harvests along the north-west shore brings a dearth that the shared-meal custom cannot carry. Families leave the coast for the interior and the east, and the north-west is thinly held from this time until the end of the age.
20 an Cèitean 790 DE Cathair dhearg
The king-list recopied
The scribes of Queen Eilidh Bhàn recopy the king-list of Rodos from its oldest surviving roll, adding the rulers since the Sundering. The new copy begins its account of the present age with the Choosing and not with the fleet.
19 an Gearran 796 DE Àth fhionn
The strand-market at Àth fhionn
Àth fhionn, the ford town where the coast road crosses the clear river, holds a market on the strand for the north coast. Fish, the flesh and oil of stranded whales, wool and barley are sold there, and the fishers of the north coast stop carrying their catch to Inis mhòr.
21 an Giblean 802 DE Cathair dhearg
Eilidh Bhàn dies without an heir
Queen Eilidh Bhàn dies at Cathair dhearg with no child, and the house of Catrìona ends with her. The seven houses meet at the vein-house rather than at the capital.
23 am Màrt 807 DE Cathair dhearg
Dòmhnall Ruadh crowned
The houses name Dòmhnall Ruadh of Clann Raghnaill, a descendant of the claimant killed at Muileann chrom. He is crowned at Cathair dhearg and keeps the mastery of the vein-house as well as the crown.
6 an t-Ògmhios 820 DE Muileann dhearg
The crown and the custody joined
Dòmhnall Ruadh's reeves write it into the custody-book that the ruler of Rodos is also master of the vein-house. From this time the heads of the seven houses sit as the king's council, and the custodian class and the court are one body.
1 an t-Ògmhios 826 DE Muileann dhearg
The custody's seal on the king's letters
From the joining of the crown and the custody the king's letters are sealed with the vein-house's own seal: a trellis of gold on blue, which the custodians read as the galleries of the mountain, with a hollow lozenge over it for Crom's slab, laid on the first break. The crown adds a white band across the field and nothing else. From this time the seal is the arms of the kingdom.
10 an Dùbhlachd 832 DE Cathair dhearg
Death of Dòmhnall Ruadh
Dòmhnall Ruadh, the first ruler to hold both the crown and the vein-house, dies at Cathair dhearg and is buried at Muileann dhearg. His son Raghnall Òg is crowned.
20 an t-Ògmhios 850 DE Cnoc bheag
The schism of the Hawk
A council of the Hawk at Cnoc bheag divides over whether Mòd's measure may ever be raised. Those who hold it fixed forever keep the name of the Hungry Hawk and the house at Cnoc bheag; those who hold that a larger flock may be fed a larger handful are called the Fed Hawk.
17 an Lùnastal 860 DE Seann Chwen
The harbour of Seann Chwen
The port of Seann Chwen builds its harbour mole, and becomes the port for the ore-carts coming down from the mountain to the coast towns of the south.
23 an Giblean 870 DE Seann Skell
The Fed Hawk at Seann Skell
The priests of the Fed Hawk, turned out of Cnoc bheag, settle at Seann Skell on the north coast, not the western river port of that name. Their teaching is written in the custody-book as an error, and the error is recorded at length.
25 an Lùnastal 880 DE Seann Skell
The Fed Hawk's petition
The Fed Hawk petitions the king's council from Seann Skell to raise the measured handful by a quarter for the hearths of the north coast. The council refuses. The petition is the first recorded request to alter the Small-Burning Law.
14 an Dàmhair 890 DE Cill ghlas
The gallery at Cill ghlas
A second tremor in the hills of Cill ghlas brings down a gallery of the vein and kills fourteen custodians' labourers. The vein-house closes the gallery and sets a stone at its mouth with the fourteen names.
12 an t-Samhain 900 DE Cathair dhearg
