Òrd Mhanannainthe order of ManannanManannan mac Lir, lord of the seathe yellow scorpion, badge of his Cup of Truth35118Seann Skell (west)

The Church is kept in three bodies. The churches of the Mission's line hold 51 burgs, with eight churches the map marks as temples; their largest house is at Cnoc ghorm. The old congregations of the north coast, Eaglais nan Tuathach, hold twelve, with three. The vigil of the Grey Night, which the Church's bishops call irregular, holds one town and its one house.

Counted by burgs, the Old Faith is the most widespread faith, and within it the druid schools are the most widespread order, with Macha's order next. Counted by the people in their towns, the Old Faith comes first by far, at nearly three million two hundred thousand. The Old Spirits come next, at a little over one million two hundred thousand, and the Church holds some five hundred and forty thousand. Among the orders Macha's is the largest in people, at nearly one million two hundred thousand, close behind the Old Spirits, and the schools come next. Òrd Bhrìde, which the kingdom treats as the orthodox keeper of the vein, holds nine towns. That is not a mistake in the count, and section VIII explains it.

Shires and temples. Counted by land rather than by towns, the faiths divide the island's 123 shires as follows. A faith holds a shire where it has more of the shire's land than any other faith, and shares one where it has a smaller part. The temples are the houses the map marks as temples.

FaithShires heldShires sharedTemples
An Creideamh Sean771365
Na Seann Spioradan341124
An Eaglais11512

That accounts for 122 shires. In Seann Vell, the shire whose lands take in the far north-western cape, most of the land keeps no faith at all. The orders between them stand first in seventy-six of the Old Faith's shires. In the seventy-seventh, Muileann dhomhain in the south-east, no order has the greater part: the Old Spirits, Òrd Bhrìde and Macha's order have almost equal shares and the schools a small one, so that the orders together hold two-thirds of the land.

Descent. The Old Spirits are the old reverence itself, kept at the hearths without a break, and they descend from nothing older that the record can name. The Old Faith grew out of the same reverence: its six orders began as the companies of the Hall's council at the end of the Holy Age (section II), though the gods they serve are older than any company. The Church came over the sea with the humans (5 am Faoilleach 1780 DE) and has no root on Rodos older than the Crossing. The vigil of the Grey Night is the only rite on the island that grew out of two faiths at once: its prayer came from the harbours of Manannan's order, and its goose from the Church (section VII).

How they spread. The Old Spirits have never sought converts beyond their own people, and neither have Òrd Bhrìde, the Hawk order or the old congregations of the north coast. Each is held where its people live and nowhere else. The druid schools and Macha's order spread with the kingdom, the one through its schools and the other through the crown's favour, and neither has gone beyond the Ròdaich. Since King Aonghas took it up, Macha's order has spread faster than any other. The Church sought converts from the day the Mission landed, and counted its first Ròdaich converts among the children of its school at Ros dhomhain (9 an Cèitean 1830 DE). It holds no Ròdaich town today. Manannan's order, the Stone and the Grey Night take in anyone of any people who comes to them. Only Manannan's has taught its prayers to a second people: the first human fishing families at Ceann mhòr learned its harbour prayers (14 am Màrt 1830 DE). The Stone, for all its open doors, is still held only in Ròdaich towns of the south-west.

Land without a faith. No faith holds the far north-western cape beyond Baile chrom. It has no town, and most of it lies outside any shire. Its few families, herders and shore-folk, most of them Tuathaich, have no house of any faith, and the first census of the restored kingdom entered them as gun chreideamh, without a faith (30 an t-Iuchar 1936 DE). The same entry covers Eilean ghorm, where the grey geese winter and are never hunted (3 an Lùnastal 9112 BDE), Eilean dhubh, where the sea-thieves' boats were burned (27 an t-Samhain 762 DE), and the islet of Eilean gheal off the south-east coast. The cape has been thinly held since the dearth on the north-west shore (19 an Giblean 780 DE).

II. The Old Reverence and Its Parting

The chronicle says plainly that the Ròdaich reverence was once one. On 11 an Gearran 144 BDE "a single unified folk practice begins visibly splitting into the distinct threads later ages will separately name." What that one practice was can be put together from the Ancient Age. The tellings of that age name the slab, the cup and the handful, and name no god over them.

The slab and the handful. A mason broke into a black vein that bled colour instead of dust (20 am Faoilleach 12,923 BDE). His people did not dig on. They laid a slab over the break and cut their well a stone's throw away (19 am Màrt 12,773 BDE). Families took turns sitting by the slab (8 an t-Ògmhios 6481 BDE) and later chose a keeper by lot (26 an t-Samhain 5198 BDE). The first was Oighrig nic Dhòmhnaill, who had a cup ground out of grey stone to the size of her cupped hand (29 an t-Sultain 5196 BDE), because by then no fire took more ore than one hand could hold (5 an Lùnastal 6590 BDE). When a keeper was found with a basket of ore in his house, it was neither burned nor kept. It was laid back under the slab: the ore went home (4 an t-Iuchar 5190 BDE). By the end of the age every household of the hills burned its handful on one night of the dark of the year, so that the colour showed on every hillside at once (9 an Cèitean 3246 BDE).

The doctrine. The oldest saying on the island is cut on the column near Cnoc ghorm (6 an t-Samhain 8048 BDE), and it was first spoken as a rule at the ford gathering (21 an t-Sultain 5178 BDE):

Cha do thàinig sinn; bha sinn ann. We did not come; we were here.

No order or house on Rodos has disowned it since, though each reads it its own way.

What the Old Ones left. Làrach an Teampaill (Làrach an Teampaill) has its altar set square to the central mountains (14 an Lùnastal 10,232 BDE), and every later temple on Rodos faces some other way. Its top stone was prised off and never found (5 an Gearran 8720 BDE). The chronicle calls it "a temple older than any recorded religion ... toward the vein, not the horizon" (7 am Faoilleach 8673 BDE). The Ròdaich walked round it and took no stone from it (13 an t-Sultain 4244 BDE). Whether its builders held the vein holy, or only knew where it lay, is not known.

The Binding and the first parting. The Holy Age opens with the Binding of the First Flame (23 an t-Sultain 2998 BDE), the flame the Old Faith calls Brìde's. At Dùn ìseal Beathag Bhàn was chosen to hold the flame (28 an t-Ògmhios 2995 BDE), and Talla na Lasrach was raised over it with one door facing the vein and none facing the sea (19 an Dùbhlachd 2984 BDE). The custom of the handful hardened into the Small-Burning Law (13 an Lùnastal 2857 BDE). The Keepers also ruled on what belonged to the vein, and each ruling drew a line. When Muireach Liath held that the fortune-stream Allt an Àigh belonged "to the ancestors and the weather, not to the vein" (16 am Màrt 2940 BDE), the Hall's reverence and the older reverence of the hearths could be seen for the first time as two things. The first became the Old Faith, and the second the Old Spirits.

By the end of the Holy Age the Hall could no longer keep one rite. Seumas Bàn's clerks listed every rite that burned the handful or claimed the vein (18 an Dàmhair 161 BDE): the Hall's own, the ancestor-keeping of the old folk, the dawn-hawk of the north coast, the wood-watchers of the west, the wolf-sworn, the sting-oath, and both schools of the stag. The council then began to sit in companies by rite. Seumas Bàn complained that he kept the flame for eight peoples who each thought themselves its only keepers (16 an t-Samhain 141 BDE). The ancestor-keepers are the Old Spirits of the map. The other companies are the roots of the six orders of the Old Faith. The Church grew from no root on Rodos.

What stayed common. Pilgrims of every rite went on walking to Allt an Àigh (Allt an Àigh) (15 an Dùbhlachd 139 BDE), and the sick of every rite were bathed at the springs of Muileann ruadh (Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh) without being asked which rite they kept (19 an t-Sultain 136 BDE). The Age of Sundering added two rites that belong to no single order. One is the Mourning Custom for the departed, "not quite grief and not quite celebration" (1 an Lùnastal 15 DE). The other is the empty-harbour rite on Cidhe an Diosail at Seann Skell (25 an t-Samhain 22 DE). The harbour saying at that rite is in no order of worship:

Dh'fhalbh iad, agus cha do dh'fhalbh iad. They went, and they did not go.

III. The Gods

The gods of the Old Faith are na Dè, and their people are the Tuath Dè, the people of the gods. The tellings of Rodos are the oldest that hold them. The Ròdaich say the gods were on the island before the people were, as the people were on it before anyone came: bha sinn ann. The priests of the Old Faith are the draoidhean, the druids; its poets are the filidhean and its judges the britheamhan. Most of the gods have no house of their own. The orders each serve one god or one pair above the rest, and honour the others at the feasts and in need.

An Dagda, the Good God, is the father of the gods, with his cauldron that no company leaves hungry, his club that kills with one end and wakes with the other, and his harp that calls the seasons in order. He is first among the gods on the map and in every order, and he has no order and no temple of his own. Every house of the Old Faith fills a cauldron for him at the four feasts.

Brìde is the goddess of the hearth-fire, of poetry, of healing and of smithcraft. The first flame bound at Dùn ìseal (23 an t-Sultain 2998 BDE) is hers, and the Keepers from Beathag Bhàn on (28 an t-Ògmhios 2995 BDE) kept it in her name. Her order, Òrd Bhrìde, keeps the flame still, and every hearth on the island is swept and relit on her feast.

Crom Cruaich, the bent one of the mound, is the god of the vein. The black vein that bled colour (20 am Faoilleach 12,923 BDE) is his, and so is the slab over it (19 am Màrt 12,773 BDE). He gives, and his price is measured: the handful, the cup and the Small-Burning Law (13 an Lùnastal 2857 BDE) are the measure. The tellings of Magh Slèacht, where his stone stood covered in gold among twelve stones, say that his due there was the firstlings of every kind, paid at Samhain; the Law holds that due to a handful. His oldest byname is Dòrsair, Uilebheist nan Geataichean, the Monster of the Gates, who stands at the door between the mountain and those who take from it. He is honoured by Òrd Bhrìde at the southern Seann Skell and at the last open face of the Sloc Mòr.

Fionntan mac Bòchra is the oldest of men, who outlived the Flood and lived through the long ages as a salmon, an eagle and a hawk, and remembers everything. His fellow in memory is the Hawk of Acaill, the grey hawk of time, as old as he is, which took one of his eyes when he swam as a salmon; the two have told each other the ages. The Hawk order takes its name from that hawk and keeps them both, and on the north coast it calls the hawk Mòd. The oldest hawk on the island, over a door at Àth mhòr (13 an Dùbhlachd 5748 BDE), is read as the Hawk of Acaill.

Flidais is the lady of the deer and the wild. The white stag first told of at the edge of Coille Naomh Muileann chiar (11 am Màrt 9392 BDE), the wood marked sacred before any order claimed it (21 an Giblean 9504 BDE), is hers in the tellings of the later ages, though the oldest tellings give it no god. The druid schools keep the wood in her name.

Macha is the goddess of sovereignty, of kingship and of horses. The tellings give her the race she ran against a king's horses when she was great with child: she won it, bore twins at the finish, and laid on the men who made her run the pangs of a woman in labour in their hour of need, and Eamhain Mhacha is named for her twins. The grey of the two horses that drew Cù Chulainn's chariot bears her name, Liath Macha, the Grey of Macha, and his yoke-fellow is Dubh Sainglenn, the black. The two were foaled on the night the hero was born, and the tellings also have them come up out of a grey pool in the mountains. Before his last battle the grey wept tears of blood, and when the hero fell the grey fought over him while the black ran on. Her order keeps the pair as its sign. Her wood is Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag, and her order makes the kings of Rodos: King Aonghas was the first king buried by her rite (31 an Dùbhlachd 445 DE), and Niall was crowned by it at Cathair dhearg (19 an t-Ògmhios 1932 DE).

Lia Fàil, the stone that cries out under the rightful king, which the Tuath Dè brought out of the north of the world and set up at Teamhair, is honoured as a power in its own right by the order of the Stone. The order holds that the Stone is one and its stones are many. Its first stone stood at the gate of Caol leathan (12 am Faoilleach 1990 BDE), and its second was dragged from the mountain to Inis thais (3 an Dùbhlachd 782 BDE). Some read the name of the oldest king-list, Rìghrean na Cloiche, the kings of the stone (9 an Lùnastal 7600 BDE), as the kings of this stone. The list itself does not say.

Manannan mac Lir is the lord of the sea, and the sea round Rodos is his, Muir Mhanannain. His mist hides the Otherworld, and the Ròdaich tell that the fleet of the Sundering sailed into it (19 an Giblean 1 DE). Until the Crossing the same mist hid Rodos from every ship beyond it. His Cup of Truth breaks in three when three lies are spoken over it and is made whole again by three truths. His order keeps the western coast, and its first seat is the western Seann Skell (1 an t-Sultain 615 DE).

Lugh Làmhfhada, Lugh of the long arm, is the master of every craft. Lùnastal is his feast, which he made in memory of his foster-mother Tailtiu: markets open, contests are held and oaths are taken before witnesses on it, and Cathal was crowned on the feast itself (1 an Lùnastal 2002 DE).

Goibhniu is the smith of the gods. The smiths of the old vein country, where the forges of Muileann chrom, Muileann dhearg and Muileann dhomhain now make arms, swear by him. No smith on Rodos could place the nails of the timber that came ashore at Ceann mhòr from beyond Manannan's mist (22 an Cèitean 1755 DE).

Dian Cècht is the healer of the gods, who made Nuadha's hand of silver. The springs of Muileann ruadh, where the sick of every rite are bathed (19 an t-Sultain 136 BDE), are his.

The Morrìgan is the goddess of war and the crows. The battlefields are hers, among them the ford of Àth shean, where the custody-book counts three hundred dead (22 an Gearran 515 DE).

Ogma is the god of letters and of eloquence. The first Ròdaich letters, the stag-letters made from the cutters' tally-notches (15 am Màrt 2085 BDE), are the ogham, which the druids call his gift.

Nuadha is the first king of the gods, who lost his hand in battle and ruled again with the hand of silver that Dian Cècht made him. Ròdais still calls an artificial limb ball-airgid, silver-limb, after him.

Danu is the mother of the gods, from whom the Tuath Dè are named. She has no house, and the tellings give her the rivers.

Donn is the lord of the dead. His house, Taigh Dhuinn, is a rock in the sea to the south-west, and the dead go to it. The Old Faith names him at Samhain and at every burial.

IV. The Four Feasts and the Otherworld

The feasts. Four feasts divide the year into quarters (Appendix D). They are older than any order now on the island, and all three faiths keep them in some form, each for its own reasons.

  • Samhain, 1 an t-Samhain, is summer's end, when the Otherworld stands open and the dead are nearest. The Old Faith names Donn and the dead of the year. In the Holy Age the Hall filled the baskets of the Small-Burning Law at Samhain and the galleries closed.
  • Là Fhèill Brìde, or Imbolc, 1 an Gearran, is Brìde's feast. Hearths are swept and relit, and Òrd Bhrìde lights its first lamp of the year from the altar-flame.
  • Bealltainn, 1 an Cèitean, is summer's beginning, the feast of the bright fire, when the cattle go up to the high pastures between two fires. The first sentence under the Small-Burning Law fell on Bealltainn itself (1 an Cèitean 2854 BDE).
  • Lùnastal, 1 an Lùnastal, is Lugh's feast of first-fruits and gathering.

The Old Spirits keep the same four days at the hearth and at the mounds, and the Church keeps them as saints' days and the feasts of the Church's year.

The Otherworld. The Old Faith holds that the Otherworld lies west over the sea, behind Manannan's mist. Its tellings give it two names: Tìr nan Òg, the land of the young, where no one ages, and Magh Meall, the plain of delight. On the way to it, on its rock in the south-western sea, stands Taigh Dhuinn, the house of Donn, where the dead gather. The fleet of the Sundering sailed west into that mist (19 an Giblean 1 DE), and the saying at the empty-harbour rite, they went, and they did not go, is read in the light of it. When the humans came in from the same quarter of sea, old sailors at Cuan shean said so aloud, and the council forbade the remark (9 an Gearran 1781 DE).

The sìth. Nearer home the Otherworld opens in the hills. The sìth, the mounds, belong to the sìthichean, the people of the mounds, whom the Old Spirits honour at the hearth and the Old Faith leaves alone.

V. An Creideamh Sean and Its Orders

The Old Faith is the faith of the gods, and it is kept in its orders. Each order has its houses, its temples, its custodians and its own history, and some have schisms of their own. All of them honour an Dagda and keep the four feasts. They differ on the vein, on the measure and on which god stands nearest to it, and they have differed since the Holy Age. The druids of every order are trained in the schools or in the order's own houses. No single council speaks for the Old Faith as a whole.

Òrd Bhrìde

Òrd Bhrìde, the order of Brìde's flame, is the Hall of the Holy Age and the Obsidian Rite of the chronicle. It keeps Brìde's flame, bound at Dùn ìseal, and Crom's stone, the vein. In its orthodox form it is "organized doctrine within the Old Faith rather than diffuse folk reverence, built around the leyline and the unbroken line of the obsidian-touched" (18 an Giblean 1935 DE). As an organised body it is the youngest of the orders. As a rite it claims to be the oldest. Both are true. Its seat is at the southern Seann Skell (Seann Skell), where its largest house stands (17 an Cèitean 1935 DE). Its saying is the Law's own:

Làn an dùirn, agus gun tuilleadh. The fill of the fist, and no more.

It holds nine burgs, all in the south-east, and four shires: Seann Skell, Tobar dhearg, Muileann naomh and Àth fhionn. It has a third of Muileann dhomhain, and the Old Spirits hold the land on every side. The largest towns are Seann Skell, Tobar dhearg (Tobar dhearg), Muileann naomh (Muileann naomh), Caol ruadh (Caol ruadh) and Àth fhionn (Àth fhionn). The map marks five of its houses as temples: Seann Skell, Tobar dhearg, Muileann naomh, Baile gharbh (Baile gharbh) on the coast road and Caol naomh (Caol naomh), the pilgrims' landing. Muileann naomh was the southernmost house of the Hawk until it took the order of worship of Òrd Bhrìde (29 an Cèitean 1935 DE). The order's history is given in section VIII.

Òrd an t-Seabhaig

What it holds. The Hawk order is the older form of Brìde's rite on the north coast. It teaches that the hawk of the vein is Mòd, the Hawk of Acaill, who is as old as Fionntan mac Bòchra and remembers the ages with him, and who must be fed the measured handful and no more, "since a hawk overfed will not hunt and a hawk starved will turn on the hand" (20 an Giblean 190 DE). Too much and too little both ruin, and the measure lies between them. The Hawk holds that the measure belongs to the hawk and not to any custodian.

Rites and sayings. Each household feeds its hawk before it eats, and the handful is burned at dawn with the hawk on the wrist. The fowlers who began the rite gave its first saying (30 an Dùbhlachd 1000 BDE):

Is acras an lasair. The flame is a hunger.

Gormshuil's sayings were written down after her death as Leabhar an t-Seabhaig, the Book of the Hawk. The copyist marked every saying he had not heard from her own mouth, and those outnumbered the rest (5 an t-Ògmhios 212 DE). The saying most often cut over hawk-house doors is:

Cha shealg seabhag sàthach. A sated hawk will not hunt.

Holy places. The oldest hawk carving on the island is over a door at Àth mhòr (13 an Dùbhlachd 5748 BDE), and it is older than any rite. The rite itself began at the Seann Skell of the northern coast (Seann Skell). The first house of the order is at Cnoc bheag (Cnoc bheag).

History. The dawn-hawk spread along the north coast in the Holy Age, and as it spread the Keeper wrote that it was no concern of the Hall's (28 am Faoilleach 927 BDE). Later it became the first rite to refuse the Hall's measure-check outright (19 an t-Sultain 159 BDE). The order was formalised, not founded, when Gormshuil nic Artair gathered the old rite at Cnoc bheag into its first house (20 an Giblean 190 DE). A second house followed at Ros gheal (22 am Màrt 200 DE) and a southern one at Muileann naomh (13 an t-Sultain 487 DE), which is now a house of Òrd Bhrìde. The schism came when a council at Cnoc bheag split over whether Mòd's measure could ever be raised (20 an t-Ògmhios 850 DE). Those who called it fixed kept the name of the Hungry Hawk. The Fed Hawk were turned out to the northern Seann Skell (23 an Giblean 870 DE), and their petition to raise the handful by a quarter was the first recorded request to alter the Small-Burning Law (25 an Lùnastal 880 DE). It was refused, and the record does not follow the Fed Hawk as a separate house after that.

Under the humans the Hawk resisted before any organised resistance existed. Murchadh Seabhag preached that Mòd starves those who eat faster than the land can feed them (6 an t-Sultain 1801 DE), and his sermon was the first Ròdaich text the Company's agents were told to confiscate. When hawk-priests were barred from the camps (12 an t-Sultain 1817 DE), the crews carried the sermons in themselves (10 an Cèitean 1855 DE). Ìomhar Seabhag's shrines served as meeting houses for the Lamp-Watch (24 an Giblean 1919 DE), and when the war came he called it Mòd's own hunger turned back on those who fed it (5 an t-Ògmhios 1929 DE). In the New Age the Hawk houses refused the written order of worship of Òrd Bhrìde (23 an Cèitean 1935 DE); only the far southern house at Muileann naomh took it (29 an Cèitean 1935 DE). The others named their own custodian at Inis ìseal (26 an Cèitean 1964 DE). They wrote out their order, which until then had been spoken and never written, and they keep the copy locked away (23 an t-Samhain 1964 DE). They accepted a place under the high custodian only on condition that they kept that order (13 an Dùbhlachd 1976 DE). The quarrel with Òrd Bhrìde has quietened, but it has not ended.

Where it is held now. Fourteen burgs, all Ròdaich, along the north-central coast and up the Abhainn ìseal. It holds Inis bhàn and Ros gheal. It is the largest order, though short of half the land, in Cnoc bheag, where Manannan's order and Macha's hold the rest, and in the northern Seann Skell, which it shares with the Old Spirits and Manannan's order. It also has a quarter of the northern Doire fhionn. Cnoc bheag is the largest, and its Hawk house is the richest house of any order outside the capital (14 an Dàmhair 1975 DE). After it come Inis bhàn (Inis bhàn), Ros gheal (Ros gheal), the northern Seann Skell and Ros leathan (Ros leathan). The map marks eight of its houses as temples: Cnoc bheag, Inis bhàn, Ros gheal and the northern Seann Skell; Àth shean on the northern march (Àth shean); the Hawk mill of Muileann uaine (Muileann uaine) and its field village Achadh fhada (Achadh fhada); and Inis ìseal (Inis ìseal), where the Hawk's own custodian sits.

Scoiltean nan Draoidhean

What it holds. The druid schools are the reasoning order of the Old Faith, and they call themselves by their oldest name, Feallsanachd an Fhèidh, the Philosophy of the Deer. They are schools more than a church. They formed around one question, why the vein answers some hands and not others (10 an Dàmhair 2896 BDE): "the first attempt within the Old Faith to reason about the obsidian rather than simply revere it." They do not deny that the vein is holy. They ask what the holiness does. Their patron is Flidais, lady of the deer and the wild, whose white stag walks in their sacred wood. None of the schools' records in the library show the stag, Camaran, being worshipped. His name first appears "in texts much younger than these events" (7 an Dùbhlachd 2881 BDE). The schools are counted among the orders of the Old Faith, and they have not objected.

Rites and sayings. Their one public observance is the yearly walking of the bounds of Flidais's wood (11 an t-Iuchar 440 DE). Everything else they do is argument. Their oldest question, as the masters put it to beginners, is:

Carson an làmh seo? Why this hand?

A student who thinks he has solved it is given Aonghas mac Coinnich's answer (19 an t-Ògmhios 1828 DE):

Chan e sin a' cheist. That is not the question.

Holy places. Coille Naomh Muileann chiar (Coille Naomh Muileann chiar), "marked sacred, long before any order of the Old Faith claims it formally" (21 an Giblean 9504 BDE), where the white stag was first seen (11 am Màrt 9392 BDE). The wood lies outside the schools' own country, among Old Spirits towns in the shire of Baile chaol, and the people of Cnoc uaine (Cnoc uaine) and Àth dhearg (Àth dhearg) on its edge, who keep the ancestors, share its keeping. Dùn thais (Dùn thais) has the first stone temple of the stag's people (21 am Màrt 110 BDE). Caol shean (Caol shean) is the schools' house in the New Age.

Where it is held now. 133 burgs, all Ròdaich, in the north-east and the eastern hills; the east coast itself belongs to the Old Spirits. The schools stand first in twenty-three shires, a block running from Tobar ghorm and Àth mhòr in the north through Caol bheag, Baile gharbh and Dùn thais to Caol shean, Muileann chiar and Muileann dhearg in the hills, and west to Baile Mòr dhomhain in the middle of the island. They share ten more, most of them with the Old Spirits along the line where the two faiths meet, and they have nearly half of Cnoc dhubh, Dùn ìseal and Cnoc gheal. The largest towns are Caol bheag (Caol bheag), Baile gharbh (Baile gharbh), Dùn thais, Caol shean and Caol gharbh (Caol gharbh). The map marks sixteen of the schools' houses as temples, though the schools call them halls: among them Dùn thais, Caol shean, Caol bheag, Ros fhionn (Ros fhionn) and the church villages whose chapels served the silver-miners and the old bridge. Muileann chaol (Muileann chaol), the library town, is a school town. The schools' history is given in section IX.

Òrd Mhacha

What it holds. Macha's order holds that "light and dark are two powers in balance, and the vein belongs to both" (31 an Dùbhlachd 402 DE). The wood-watchers held that their black beast has two natures, one that keeps and one that devours, and that so has the vein (13 am Faoilleach 147 BDE); the order tells it of the two horses that drew one chariot, the black Dubh Sainglenn and the grey Liath Macha. It is the order of the capital and the court, and the kings of Rodos are made by its rite. Its oldest saying is the wood-watchers':

Tha dà nàdar aig a' bhèist, agus aig an fhèith. The beast has two natures, and so has the vein.

Its own saying is of the pair:

Dà each, aon chuing. Two horses, one yoke.

Rites and holy places. Its priests read omens for rulers and bury by their own rite. King Aonghas mac Uisdein was the first king buried that way (31 an Dùbhlachd 445 DE). Its floors are laid in black and white, and the floor of its great house at Cathair mhòr (Cathair mhòr) took eleven years (14 am Màrt 1420 DE). Its sacred wood is Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag (Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag), near the lesser Cnoc bheag south of the capital (Cnoc bheag). That town is not the Hawk river port of the same name.

History. The order began as a watch. A small company settled at the edge of a wood no one had ever cleared and watched for a black horned beast that walked in it (15 an t-Samhain 1430 BDE), the beast the order takes for a sign of Dubh Sainglenn, the black horse. Its quarrel with the stag's people over both sacred woods became the holy-wood dispute, "settled by dividing custody rather than choosing a winner" (10 an Gearran 1410 BDE). Anna Ruadh took a wood-watcher into her household at Cathair dhearg to read the omens (23 an t-Iuchar 177 BDE). Cathair dhomhain refused one, and the rivalry between the two towns took a religious turn "it never loses" (24 an t-Ògmhios 173 BDE). Cathair dhomhain is a town of Macha's order now, with its own temple. The order was formalised when King Aonghas took up the wood-watchers' rite of Macha (31 an Dùbhlachd 402 DE). By royal grant its priests then took sole custody of the western wood, and the other claimants withdrew for reasons the record does not give (14 am Faoilleach 432 DE).

Under the humans it split over the Residency's coin. The priests at Cathair dhearg blessed it (24 an Gearran 1864 DE). Those who refused went to the sacred forest, where they received custodians who had lost their seats (25 am Màrt 1866 DE). Sixty years later the capital's temple sheltered the council that Strake had locked out (26 an Gearran 1926 DE). In the forest the dissenters sat with custodians and the Lamp-Watch when the council of the mining regions was formed (20 an Lùnastal 1927 DE). In the restored kingdom the house at Cathair dhearg got back the keeping of the regalia and refused Òrd Bhrìde a share of it (26 an Gearran 1936 DE).

Where it is held now. 103 burgs, all Ròdaich, across the middle and south of the island. It stands first in twenty-nine shires in one block, from the capital's own shire (Cathair dhearg) and its neighbours in the middle of the island south to Ros dhomhain, Cathair fhada and Doire fhiadhaich, and east to Cathair mhòr and Seann Chwen. Manannan's order holds more than a third of Cathair dhomhain, the shire of the capital's old rival, and in Baile ghlas the Stone holds most of the land, though the harbour town is Macha's. The largest towns are Ros dhomhain (Ros dhomhain), Cathair mhòr, Àth shean (Àth shean), Seann Chwen (Seann Chwen) and Baile ghlas (Baile ghlas). The map marks seventeen of its temples. Five are the great houses of Cathair mhòr, Cathair dhomhain (Cathair dhomhain), Cathair dhearg (Cathair dhearg), Ceann leathan (Ceann leathan) and Cuan uaine (Cuan uaine); the others are the priests' towns, such as Cathair naomh (Cathair naomh) and Cnoc bhàn (Cnoc bhàn), where acolytes are trained for the capital's temples, and the chapels along the roads to the capital. Cnoc naomh, whose people once kept the old reverence "with no hawk, wolf, sting or stag in it" (16 an t-Ògmhios 73 BDE), is a town of Macha's order on the map.

Òrd na Cloiche

What it holds. The order of the Stone holds that the Stone watches the whole island as a guard watches a road, and will cry out under the rightful king (21 an Lùnastal 156 BDE). The Stone is Lia Fàil, and its sworn guards are the Fianna, "who keep the island as a wolf keeps its range" (28 am Màrt 370 DE). The Stone's plain name is Clach, the common word for stone. The first stone was a white stone carved as a wolf at the gate of Caol leathan, on which road-guards swore their watch, and the annals say that "later ages will read more into the stone than they did" (12 am Faoilleach 1990 BDE). The tales of Fionn and his Fianna are the order's own. The record does not show the Stone claiming the vein. When Òrd Bhrìde was formalised, the houses of the Stone sent no witnesses, only "a letter saying they wish it well" (2 an Gearran 1936 DE).

Rites and sayings. Oaths are taken before the Stone. The houses of the Stone nurse the sick. At Inis chrom the Fianna died doing it, "and the town becomes the Stone's for good" (3 an t-Sultain 585 DE). Its saying comes from the road-guards:

Mar a ghleidheas am freiceadan an rathad, gleidhidh Clach an t-eilean. As the guard keeps the road, Clach keeps the island.

Holy places. Caol leathan (Caol leathan), whose house of the Stone is the largest of the order and rings a bell for the hours (7 an Cèitean 1950 DE); Inis thais (Inis thais), where a second stone of white quartz was dragged from the mountain (3 an Dùbhlachd 782 BDE) and the first temple to Lia Fàil by name was built (16 an Dùbhlachd 380 DE); and Baile gheal (Baile gheal).

History. The wolf-sworn were soldiers before they were an order. The order was formalised when Dòmhnall mac Ailein, a net-maker of Inis thais, preached that their stone was Lia Fàil and its guards the Fianna (28 am Màrt 370 DE). Its schism was over the dead. Those who would not pray to the Stone for the dead kept the temple at Inis thais, and those who would built a house at Baile gheal (25 an Dùbhlachd 1350 DE, 8 an Lùnastal 1360 DE). The record does not say the two houses have been reconciled. In the New Age the houses of the Stone have acted as banks as well as churches. They issued chits on house paper when coin ran short (3 am Màrt 1935 DE) and lent the money for Doire shean's harbour (24 an t-Ògmhios 1959 DE). They also published a count of their own people that matched the kingdom's to within a hundred (28 an Lùnastal 1994 DE).

Where it is held now. 21 burgs, all Ròdaich, in the south-west. It holds six shires outright, Doire shean, Inis chrom, Baile ghorm, Caol fhiadhaich, Cnoc àrsaidh and Baile gheal, and most of Caol leathan and Baile ghlas. In Inis thais, the shire of its chief shrine, Manannan's order holds three-fifths of the land. The Stone also has a share of Seann Dunn, Baile chiar and Seann Warr, where Seann Warr is a town of the Stone in Manannan's country. The largest are Doire shean (Doire shean), Inis thais, Inis chrom (Inis chrom), Baile ghorm (Baile ghorm) and Seann Warr (Seann Warr). The map marks temples in eight of its towns: Inis thais, still the chief shrine of the order, Caol leathan, Baile gheal, Doire shean, Inis chrom, Caol fhiadhaich (Caol fhiadhaich), Baile Mòr fhionn (Baile Mòr fhionn) and Cnoc àrsaidh (Cnoc àrsaidh), which holds the oldest shrines of the Stone.

Òrd Mhanannain

What it holds. Manannan's order holds that the lord of the sea sees the liar wherever he is, and that his Cup of Truth breaks at the lies spoken over it and is whole again at the truth; the yellow scorpion is the old sign on the Cup, and the order's badge. It was the first teaching on the island to call itself the only true one (3 an Dùbhlachd 153 BDE). Its central teaching is about the sea: Manannan shut the western sea behind the fleet of the Sundering with his mist, which hid the island from every ship beyond it, and it must not be tried again (1 an t-Sultain 615 DE). The order keeps the sea shut by prayer. Its priests recorded the mist thinning in the last years of the Age of Sundering (27 an Dàmhair 1774 DE), and it lifted in the winter the humans' ships came out of it (13 am Faoilleach 1780 DE). They held the Crossing to be the price of a prayer grown slack. When no ship came from the west after the Severance, and the council's ship found only open water, they said the lord of the sea had shut the sea again (11 an t-Ògmhios 1932 DE).

Rites and sayings. Oaths of trade were first sworn on a scorpion's sting kept in a box (19 an t-Samhain 2120 BDE). Since the sting-oath became a creed they have been sworn over a cup marked with the scorpion, Manannan's Cup of Truth. No boat of the faithful may go out of sight of the headlands, and on the west coast steering by the stars was lost entirely (27 an t-Samhain 655 DE). At the harbour mouth the priests pray (13 an Giblean 1551 DE):

A Mhanannain, cùm a' mhuir dùinte. Manannan, keep the sea shut.

Since 1675 DE that prayer has been said on the day of the empty-harbour rite. So on one quay, on one day, some mourn the departed and some pray that no one follows them. Neither side is pleased.

Holy places. Seann Skell in the west (Seann Skell), where the teaching was declared; Baile àrsaidh (Baile àrsaidh), where the sting-oath began; and Seann Vell (Seann Vell), which has the first scorpion carved in yellow stone for worship (4 an t-Samhain 150 BDE).

History. The sting-oath went from Baile àrsaidh up the coast to Ros bheag (1 am Faoilleach 854 BDE) and became a creed at Seann Skell. The order was formalised when Mànas mac Ruairidh named its power Manannan mac Lir (1 an t-Sultain 615 DE). A worked timber longer than any tree on the island, held with nails no smith on Rodos could place, came ashore at Ceann mhòr. It was carried to Seann Skell, shown to Manannan's priests, and burned (22 an Cèitean 1755 DE). That was twenty-five years before the humans came. The first human fishing families on the north-west coast learned the order's harbour prayers at Ceann mhòr (14 am Màrt 1830 DE), and its priests there say the Grey Night grew from them (section VII). In the New Age the house at Seann Bhral turned away the Tuathaich of the north who came for its feast of the sea, and the northerners made a feast of their own at Cnoc ghorm (2 an t-Sultain 1954 DE, 11 an Gearran 1955 DE); that quarrel belongs to the Church's history. On the eve of the Long War Manannan's house at Seann Skell refused to bless the enforcers' depot (23 am Faoilleach 2018 DE). In the present year its priests said the prayer to keep the sea shut on the day the first dubhan was shipped off the island under Dubhan's charter (7 an t-Sultain 2026 DE).

Where it is held now. 35 burgs, all Ròdaich, on the west coast. Its seat, the western Seann Skell, is the largest town on Rodos. It stands first in eight shires in the west, from Muileann naomh and Baile fhiadhaich south through Seann Skell, Ros bheag and Baile àrsaidh to Cuan shean and the Stone's holy shire of Inis thais, with Seann Warr inland. It also has more than a third of Cnoc bheag and Cathair dhomhain in the middle of the island and a quarter of Caol leathan. The map marks eleven of its houses as temples; besides the holy places above they include Ros bheag (Ros bheag) and the western Seann Bhral (Seann Bhral). After Seann Skell its largest towns are Cuan shean (Cuan shean) and Baile fhiadhaich (Baile fhiadhaich).

VI. Na Seann Spioradan

What it holds. The Old Spirits keep the reverence of the hearths as it was before the Hall: "reverence for ancestors, for the vein, for the weather that decides the mining season" (17 am Faoilleach 2978 BDE). The chronicle calls it the island's oldest continuous tradition. It keeps no priests, no order of worship and no council. Its powers, as the map gives them, are na Sìthichean, the people of the mounds, and its tellings speak of the ancestors, the sìth of the hills and mounds, and the spirits of weather, wells and streams, not of any one power over them. The gods belong to the Old Faith. When the hearths first called the powers of the mounds by that name, or who first did, is not known.

Rites and sayings. The living heads of families name their ancestors aloud. The names of the dead are cut on wooden posts, which are recut each generation as the old ones rot (7 an Dàmhair 140 DE). The faith keeps the walk to Allt an Àigh as its own, and after the Keepers declined the stream it took Muireach Liath's ruling for its saying:

Buinidh an t-allt do na sinnsearan agus don t-sìde. The stream belongs to the ancestors and to the weather.

It blesses what comes from the vein and nothing else. When copper was found behind Àth fhiadhaich, the town's Seann Spioradan house held no blessing for it (28 an Lùnastal 1989 DE).

Holy places. Dùn ìseal (Dùn ìseal) and its spirit-house; Seann Dunn (Seann Dunn), where the east-coast houses built a common hall for naming the ancestors of forty families (28 an Dàmhair 1951 DE); Allt an Àigh, which lies in the schools' country behind Caol shean, with the walkers' hall at Achadh gharbh, a school village (11 an Gearran 1940 DE); and Làrach an Teampaill, which at the houses' request was entered by the library as "measured and let be" (7 an Dàmhair 1960 DE).

History. By the end of the Holy Age the Hall's list counted the old folk as "a company of its own" (16 an t-Ògmhios 73 BDE). In the Age of Sundering they built a guest-house at the stream, and its book records pilgrims from every shire (10 an t-Samhain 1220 DE). Under the humans this was the first faith to refuse the Company's ore on principle. The households of Achadh naomh burned peat, and their elders taught "that ore burned for wages is ore burned without the ancestors' leave" (16 am Màrt 1802 DE). In the Long Drought the Administration's watchman at Allt an Àigh, posted to charge pilgrims for the water, was recalled after one season (1 an Cèitean 1887 DE). In the New Age the custodians of Òrd Bhrìde discouraged the walk and did not forbid it (8 an t-Iuchar 1939 DE).

Where it is held now. 126 burgs, all Ròdaich, and more land than any single order of the Old Faith. It holds thirty-four shires: the whole south-east, from Seann Bhral and Achadh mhòr to Baile ghorm and Ceann mhin; the east coast from Ceann leathan north through Seann Tarr and Achadh shean to Baile ruadh; the hills round Dùn ìseal, where the schools hold nearly as much (Dùn ìseal, Cnoc dhubh, Cnoc dhìreach); and a band of the north coast between the Hawk and the schools, from Baile Mòr mhòr and Seann Bhrenn to Seann Toll and Caol ìseal. It has a share of eleven more, among them Muileann bheag, which it divides almost evenly with the schools. The largest are Seann Bhral (Seann Bhral), Achadh mhòr (Achadh mhòr), Baile Mòr mhòr (Baile Mòr mhòr), Muileann bhàn (Muileann bhàn), Achadh naomh (Achadh naomh) and Dùn dhearg (Dùn dhearg). The map marks temples in twenty-four of its towns, more than for any single order. The chief are Dùn ìseal, Seann Dunn, Seann Tarr (Seann Tarr), whose shrine draws the whole north-east at the great feasts, and Cathair naomh (Cathair naomh), whose elders the shrine-keepers of the north answer to. The rest are the shrines of wells, springs, fords and holy woods, and the houses of the largest towns.

VII. An Eaglais

What it holds. The Church is the faith the humans brought over the sea at the Crossing (5 am Faoilleach 1780 DE). It holds that there is one God, Dia, and that Crìosd, Christ, is his son. Its book is am Bìoball, the Bible. Its clergy are sagairt and ministearan, priests and ministers, under easbaigean, bishops; it has had manaich, monks, and it keeps the days of its naoimh, its saints. On Rodos it is the faith of the human labourers and the Residency in the Age of Strangers, and of the Tuathaich, their descendants, since.

The Mission. The Church came to the Ròdaich as the Mission. It raised a timber chapel on the quay at Ros dhomhain, the first church on the island (30 an Dùbhlachd 1792 DE), and ran a school there that taught Ròdach children in the humans' tongue (9 an Cèitean 1830 DE). Samuel Wren made his grammar of Ròdais for its use (21 an Lùnastal 1791 DE), and the hawk-priests of Cnoc bheag asked it for a copy (4 an t-Iuchar 1792 DE). The Mission kept lists of the dead in the camps, and the custodians wrote their own count in its margins (11 an Dàmhair 1818 DE). Samuel Wren asked the masters of the schools why the vein should be holy, and they asked him why his fuel should be burned (3 an Dùbhlachd 1797 DE). The Mission's house in the north was at Cathair gheal (Cathair gheal).

The churches of the north. Most Tuathaich towns keep the Church their forebears brought at the Crossing, in the line the Mission left, while the Ròdaich of the west coast beside them keep Manannan's order (30 am Màrt 1938 DE). How the churches of the Mission's line came to outnumber the older congregations of the north coast the record does not say. Their largest house is at Cnoc ghorm (Cnoc ghorm). It opened a school for its priests that taught in the humans' tongue and read the Bible in the Ròdais text its preachers use on the west coast, the only place in the north where both are taught (29 an Giblean 1939 DE). In the early New Age the northerners came south to the feast of the sea at Seann Bhral, as their forebears had learned to from the Ròdaich harbours. The house of Manannan's order there turned them away, and its keeper said "the sea is the same and the house is not" (2 an t-Sultain 1954 DE). They kept the feast at the church at Cnoc ghorm instead, as a blessing of the boats, and within a generation it was the larger of the two (11 an Gearran 1955 DE).

These churches hold 51 burgs. They hold seven shires in the north-west, Cnoc ghorm, Ceann mhòr, Cnoc thais, Muileann àrsaidh and Baile ìseal, and on the north coast Caol mhòr and Àth àrsaidh. The map marks eight of their houses as temples, among them Cnoc ghorm and Cathair gheal. Their largest towns are Caol mhòr (Caol mhòr), the Moot's town, Ceann mhòr (Ceann mhòr) and Cnoc ghorm.

Eaglais nan Tuathach and the voyage of Naomh Breandan. The old congregations of the north coast keep the Church in their own way (13 an Gearran 1938 DE), "including, quietly, the telling of the First Canoe, the voyage of Naomh Breandan to the Isle of the Blessed, which the Ròdaich priesthood still calls superstition." Beyond that the record holds almost nothing, and what it has comes from outside them. Few Tuathaich would speak to the chronicle clerks (25 am Màrt 1948 DE). The north's books stayed in private keeping (3 an Lùnastal 1996 DE). The request to archive Tuathaich oral history at the library was tabled rather than rejected, and it is still tabled (15 an Gearran 2016 DE). This appendix does not know their rites or their sayings, or how far they differ from the churches of the Mission's line. Of their holy places it knows three, the houses the map marks as temples: Doire ghlas, called the heart of the Church in the north, whose keepers are said to hold the First Canoe fragment and have not let the library copy it; Muileann leathan; and Cill chaol (Cill chaol), a Ròdaich chapel village whose chapel the Tuathaich made a church, leaving the old carvings on its doorposts beside their own.

The only one of their tellings known outside the north is the fragment its tellers set in the Ancient Age: "a named steersman, a first crossing" (9 an t-Samhain 10,073 BDE). The steersman is Naomh Breandan, Saint Brendan the Navigator of the humans' Church, who sailed west from an Tìr Thall in a boat of hides to the Isle of the Blessed, and the north's tellers say that isle was Rodos. His name is in no Ròdaich record. His voyage has a mist at sea and an island of the blessed in the west, as the Ròdaich tellings of Manannan's sea have, and the Library notes the likeness and draws nothing from it. The record does not say how families whose forebears came over the water in 1780 DE came to keep a telling of a crossing set so long before the Sundering. This appendix leaves it where its tellers set it, notes that the north still keeps it in the present day (21 an Dùbhlachd 2026 DE), and does not resolve it.

The old congregations hold twelve burgs, all Tuathaich, along the north. They hold three shires, Doire ghlas, Muileann leathan and the island shire of Eilean dhìreach off the coast to the west of them, and have a share of six more, among them the land west of Baile chrom on the north-western cape, a quarter of Àth àrsaidh and a sixth of Inis mhin and Caol mhòr. The largest are Doire ghlas (Doire ghlas), Muileann leathan (Muileann leathan), Inis mhin (Inis mhin) and Baile ghlas in Siorrachd Àth àrsaidh (Baile ghlas).

Rùn-dìomhair na h-Oidhche Glaise. Of the Mystery of the Grey Night the record knows the name, the goose, one custom and one town. The goose is Sìne, an Gèadh Sìtheil, the Peaceful Goose, the keepers' name for an Gèadh Fiadhaich, the wild goose of the Holy Spirit. The custom is "one night of silence in the year", a vigil, and outsiders are not told which night it is (14 am Màrt 1938 DE). No saying is known.

The vigil first appears in a Mission report that human labourers near Baile chrom were keeping a vigil at night in the fields, praying in silence under the sign of a grey goose, which they called the wild goose of the Spirit (28 an Lùnastal 1912 DE). The Mission called it irregular, a superstition learned from the Ròdaich, and the Ròdaich of Baile chrom disowned it. Manannan's priests at Ceann mhòr said the Mission was half right. The first human fishing families on that coast had settled at Ceann mhòr (14 am Màrt 1830 DE) and learned Manannan's night prayer to keep the sea shut there, and the labourers inland kept it as a Christian vigil, a night of silence under the wild goose of the Spirit instead of a prayer to Manannan. The priests called it Manannan's prayer gone astray and would not have its keepers in their house (21 an Dàmhair 1912 DE). The Church's bishops call the vigil irregular and have not put it out. From the Ancient Age the record keeps a telling of the grey geese that winter on Eilean ghorm and are never hunted there (3 an Lùnastal 9112 BDE). The record does not connect the two, and this appendix does not either. After the Severance the vigil-keeper Hannah Crane held the vigil openly (14 am Màrt 1938 DE). A magistrate fined her, and the vigil moved indoors (15 an t-Ògmhios 1956 DE). The keeper of Taigh-solais Baile chrom (Taigh-solais Baile chrom) reported that the vigil was kept in the lighthouse's shadow (27 an Giblean 1961 DE). In the Long War soldiers searched the town on a night when it was wholly dark and silent, and they found nothing (9 an Dùbhlachd 2020 DE).

The vigil holds one burg, Baile chrom in the far north-west (Baile chrom), and with it the whole of its shire (Baile chrom) and a tenth of Ceann mhòr next door. It is not the Baile chrom in the hills (Baile chrom), and the record takes care to keep the two apart (11 an Gearran 1853 DE).

Where the Church is held now. 64 burgs, every Tuathaich town on the map, and eleven shires, all in the north and north-west. It has a share of five more: a quarter of Seann Skell and of Seann Vell, a sixth of Inis mhin, and smaller parts of Baile fhiadhaich and Muileann naomh. The map marks twelve of its churches as temples.

VIII. Of the Obsidian Rite

The Rite is older than any name for it. Its root is the slab over the crack and the handful in the cup. What the chronicle calls the Obsidian Rite, and the Old Faith calls Òrd Bhrìde, is the part of the old reverence that holds the vein itself to be sacred. The vein is Crom's, and Brìde's flame is lit from what it gives, but the Rite does not hold it to be the sign of a god or the seat of a spirit. It is the holy thing.

The vein as sacred. The Rite holds that the vein bleeds because it is alive in some way the Ròdaich are not asked to understand. What is broken from it must be burned in measure or returned. The vein answers a line of people, and that answering is itself holy. The doctrine of 1935 is "built around the leyline and the unbroken line of the obsidian-touched" (18 an Giblean 1935 DE): the vein under the ground and the blood of those it has answered. Fionnghal nic Artair's defence of the Small-Burning Law, the only one that survives, argued that "the Law was never about the ore but about the people who would become whatever the burning made them" (11 an t-Ògmhios 1801 DE). She wrote it two generations before Aisling was born, and it has been read as prophecy since. She did not claim to be prophesying.

Under the Keepers. In the Holy Age the Rite belonged to the Hall. The Keepers held the cup, took the census of hands (22 an t-Ògmhios 1264 BDE) and sentenced households that burned beyond the measure (1 an Cèitean 2854 BDE). Their roll holds one hundred and forty names (2 an Giblean 60 BDE).

Under the vein-house. Each ship of the Sundering carried one sealed measure of ore and no more (17 an t-Ògmhios 15 BDE). The vein-house above Muileann dhearg kept the custody-book, and in 820 DE the crown and the custody were joined. The Rite's worst hour in that age came in war, not heresy. Raghnall Ruadh, holding the vein-house, refused the handful to every hearth in the shires that stood against him, "and the act turns more people against him than any battle" (24 am Faoilleach 519 DE). The council refused the Fed Hawk's petition and refused Clann Choinnich's request to smelt silver with the ore (31 an Lùnastal 1520 DE), "the first request to burn the ore for work rather than worship."

Under the humans. The Small-Burning Law lapsed without repeal "once it stops being profitable to enforce" (2 an Dùbhlachd 1800 DE). The Rite lived on in shrines at the pit mouths. At Cill dhìreach the crews left the first piece of ore from each new gallery, and the Company allowed it "because it costs a stone a gallery" (19 an t-Sultain 1851 DE). At Cill ghlas the custodians kept the rites at the mouth of the oldest cutting (18 an Dàmhair 1851 DE). They agreed the word fuil-ghuail there (21 an Gearran 1905 DE), and the Rending swallowed that shrine (3 an t-Iuchar 1916 DE).

Formalised. The Rite was formalised on 18 an Giblean 1935 DE. Dòmhnall mac Thormoid was seated at the southern Seann Skell as Àrd-choimheadaiche, and his first charge was a written order of worship: "there had never been one" (17 an Cèitean 1935 DE). The Hawk refused the order and the Stone stood aside. When the council kept the night shift, the custodians "enter a protest and then bless the shafts" (18 an t-Samhain 1940 DE). The Rite has worked that way ever since. It protests how the kingdom uses the vein, and then it blesses it.

The Depletion. The high custodian ruled that dubhan was "not forbidden, since it is not ore, and not blessed, since it is not ore" (25 an t-Samhain 2003 DE). When the beacons were converted (22 an Cèitean 2005 DE), the obsidian flame of Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg was carried to Seann Skell and left to burn out on the altar (19 an t-Iuchar 2005 DE). When the coinage seal lost its obsidian ink, the high custodian protested. The council replied that the kingdom had never said it held the vein sacred (31 an t-Iuchar 2014 DE).

The Rite now. One face of the Sloc Mòr is kept open under the Rite's custody (17 an Cèitean 2025 DE). Twelve hewers work it, the last of their trade (15 an t-Ògmhios 2025 DE). On 6 an Dàmhair 2026 DE they cut the year's altar-ore. It filled four baskets, and the high custodian divided it among the houses by lot.

That is why Òrd Bhrìde holds only nine burgs. Most Ròdaich who hold the vein sacred keep it at the hearth, as the Old Spirits do, or at the local altar, as the Hawk does. The Rite is their orthodoxy in name, and it is their whole practice in only nine towns. It was formalised after the vein had begun to fail. In less than a century it went from an order of worship for the whole island to four baskets of ore.

IX. Of the Schools' Question

Carson an làmh seo?

The druid schools began with one question, asked at Muileann chiar in the Holy Age: why does the vein answer some hands and not others (10 an Dàmhair 2896 BDE)? Some have made much of how close fèidh, deer, sounds to fèith, vein. The schools' own texts do not.

Forbidden and allowed. The Hall shut the galleries to the stag's people "on the ground that a question asked of the vein is a demand made of it" (18 an Cèitean 2874 BDE). They were later let back in on an oath "to ask nothing of the vein aloud" (26 an Gearran 2425 BDE). The Hall called that a reconciliation, and the schools called it a truce. Long after the truce the stag's people made the first Ròdaich letters out of cutters' tally-notches (15 am Màrt 2085 BDE), the letters the schools call ogham, and nearly every later hand on the island descends from them.

Birth or effort. Apprentices kept strike-books, written accounts of every blow (23 am Màrt 1358 BDE). Reading them, Donnchadh mac Iain found that the ore bled brighter for older cutters, whatever house they came from (28 an Gearran 709 BDE). The chronicle records the split that followed: "a breakaway school of druids argues the vein answers effort, not birth — a quiet, centuries-early rehearsal of the argument the Long War will eventually be fought over" (7 an t-Sultain 682 BDE). The breakaway school at Muileann chaol did not write a cutter's parentage in the book at all (9 an Lùnastal 669 BDE). The Keeper Raonaid Dhubh heard both schools and gave no ruling, "saying the vein has not asked the Hall to decide" (4 an t-Samhain 633 BDE).

The years of disputation. At Dùn thais the question was argued by rule (29 an Cèitean 275 DE). Eilidh Dhubh's tracts for the effort-school were read aloud at harvest gatherings across the north-east (23 an t-Ògmhios 445 DE). Then Raghnall mac Chaluim showed that the heads of the custodian houses lived a few years longer than their tenants, and asked whether the vein answers the hand that holds it (29 an t-Samhain 1170 DE). The house was later reopened only on condition that the question of longer lives was not raised (20 an Giblean 1720 DE). His table is nearly seven hundred years older than the first of the immortal generation.

Under the humans. Samuel Wren asked the masters why the vein should be holy. They asked him why his fuel should be burned (3 an Dùbhlachd 1797 DE). Aonghas mac Coinnich asked why the humans cannot see the colour in broken ore, and said it was the wrong question (19 an t-Ògmhios 1828 DE). Tolley closed the hall at Dùn thais (14 an Dùbhlachd 1868 DE). The last public disputation asked whether a question may be forbidden, and the Administration's clerk recorded that it may (30 an Giblean 1869 DE). After that the masters taught under the trees (15 an t-Ògmhios 1869 DE), until the last of them died in 1902 DE.

The revival. The schools reopened in 1975 DE, when their question became "suddenly urgent again as the vein itself starts running short." Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain lectured in the sacred wood (11 an Dùbhlachd 1975 DE), and the schools took a house at Caol shean, where students debated the census note on the obsidian-touched openly (5 an Dùbhlachd 1976 DE). When the Mine Board searched for a second vein, she wrote that "nobody has asked why there is one vein" (13 an Giblean 1980 DE). The Board filed her letter, and the search found nothing (21 an Giblean 1980 DE). The schools' own word for their revival is dubhan-tùsail (22 an Dàmhair 2010 DE).

What the question has come to. In the Holy Age it asked whether the ore bled for birth or for practice. In the Age of Sundering it asked whether the vein lengthened lives. Under the humans it asked why the humans could not see the colour. Since 1905 DE, when the custodians agreed a plain word for what the vein had begun to do to a few children, the answer has had a name but no reason. The masters do not claim that the question caused the Long War, and no one has accused them of it. They would say only that it was asked in the Holy Age and has not been answered since.

Appendix C — Hosts, Wars and Calamities

This appendix gathers from the annals every war and armed struggle the record keeps, the hosts that stand on the map today, and the calamities that have fallen on the island, whether sent by the sea, the ground, the weather or the vein. It adds nothing the annals do not hold. Where the annals disagree with one another the entries are given as they stand. Where the record is sealed, or was never made, this appendix says so and goes no further.

The reader should know how much is missing. The Ancient Age cut its dead on tally stones and did not say what killed them. The Age of Sundering left two histories of its wars, and one was written to praise a king. For the Age of Strangers the custodians' rolls, the Mission's lists and the Residency's letter-books seldom give the same number. The complete record of the Long War is sealed at Leabharlann Muileann chaol until the fifty years run out (14 am Faoilleach 2023 DE).

Part I. The Wars

Before the wars

The oldest act of force the record knows is not a war, and nobody knows who did it. On 29 an Dàmhair 8944 BDE the single gate of Làrach an Dùin-fhaire was blocked with rubble from the inside, by people who left by another way or did not leave. More than a century later the cistern of Làrach an Dùin, which had served four hundred people, was found choked with the bones of whole cattle (4 an Giblean 8832 BDE). Both are works of the Seann-Dhaoine. The record will not guess at what was being fought over there, or by whom.

The first war in either of the oral king-lists is the salt-flats raid. On 9 am Faoilleach 6929 BDE Mòrag Chruaidh, fifth of the Stone Kings, led the hill-folk down to the salt-pans at Baile ghorm and carried the salt away. Seven died on the hill side, and the telling keeps that number. Her successor Iain Dubh went down to repeat the raid and was killed on the shingle (8 an t-Ògmhios 6874 BDE). The list says only that he was brought home. After him the Ancient Age records no war.

The War of the Roads

Cause. In the Holy Age the carriers' road ran from the mountain to the sea, and its tolls went to the rìgh of Dùn dhearg. Lachlann Ciar, head of the leading family of the harbour town of Caol leathan, began to keep the southern tolls for himself and send none of them to Dùn dhearg (14 an Gearran 2008 BDE). Iain Garbh, son of Sìleas Dhonn, took the hall at Dùn dhearg and demanded the western tolls, and Lachlann Ciar sent him back a basket of fish-bones (12 an Cèitean 2005 BDE).

Sides. On one side were Iain Garbh of Dùn dhearg, the road-guards and the lowland levies. On the other were Lachlann Ciar and the men of Caol leathan. The Hall at Dùn ìseal refused to bless either side.

Course. On 13 an Giblean 2000 BDE Iain Garbh marched west and burned the toll-house at Muileann òg, which Lachlann Ciar's people had taken. The annals call this the first war between Ròdaich and Ròdaich. At the ford of Àth fhiadhaich the men of Caol leathan held Iain Garbh's levies for a day before they gave way (21 an Dàmhair 1998 BDE). Forty were dead on the two sides together, and for a long time afterward the carriers called it the ford of the forty. Falling back, Lachlann Ciar's men burned Baile ghlas so that the levies would find no grain there (16 am Faoilleach 1997 BDE). Its people walked to Cathair dhomhain, and many of them never came home. Baile chiar shut its gate against both armies and fed the burned-out people of Baile ghlas through the winter (18 an Dùbhlachd 1996 BDE). Neither side forgave it and neither side attacked it. Iain Garbh then closed Caol leathan from the landward side for a season, but its boats brought in fish and he could not close the harbour. His levies drifted home for the harvest, and the siege ended without an assault (2 an t-Samhain 1994 BDE).

End. The two leaders met under the roof of the waypoint house that would later be called Am Buabhall Fortanach, where by the road-peace neither of them could draw (4 an Dàmhair 1993 BDE). Caol leathan kept half its tolls and sent the other half to Dùn dhearg, and Lachlann Ciar swore to the Law with the Keeper as witness. So the war ended in a house built to feed carriers. Muileann òg was rebuilt as a market town, and its fair is the ancestor of Fèill Muileann òg (5 an t-Iuchar 1334 BDE).

Lesser strife of the Holy Age

The Silver Feud (17 an t-Sultain 1253 BDE) was a closing and not a war. For three seasons no silver left Muileann chiar. The road-guards went unpaid and the eastern tolls went uncollected. The record gives the feud its name while noting that no one was killed in it. At sea, outlaw boats from the eastern islets began raiding the fishing strands. Sliochd Raghnaill armed its boats at Seann Tarr and burned two of them (10 an t-Ògmhios 544 BDE), and the rest were never caught. Late in the age raiders from the north-western waters took a season's dried fish from the north-western strands. The sting-sworn merchants of Ros bheag paid for two armed boats to watch the shore, and the raiders moved north (28 an Gearran 252 BDE).

The War of the Three Claimants

Cause. King Tormod Bàn's two sons were drowned together when a ferry overturned on Abhainn fhionn (18 an t-Ògmhios 495 DE). The king died at Cathair dhearg without naming an heir (8 an t-Sultain 508 DE), and three claims were laid before the houses at once.

Sides. The claimants were Catrìona nic Aonghais of Inis thais, the late king's niece; Dùghall Garbh of Baile Mòr dhomhain, his half-brother; and Raghnall Ruadh, head of Clann Raghnaill and master of the vein-house above Muileann dhearg (21 an Giblean 513 DE). The seven houses divided among the three. Seann Warr, the western port nearest the capital, shut its gates to all three and declared for none (20 an Cèitean 514 DE). It was besieged twice during the war and taken by neither claimant.

Course. Dùghall's host broke Raghnall's at the ford of Àth shean on 22 an Gearran 515 DE. The custody-book counts some three hundred dead, most of them drowned in the ford. Raghnall's men burned Doire mhin and its granary as they fell back (24 an t-Sultain 516 DE), and the villagers spent the winter at Cathair mhòr on the charity of Macha's priests. Catrìona besieged Cathair dhomhain, which had declared for Dùghall, and took it after forty days, when the dead of the siege lines had poisoned its wells (26 an Dùbhlachd 518 DE). She let the garrison go free on their oath. Raghnall, who held the vein-house, then refused the measured handful of ore to every hearth and temple in the shires that stood against him (24 am Faoilleach 519 DE). Hearths that had burned ore for generations went cold. The annals judge that this act turned more people against him than any battle did. Catrìona and Dùghall joined their hosts for the purpose and met Raghnall below Muileann chrom on 14 am Faoilleach 521 DE. Raghnall was killed on the field, and his own custodians opened the vein-house the next day.

End. Catrìona was crowned at Cathair dhearg on 13 am Màrt 523 DE and was known afterward as Catrìona Bhuadhach. The war had lasted about a decade. Her first great law bound the custodians themselves: no claimant, house or king could withhold the handful from a lawful hearth (12 an Gearran 526 DE). Seann Warr's neutral gates were later honoured by the crown (11 an Giblean 555 DE). Seònaid nic Coinnich's Book of the Three Claimants (8 an t-Ògmhios 585 DE) is the oldest history on Rodos written as one narrative rather than as a list of entries.

The sea-thieves of the north-west

Boats working out of the small islands off the north-west coast began to take fish and grain from coasting traders (24 am Faoilleach 745 DE). The thieves were Ròdaich, men of the north-west shore, and the harbour rolls give some of their names. A force sent by Queen Eilidh Bhàn landed on Eilean dhubh and burned their boats on the strand (27 an t-Samhain 762 DE). Their leader, Uilleam Ruadh, was taken to Cathair dhearg and hanged.

The Brothers' War, Cogadh nam Bràithrean

Cause. King Ailean mac Raghnaill died at Cathair dhearg leaving two sons by different mothers, Iain Ciar and Alasdair Bàn, and each of them had been told that he was the heir (7 an t-Iuchar 1227 DE).

Sides. The seven houses divided four to three between the brothers.

Course. Alasdair Bàn's men seized Cnoc naomh, and Iain Ciar took it back on 8 an t-Ògmhios 1231 DE. The war is named from that battle. Alasdair's ships burned the waterfront of Ceann mhin, which held for his brother, taking the rope stores and the granary, and the town had to beg its bread from Cathair mhòr (17 an Lùnastal 1233 DE). Iain Ciar defeated Alasdair below Muileann ghlas on 19 an t-Iuchar 1235 DE. Alasdair was taken alive, and his captains were allowed to go home.

End. The brothers made peace at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr, on neutral ground between their lands (12 an t-Sultain 1237 DE). Alasdair gave up his claim and was given the lordship of Seann Chwen for life. Iain Ciar was crowned. Alasdair kept the peace until his death (8 an Dàmhair 1252 DE), and his lordship went back to the crown. Iain Ciar, having seen Ceann mhin beg for bread, ordered every shire seat to keep a year's grain in store against the next war (20 an Giblean 1260 DE). The only surviving account of the war was written by his clerk Pàdraig mac Ruairidh (14 an Lùnastal 1265 DE). It praises the king at every turn, and later readers have found it inconvenient.

The humans' campaigns and the forerunners of war

For most of the Age of Strangers the humans made war only at sea. Raiders stripped a Company brig off the north-west coast (10 an Giblean 1795 DE) and burned an ore ship off the east (20 an Dàmhair 1825 DE). The Company's first armed reply was a gunboat that burned every boat on the shingle of a cove near Ceann leathan (25 an t-Iuchar 1826 DE). Most of them belonged to the town's own fishermen, and the raiders were not found.

On land the Administration kept no standing force until Charles Merriman brought a company of armed constables (24 an Lùnastal 1911 DE). They broke the dockers' strike at Ros dhomhain (1 an Giblean 1913 DE). After the Rending the roll records the first violent clash between the two peoples (17 an t-Ògmhios 1916 DE), placed by its fuller entry at Muileann chrom (13 an Dùbhlachd 1916 DE): a gallery drowned seven when the pumps were stopped to save fuel, the crews stoned the Company's agent, and the constables fired. Four Ròdaich and one constable died. Merriman answered the second petition by tripling the constabulary and fortifying the stores of four mining towns (25 an Gearran 1919 DE). The roadside houses became waypoints for a militia with no name (9 an t-Sultain 1920 DE). The first coordinated stoppage was broken by closing the Company stores (30 an Dùbhlachd 1922 DE). After the confiscation edict (25 an Giblean 1926 DE) the silver guild began buying rifles from the eastern pirates (21 an t-Iuchar 1927 DE), a council for the mining regions met in the sacred forest at Cnoc bheag (20 an Lùnastal 1927 DE), and Strake ordered its arrest (3 am Faoilleach 1928 DE).

The War of the Hills

This history calls it the War of the Hills, after the country where it began. Later rolls call it the Severance war, after the way it ended.

Cause. On 20 an Gearran 1928 DE Ròdaich resistance, coordinated for the first time across several mining regions, passed from grievance to open war. The grievances are those listed above. The one cited most often is the confiscation edict.

Sides. On the Ròdaich side stood the council of custodians and crew-leaders under Eilidh nic Raghnaill, with the crews of the camps, the Lamp-Watch, the silver guild of Muileann chiar and its riflemen, the riflemen of Cnoc leathan (1 an Gearran 1929 DE), the company of the Hawk order's faithful mustered at Seann Skell (8 an t-Ògmhios 1929 DE), and the towns that declared for the council one after another. On the Administration's side stood Commissioner Strake, the constabulary, the Company's guards, and the Company's steamships and coasters. Some towns held apart. The human town of Cathair gheal shut its gates and raised a militia that it sent to neither side (24 an Cèitean 1929 DE). The concession town of Muileann àrsaidh closed its road against both sides for the rest of the war (28 an Cèitean 1929 DE). The Ròdaich city of Ros dhomhain, below the Residency, neither joined the rising nor opposed it until late in the war.

Course. The war opened in the hills. Crews under Mòrag nic Iain rushed the store at Muileann chrom at first light, and its eleven constables surrendered without a shot (28 an Gearran 1928 DE). Crews sank two barges across the mouth of the ore quay at Ceann fhada (24 an Cèitean 1928 DE). At Baile thais the constables held their walled pithead for eleven days and surrendered on the twelfth, when their water ran out, and Eilidh nic Raghnaill sent them to the coast unharmed (1 an t-Ògmhios 1928 DE). The northern pits rose (30 an t-Ògmhios 1928 DE), and An Taigh-seinnse Mòr shut its gates across the ore road, which stayed cut (9 an Lùnastal 1928 DE). The capital rose next and barricaded Drochaid Cathair dhearg with ore-carts (18 an Lùnastal 1928 DE), and Strake drew the Administration into the Residency above Ros dhomhain (27 an t-Samhain 1928 DE).

The first relief column, under Major Peter Ashdown, was met at the ford of Àth chiar on 5 an Dùbhlachd 1928 DE. Ashdown lost forty men and his baggage. The rebels lost nineteen, and the council's roll names them all. Dùn chrom shut its gates behind the retreating column and nursed the wounded it left (3 am Faoilleach 1929 DE). In the east the silver town rose (15 am Faoilleach 1929 DE), and the post at Dùn ìseal surrendered after one exchange of fire (17 am Faoilleach 1929 DE).

The humans struck back from the sea. A Company steamship came up the Abhainn uaine and shelled the ore stage at Seann Toll and burned the town behind it, killing twenty-three (15 an Gearran 1929 DE). On 10 an Cèitean 1929 DE fishing boats from Seann Chwen and Ros ruadh burned a Company coaster at anchor. The keepers of the southern beacons put out their fires, and two Company ships were lost on the reefs (9 an t-Ògmhios 1929 DE).

Through the first winter neither side could attack the other (26 an t-Ògmhios 1929 DE), and the capital went hungry (8 an t-Iuchar 1929 DE). In the stalemate the rebels burned the tithe ledgers in three raids (9 an t-Iuchar 1929 DE), at Ros dhomhain, Ceann àrsaidh and Muileann chrom. The Administration's last sally toward the mining country was driven back at Cnoc ghorm on 25 an Lùnastal 1929 DE. The Ros dhomhain harbour quarter opened its gates to the council (4 an t-Sultain 1929 DE), Strake left the Residency by water (21 an t-Sultain 1929 DE), and Ros bheag became the last seat of the Administration (23 an t-Sultain 1929 DE), where the human families went hungry within weeks (4 an Dàmhair 1929 DE).

End. The last ship recorded from an Tìr Thall came to Ros bheag with a sealed letter and left on the next tide (1 an t-Samhain 1929 DE). Envoys met at Àth àrsaidh and agreed a truce (2 an t-Samhain 1929 DE). The humans still on Rodos would go into the north-west under the council's safe-conduct, and the council would leave the concession towns standing. The columns went north (29 an t-Samhain 1929 DE) and camped a night at Àth leathan (1 an Dùbhlachd 1929 DE), where several of the humans wrote down the name of the place. Strake sailed west in the last ship able to make the crossing (5 an Dùbhlachd 1929 DE). On 1 am Faoilleach 1930 DE the war ended with the crossing itself closed. That is the Severance. The war-companies were stood down, but never formally abolished (3 an t-Ògmhios 1930 DE).

Raiders in the New Age

After the Severance, ships flying no flag, some crewed by men who had served the Administration, raided the coast off Cathair gheal (4 an t-Sultain 1941 DE). The council sent no help, and in the end the fishermen armed their own boats, drove the raiders out, and were fined for bearing arms without licence (8 an Giblean 1949 DE). Only after the patrol boats were refitted for dubhan could they outrun the raiders (15 an t-Sultain 2012 DE).

An Cogadh Fada, the Long War

Cause. Some northern communities refused to take their place in the new economy (25 an Giblean 2015 DE) and kept working the last coal seams rather than depend on one man's fuel. When the Mine Board's northern revenue fell by a quarter (22 am Màrt 2017 DE), it declared the western seams Crown property and ordered the pits closed. Enforcers were posted at Seann Skell (16 an Dàmhair 2017 DE), the first armed company sent north since the Severance. Skirmishes too small to name followed (29 an t-Sultain 2018 DE). Ruth Calder's offer to pay the Crown's fifth in coal went unanswered (25 an Dùbhlachd 2018 DE). The mobilization order reformed the regiments (28 an Dàmhair 2019 DE) under Somhairle mac Lachlainn (26 an t-Samhain 2019 DE), and the Moot's last petition was filed (25 an Dùbhlachd 2019 DE).

Sides. On the kingdom's side were the Board's enforcers, the reformed regiments and later the fleets, all running on dubhan, in the reign of Cathal. On the other side were the holdouts of five western towns, Àth leathan, Muileann àrsaidh, Cnoc thais, Àth naomh and Tobar dhearg, with Ruth Calder and Tom Varley named among them. The Moot stood apart and fed the hungry.

Course. Arms went west by the ore line (12 am Faoilleach 2020 DE). The hewers gathered at Àth leathan (20 am Faoilleach 2020 DE), and the regiments marched west (23 am Faoilleach 2020 DE). The Battle of Àth leathan, fought on 11 an Giblean 2020 DE at Àraich Àth leathan, was the first great engagement of the war. The open record counts only the kingdom's dead. Tuathaich telling puts the holdouts' in the hundreds, and Ruth Calder's name does not appear in the open record again (11 an Giblean 2020 DE). The holdouts fell back into the hills (11 an Giblean 2020 DE). The regiments besieged Muileann àrsaidh, which held for weeks on stored coal and potatoes (21 an Cèitean 2020 DE). Cnoc thais was taken after its road was cut (2 an Lùnastal 2020 DE), and Àth naomh and Tobar dhearg opened their roads without a siege (17 an Dùbhlachd 2020 DE). In the autumn of the next year a column of several hundred holdouts left the hills and moved south-east toward the capital (29 an Dàmhair 2021 DE). Why it did so is in the sealed archive. Tuathaich telling names its leader Owen Barrow, and the open record gives no name. It made camp by Muileann ghlas, a day's walk from the capital (6 an Dùbhlachd 2021 DE), and the first and third regiments were brought down the fair road to meet it. The Battle of Muileann ghlas, fought on 10 an Dùbhlachd 2021 DE at Àraich Muileann ghlas, was the second and last great battle of the war. The open record gives no count of the column's dead (10 an Dùbhlachd 2021 DE). It is the second battle fought below Muileann ghlas that the annals record. The first was fought there in the Brothers' War.

End. When word of the battle reached the hills, the last holdouts came down to the seventh regiment's posts and were disarmed and sent home (10 an Dùbhlachd 2021 DE). An Cogadh Fada ended on 10 an Dùbhlachd 2021 DE, and nine regiments and four fleets remained on their stations. By the Board's order the western seams were flooded and capped (24 an Gearran 2022 DE). The wartime tithe (21 an Giblean 2020 DE) was carried forward in the Treasury's accounts, and no council minute records a decision to keep it (27 an Giblean 2023 DE). Tuathaich families built a cairn on the field of Àth leathan (6 an Giblean 2023 DE). The kingdom raised a stone with the regiments' dead at Cathair mhòr (15 an Dùbhlachd 2022 DE).
