Of the Sundering the language also keeps one strange relic. A work-song of the rope-makers of Cuan shean names the parts of a deep keel, and half its words have no meaning to anyone who sings it (5 am Màrt 1350 DE). It is the only record of the fleet's techniques to survive in any form. Whether the lost words are old Ròdais, wrights' cant, or something else, no one has shown.

The tongue of the Seann-Dhaoine

Of the Old Ones' speech nothing survives but names. Ten roots are known, each standing after the Ròdais word seann, "old", which lenites it where Ròdais lenites:

RootAs written on the mapBurgs bearing itShires named from it
DunnSeann Dunn3yes
CwenSeann Chwen3yes
SkellSeann Skell4yes (three)
BralSeann Bhral3yes
TarrSeann Tarr3yes
VellSeann Vell5yes (three)
MornSeann Mhorn2—
BrennSeann Bhrenn2yes
TollSeann Toll3yes
WarrSeann Warr2yes

Thirty burgs on the map bear these names, and thirteen shires are named from them.

The Ròdaich did not translate these names; they took them over. The fishers who resettled Seann Mhorn in the Holy Age kept "the name they found there, which is not in their own tongue", and said the old name came with the stones (23 an t-Sultain 2821 BDE). It is the first such taking-over on record. The pattern is the one other lands know, where an older people's harbour-names outlive them inside a newer tongue: borrowed and fossilized, not translated.

What can be said. The roots are single syllables. Seven of the ten end in a doubled consonant (-nn, -ll, -rr). Three of them hold letters that Ròdais writes nowhere else: k in Skell, v in Vell, w in Cwen and Warr. Ròdais spelling turns every sg into sc, but it has never turned Seann Skell into Seann Scell; the scribes kept the foreign k as they found it, and the grammar counts sk- among the clusters that do not lenite.

What cannot be known. What any root meant. Whether seann was ever the Old Ones' own element, or only the Ròdaich's label for places they found already named (the second is the usual reading, and the likelier, but it is a reading). Whether the roots come from one tongue or several. Two of them look like Ròdais words, toll, a hole, and dunn beside dùn, a fort; the resemblance has tempted scholars in every age and proves nothing, and the Library does not take a side.

The script. The Seann-Dhaoine also cut signs. Rows of them stand on the cliff above Seann Tarr (5 an Giblean 11,595 BDE), in the script that turns up again on the standing stones. It is not Ròdais, and it has not been read. Not one sign of it has an agreed meaning. The stag-scholars of the Holy Age set their own new letters against the obelisk at Carragh Cnoc bheag and found that they matched nothing, and wrote down that the stone's writers were not their teachers (12 an Cèitean 2085 BDE). Samuel Wren copied the obelisk and sent it west to the scholars of an Tìr Thall; no reply is recorded (5 an Gearran 1796 DE). Edwin Lowe copied the pillar near Cnoc chiar, compared it with Wren's copy, and decided that the two were not the same script and that neither was Ròdach; his notes stop there (9 an Lùnastal 1844 DE). The strokes on the midden stones are not this script; they are a count. Whether the script records the Old Ones' tongue, or some other, or no tongue at all, is not known.

The humans' tongue

The humans spoke a plain tongue, and this history renders it in English (see Of Translation below). The names they carried were names of that tongue: Edmund Harrow, Thomas Pike, Samuel Wren, Josiah Pell, Henry Maddox, Arthur Lisle, Samuel Hale, Edwin Lowe.

The season of translation. Human clerics and Ròdach custodians spent a full season trying to build a shared vocabulary, and neither side's account of what was agreed survives intact (27 am Màrt 1781 DE). Samuel Wren and the custodian Gormshuil nic Fhearchair kept parallel word-lists. Wren's survives in the Administration's letter-books; Gormshuil's was lost, and only its first leaf is known from a copy: forty words for the colours of broken ore (13 an Dùbhlachd 1781 DE). Against those forty the humans had one word, and it was coal.

The tongue of rule. The humans wrote their agreements in their own tongue only. The first written treaty (27 an Giblean 1787 DE) was signed at Cathair dhearg by Tormod mac Ailein, who could not read the tongue it was written in; the record does not say who read it to him (7 an Cèitean 1787 DE). The Harbour Articles were written the same way, and that time two custodians refused to sign (16 an t-Samhain 1798 DE). The Mission's school at Ros dhomhain taught Ròdach children in the humans' tongue (9 an Cèitean 1830 DE); a generation later Iain Maor, the first overseer schooled there, kept his reports in the humans' tongue and his household in Ròdais (23 an Giblean 1866 DE). The Levy's officers read the names of the chosen at Caol mhòr from a list in the humans' tongue, and the custodians took the names down again in Ròdais, "so that they will know whom to look for" (3 am Màrt 1867 DE).

Loanwords. Few crossed, and most of those late. In the first generations Ròdais took the humans' goods and named them in its own way, as above, and kept few of the humans' words for them. The humans, for their part, so far as the record shows, used the Ròdais names of places as they found them, and took fuil-ghuail not as a loan but as a translation, obsidian-touched; that word, and not the Ròdais, is the one the kingdom's own later entries use of the Rite's "unbroken line". What went the other way, into the humans' speech, is best seen after the Severance, in the north.

The Ròdais word for the humans' country, an Tìr Thall, is the only name the island has for it.

Tuathaich speech

The speech of the north is a mixed speech, and the chronicles describe it only in passing. They say this much:

The Tuathaich kept the humans' tongue. Walter Hale asked the council for leave to open schools in the north teaching in it, and was refused (10 an Gearran 1936 DE); Agnes Pike opened one at Doire ghlas anyway, with Moot money and without the council's leave, and within a decade there were nine (14 am Faoilleach 1944 DE). The Moot later counted eleven such schools, and three that had begun to teach Ròdais as well, at the parents' asking (7 an t-Ògmhios 1958 DE). The church at Cnoc ghorm taught its priests in the humans' tongue while reading the Bible in the Ròdais text its preachers use on the west coast: the only place in the north where both are taught (29 an Giblean 1939 DE).

The Tuathaich live among Ròdais names and use Ròdais words. The words the north has added to the island's speech in the present age are Ròdais in form: fadachadh, from fada, long, the name of the war they lost (10 an Dùbhlachd 2021 DE), and seann-chunntas, an old reckoning, which official Ròdach usage pointedly does not take up (18 an Giblean 2025 DE). The word dubhan for the fuel came out of the north, from the name of Dubhan, a Tuathach, and it spread before the fuel did (23 an t-Sultain 2010 DE); the royal chronicler who first set it down spelled it three ways in two lines (21 an t-Samhain 2000 DE).

Beyond this the chronicles do not go. The northern towns' own accounts are among the things the royal record says it does not hold (25 an Giblean 1972 DE). How far the humans' tongue has drifted in the north since the crossing closed, how much Ròdais is spoken at a Tuathach hearth, and in which tongue the First Canoe is told: this archive does not know, and it would be wrong to pretend otherwise.

Names and naming

Personal names. Ròdach names are Gaelic personal names: Ailean, Beathag, Catrìona, Dòmhnall, Eilidh, Fearchar, Gormshuil, Iain, Mòrag, Raghnall, Sìleas, Tormod. A person is further named from the father, with mac, son, or nic, daughter, and the father's name in the genitive, lenited where Ròdais lenites: Tormod mac Iain; Eilidh nic Iain; Gormshuil nic Fhearchair; Donnchadh mac Thormoid; Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill; Oighrig nic Lachlainn.

Bynames are as common as patronymics and often outlast them. They name a colour, a trade, a size or a deed. After a woman's name the byname is lenited, after a man's it is not: Seònaid Mhòr, Eilidh Dhubh, Beathag Bhàn, but Ailean Mòr, Calum Liath, Dùghall Garbh. Trade-names are nouns and stand as they are: Alasdair Saor, the wright; Iain Maor, the overseer. Some bynames are earned: Tormod mac Iain, the first of the royal kin to read, was called Tormod Scrìobhaiche, Tormod the Writer, for the rest of his life (3 an Lùnastal 1744 BDE).

Kindreds take Sliochd, the seed or line, or Clann, the children, with a founder's name in the genitive: Sliochd Ìomhair, Sliochd Mhuirich, Clann Choinnich.

Human and Tuathaich names are of the humans' tongue and are kept in their own spelling: Walter Hale, Agnes Pike. Unlike the humans' names for the island's things, the humans' names for themselves survived the Severance.

Place names. Ròdach places are named by a generic noun and a describing word after it. On the map the describer is always lenited, whatever the gender of the generic (Baile ghorm, Cnoc bheag, Dùn thais); in speech it would not be after a masculine noun, and the map's form is a fixed naming pattern, kept as one might keep an old compound. The generics:

GenericSenseUsed for
Cathairstone fort; citycapital, city
Dùnfortified hillcapital, city
Baile Mòrgreat settlementcity
Bailesettlement, towntown
Àthfordtown
Cnochilltown
Muileannmilltown
Cillholy cell, shrinevillage, hamlet
Tobarwellvillage, hamlet

The describers are colour, size and character words: mòr, beag, dubh, geal, bàn, dearg, ruadh, uaine, glas, fada, domhain, ìseal, fiadhaich, naomh, fionn, ciar, gorm, sean, òg, garbh, min, caol, leathan, crom, dìreach, àrsaidh. The great rivers are Abhainn with a describer; the small ones take a root and the ending -as or -eas by broad and slender. A shire, siorrachd, takes the name of its seat, or, where it has no town, of its island (Appendix H). Names repeat freely; there are four Baile chrom and four Seann Skell, and the rolls tell them apart by where they are.

Beside these stand the Old Ones' names, which follow none of the rules above except that the Ròdaich put seann before them.

Writing

Before letters. The first marks on Rodos made on purpose are the Seann-Dhaoine's: the notched net-weights of Seann Chwen, their unread script, and their tally strokes. The Ròdaich's forebears kept counts too, but not in letters. Someone began marking the high-water line against a fixed rock in the Ancient Age (28 am Faoilleach 5930 BDE), and at Ros dhomhain Seònaid Mhòr cut her marks in pairs, one for the high water and one for the low (25 an t-Iuchar 5177 BDE). The king-lists of that age were oral, and the Small-Burning custom was "nowhere written and everywhere kept".

The Ròdais words on the stones. Bha teine sa chloich on Carragh Cnoc bheag, Cuimhnich an teine on Colbh Cnoc chiar, Cha do thàinig sinn; bha sinn ann on Calbh Cnoc ghorm: these are the oldest Ròdais words in stone. When they were cut no roll says. The stones were raised in the Ancient Age; the Ròdais on Carragh Cnoc bheag was cut later, by another hand. The words on Calbh Cnoc ghorm were recut along their old grooves by a hand from the Stone Kings' hill, and some later readers say the recutting changed a letter (2 an t-Samhain 3237 BDE). That there were letters to change then is not proved by this; the Library keeps the claim and makes no judgment on it.

The stag-letters. The first letters in use by the Ròdaich were made at Muileann chiar in the far east, where the teachers of the stag's people, the first of the druid schools, later called Feallsanachd an Fhèidh, turned the cutters' tally-notches into signs for sounds, "so that a teaching can be kept without a teacher" (15 am Màrt 2085 BDE). The druids call them the ogham, the gift of Ogma, god of letters. Nearly every later hand on the island descends from them. From these came the first written king-list (20 an Lùnastal 1700 BDE), kept by Tormod Scrìobhaiche at Dùn dhearg; the Keepers' own roll, written down at Dùn ìseal in answer to it (17 an Dàmhair 1679 BDE); boundary stones cut with treaty terms (11 am Màrt 1404 BDE); and the first teaching of letters for their own sake, to fishers' children at Inis bheag, which the Hall recorded with the remark that fish do not need reading (22 an t-Ògmhios 1145 BDE).

Books and paper. The Age of Sundering is the age of the custody-book, kept by the vein-house, and of the first books: Leabhar an t-Seabhaig, the sayings of Gormshuil (5 an t-Ògmhios 212 DE), and Seònaid nic Coinnich's Book of the Three Claimants, the oldest surviving history on Rodos written as one narrative (8 an t-Ògmhios 585 DE). Aonghas mac Uisdein was the first king to learn his letters as a child (25 an Cèitean 355 DE). A mill at Muileann chaol began making paper from rags, the first on Rodos, and the custody-book was copied onto paper in that generation (28 am Faoilleach 1635 DE).

Two tongues of record. The humans brought paper in quantity, and the custodians of Cathair naomh asked for their first payment in paper and ink (19 an Lùnastal 1782 DE). They brought, too, a written tongue the Ròdaich could not read, and for a century the island kept its records in two. Whether the humans' letters and the stag-letters share their shapes, the record does not say. The earliest Ròdach grievance text to survive, Leabhar Baile thais, was set down in Ròdais by many hands (18 an t-Sultain 1880 DE).

The kingdom's record. After the Severance the kingdom founded Leabharlann Muileann chaol (1 an Cèitean 1945 DE) and the office of royal chronicler (20 an t-Samhain 1947 DE), and in time drew the provincial archives into one place (26 an t-Iuchar 1996 DE). This appendix is written from that library.

Of Translation

This history is written in English for the next reader, and some account is owed of what that has done to the tongues it describes.

The humans' speech is rendered in English. The humans did not speak English. They spoke the tongue of an Tìr Thall, whose name for itself, like the name of their country, is not recorded on Rodos. It was a plain tongue, as English is plain beside Ròdais; its speakers were strangers to the island and its things; and it has become, in the north, the ordinary speech of the Tuathaich. For those reasons it is given here as English, and its names are given as English names, as the letter- books would have them. When this history says the humans called the ore coal, it means that they used their ordinary word for their ordinary fuel, and that coal is the nearest English word for what they meant. When it gives a custodian's title as "keepers of the coal", it is rendering Wren's rendering. Obsidian-touched is likewise an English stand-in for the humans' word, chosen because it keeps the plainness of the original and the error in it. The ore is not obsidian, and it is not coal.

Ròdais is kept as it is. The Ròdaich are the people of this history and Ròdais is its first tongue, and it is not translated into something else here. Names of places, persons, faiths, laws and offices are left in Ròdais spelling, with the grave accent and the sc, and with their lenitions: Cathair dhearg, not "Red City"; fuil-ghuail, not "coal-blood", except where a gloss is wanted. Where a Ròdais phrase is translated, the translation follows it in quotation marks and is meant as a help, not a replacement. The five ages have Ròdais names and are also given English ones for convenience; the English names are this archive's, not the chroniclers'. The adjective Rodian is English, and is used as such.

The island's own name. Written in Ròdais it is Ròdos, with the accent. In the English text of this history it is written Rodos, the form the humans used and the form in which most readers will have met it. It is the same word.

The Seann tongue is not translated, because it cannot be. Its ten roots are given as the Ròdaich wrote them, with the foreign letters the Ròdaich kept. No meaning is offered for any of them.

What has been lost in the rendering. Some things do not cross. The forty colour-words on Gormshuil's leaf are one; the Tuathaich jokes about being long-warred are another, since fadachadh is funny, and not funny, only in a tongue where fada is also the name of the war. Where this history has had to choose between a translation that reads easily and one that keeps what the words did, it has tried to keep what they did.

Appendix G — The Goods and Markets of Rodos

This appendix describes what the island grows, digs, catches and makes; the sixteen market towns through which almost all of it is bought and sold; the main roads of trade between them; and the taxes the Treasury takes on that trade. The present-day account is drawn from the Treasury's market roll for the last full year, which the clerks of the market-due keep in each of the sixteen market towns and send to Cathair dhearg, and from the books of the fair-court at Muileann òg. The older history is drawn from the annals, and where a trade has a first date in them the date is given.

The roll counts goods in the measures the markets use: grain, fish, clay and sand by the wain; timber by the pile; stone by the pallet; ore by the wagon; silver and gold by the bar; cattle, sheep, horses and oxen by the head; oil, dubhan, wine, honey and tar by the barrel; salt and dyes by the bag; cloth by the bolt; books by the volume. Prices in this appendix are in the realm-coin.

I. The Countries of the Island and What They Grow

Rodos is a wet and windy island, mild for its northern place, and most of it is forest and moor. Its farming follows five kinds of country.

The high bare north. Along the northern coast from Ceann mhòr to Seann Tarr, and inland over the moors behind the Hawk bay, the ground is bare and windswept, with snow on the high moor in winter. It still grows more than its look suggests. Barley and oats are sown in every sheltered hollow, hemp grows in the valley bottoms, and the heather feeds bees and sheep. The shore is the richer half. The northern and north-western waters hold the island's herring grounds and its whales, and amber is gathered from the wrack on the strands of the Hawk bay and the north-west. The market towns of this country are Ceann mhòr, Seann Skell, Àth fhionn, Muileann fhionn and Seann Tarr.

The birch and pine hills. The largest single country on the island is the belt of birch, pine and hill pasture that runs from the western plain across the middle of Rodos into the eastern hills. It is cattle and sheep country before anything else, and it also gives timber, venison, honey and a dark wine pressed from blaeberry and bramble. Almost all of the island's ore-bearing ground lies in these hills: the silver of Muileann chiar — baile mèinne airgid and of the hills of Cuan ghlas, the copper and tin of Ceann àrsaidh, Cnoc bhàn and Doire fhionn, the gemstones of the Muileann dhearg hills, the marble of Baile Mòr dhomhain, the old spoil-heaps where dubhan is made for the forges, and the charcoal woods that fed the forges before it. Copper was little worked before the New Age. The humans shipped theirs in for the first coinage (10 an Lùnastal 1796 DE), and the first great working is the copper-town of Àth fhiadhaich (2 an t-Ògmhios 1990 DE). The market towns of the hills are Baile Mòr dhomhain, Ros fhionn, Dùn ìseal, Baile Mòr dhìreach and Ros bheag.

The wet western and southern woods. South and west of the capital the forest is oak, alder and hazel, dripping for half the year. Timber, game, clay, white sand, hemp and honey are its chief goods, with barley on the cleared ground. The potteries and glass-houses stand in this country because its clay and sand are the best on Rodos, and the dyers of the south take their colours from its plants. Its market towns are Baile Mòr fhionn, Cathair fhada, Cnoc bhàn and Caol ruadh.

The oak country of the capital and the east. Around the capital and along the eastern road the woods are broad-leaved and the soil is deeper. This is the island's best mixed farming: cattle and sheep, grain, wine, hemp, and the horses of the Doire chaol country. Its farms sell through Cathair dhomhain, Ceann leathan and Dùn ìseal.

The eastern plain and the mosses. The open grassland east of Dùn ìseal, where the herders of the Ancient Age drove their cattle to the warm springs (7 an Lùnastal 3830 BDE), is thin pasture and bees. The wet mosses of the west coast and the western plain give peat, reeds and wildfowl, and at Baile ghorm the salt-pans the Stone Kings fought over (12 an Gearran 6918 BDE).

Some goods grow in only one or two places. Flax grows only in the lake-shore fields of Seann Warr, and its seed is pressed there for linseed oil, in which the road-houses were frying their oatcakes as early as 265 DE. Tobacco grows only on the old concession farms behind Ceann mhòr, where the humans first planted it (31 an Dàmhair 1831 DE). Gold is washed only from the streams below Baile dhìreach and Cnoc dhìreach, and the pearl-mussels lie only in the shallows of the south-eastern coast off Cnoc bhàn and Caol ruadh.

Rodos grows no spices, tea, sugar, silk or dates, and has no camels or elephants. Before the Severance the ships of an Tìr Thall brought small amounts of spice, tea and sugar to the Company's stores. No ship has come from the west since the last one sailed from Ros bheag (1 an t-Samhain 1929 DE), and those goods are not sold on the island now.

The vein itself no longer appears in the roll. Ore-fuel from the Sloc Mòr was sold at the fair by the cartload until 22 am Faoilleach 2002 DE, and the western coal seams sold their coal to the north until the Board closed them. The western seams were flooded and capped in 2022 DE, the upper galleries of the Sloc Mòr were closed in 2025 DE, and the few baskets of altar-ore cut each year under the Rite's custody are not sold in any market. Dubhan, the fuel that took the ore's place (19 an t-Ògmhios 2000 DE), is the one wrought good the roll counts among the raw goods. It is made from the spoil of the old workings (1 an t-Iuchar 1990 DE) at the works of Seann Skell on the southern coast and in the east and north (27 an t-Ògmhios 2026 DE). The works sell it by the barrel into the markets for the forges, kilns and glass-houses, which burned charcoal from the hill woods before it, as the charcoal-burners of the eastern woods had burned it since the Age of Sundering (17 an t-Ògmhios 1430 DE). Lamps, engines and lorries buy it at the works' own depots and pumps and at the inns that keep a pump (4 am Màrt 2009 DE), and the wartime tithe on it is taken at the pump by a clerk of the Treasury (29 an Giblean 2020 DE).

Dubhan is also the one good of Rodos sold off the island. In the present year Dubhan, who made the first working fuel, won from the council the right to export it (7 an t-Sultain 2026 DE), the first leave for any good to go beyond the kingdom's waters since the Severance. The export is held to a measure the Treasury sets each year and is loaded only at the quay of Ros dhomhain, where a clerk of the Treasury takes the tithe on every barrel and the custodians of Òrd Bhrìde seal every hold, so that nothing of the vein goes with it. The kingdom's own depots and the Moot's are served first. As of the present year dubhan is exported under that charter, and under no other.

II. The Wrought Goods

Most of the value that passes through the markets is in goods made in the towns rather than in raw goods. In order of value in the last roll they are these.

Salted and smoked food. Salt fish, salt meat and smoked meat are made in almost every town and are the largest trade on the island by value. Salting is as old as the fish-kilns of Seann Mhorn (17 an Giblean 11,516 BDE) and the salt road of the Ancient Age (5 an Dàmhair 5133 BDE); the mining shires have eaten salt fish in the lean season since 355 DE. The biggest salting towns are Cathair mhòr, Dùn ìseal, Seann Dunn and the harbours of the gulf.

Arms and field-guns. The forges of the old vein country, of Àth naomh in the west and of Caol ìseal on the north coast smelt bog-iron and bronze into arms, and a few of them cast field-guns. Every market in the kingdom sells arms back to its towns, where the regiments and fleets raised in An Cogadh Fada are stationed. The trade is recent. It grew from the Crown's contracts for the regiments (20 an t-Ògmhios 2023 DE), and arms are now the dearest common goods in every market. The forge-town of Muileann dhearg, where Uilleam Gobha made the rebels' grenades (17 an Lùnastal 1928 DE), stands in the same hills.

Books, paper and ink. Rodos is a country of copyists. Paper has been made from rags and hemp at Muileann chaol since 1635 DE and at Tobar dhìreach since 1947 DE, and books are bound and sold in more than eighty towns. The largest trade in books is at Dùn ìseal, Cathair dhomhain, Baile Mòr ruadh, Inis àrsaidh and Dùn chrom.

Soap and candles. Soap is boiled from tallow and seal-oil, and candles are dipped from beeswax and tallow, in most towns of the north and the gulf. The wax lights of the ancestor shrines were the first of this trade (26 an Dàmhair 605 DE).

Ships, sails and rope. Seagoing ships are built at nine yards: the two Seann Dunns on the east coast, Inis thais, Seann Skell of the Hawk bay, Ros fhionn, Inis ìseal, Ceann leathan, the royal quays of Cathair dhearg and Inis mhòr. Their sails are cut from hemp cloth in the same towns, and their rope comes from the rope-walks of Baile ghlas and Seann Tarr. The first deep keels since the Sundering were measured from the humans' hulls at Inis mhòr (14 an t-Samhain 1783 DE).

Glass and pottery. Glass is blown from the white sand of Cuan ruadh, Ceann mhòr and the southern Seann Skell in some seventy towns, most of all at Cathair mhòr on the north road, Baile Mòr dhìreach and Seann Vell. The first glass-house on Rodos was built at Baile Mòr dhìreach in 1845 DE. Pottery is older. The red ware of the western road was fired at Baile ghorm and Cnoc àrsaidh in the Holy Age (8 an t-Samhain 81 BDE, 19 an Giblean 79 BDE). Today the largest potteries are at Dùn fhiadhaich, Ros dhìreach and Àth bheag, and Cathair fhada sells their ware to the north.

Cloth, garments and leather. Wool is spun and woven in every sheep country. The chartered weavers are those of Baile chiar (6 am Faoilleach 1944 DE) and the mills of Doire ghlas (27 an Giblean 1988 DE). Hides are tanned at Baile ghorm (13 an t-Iuchar 1991 DE) and Muileann dhomhain (9 an Giblean 1982 DE), and boots and harness are made in most of the market towns.

Scent. Scent waters are distilled from bog-myrtle, meadowsweet and heather honey and sold in small glass flasks. This trade belongs to the capital shore and the western plain: Seann Vell, Caol fhiadhaich, Cnoc àrsaidh, Baile ghlas and Doire shean. It began at Seann Vell in the first years of the restored kingdom (15 an Gearran 1956 DE).

Drink and cheese. Barley spirit, the fire-water of the northern road (15 an Dùbhlachd 327 BDE), is distilled in some forty towns. Ale is brewed for sale only at Ceann chaol, Muileann fhada and Seann Bhral in the south-east. Cheese is made in the cattle towns, most of all at Ceann leathan and Cathair fhada.

Coin. The realm-coin is struck only at the mint at Cathair dhearg (9 an Dàmhair 1934 DE). The blanks it is struck from are refined in the villages of the eastern hills from the silver of Muileann chiar and the gold of Baile dhìreach (19 an t-Sultain 1966 DE), and the Treasury counts those blanks among the goods of the Dùn ìseal market.

III. The Sixteen Market Towns

Every town on Rodos belongs to one of sixteen markets. A town sells its surplus into its market and buys what it lacks there. The market town holds the market-court, weighs goods on the Crown's weights and keeps the clerk of the market-due. Each of the sixteen has a market square, and so do some hundred and seventy lesser towns that hold a weekly market of their own. Only the market towns keep a tithe-clerk.

Ceann leathan is the largest and dearest market on the island. Its reach runs from the gulf shore up into the old vein country of Muileann chrom, Muileann dhearg and Muileann dhomhain, whose forges now make arms where their pits once sent up ore. It became the market of the southern fishing in the Holy Age (16 am Faoilleach 2415 BDE), and its harbour-master's notched tallies are the oldest counted objects in the library. Today the crowds of the Còmhrag keep its prices the highest on Rodos. Grain, timber, honey and wine all cost it nearly twice what they cost on the south coast. It sells nothing to other markets and buys from eight of them: scent from the capital, amber from the Hawk bay and the north-west, pearls from Cnoc bhàn, cattle, sheep and venison from the northern hills, coin-blanks from Dùn ìseal, oxen and linseed oil from the western plain, and seal-oil, whale-oil and dyes from Ceann mhòr.

Cathair dhomhain is the market of the capital shore: the three harbour towns of Cathair dhomhain, Ros dhomhain and Baile ghlas, the royal precinct of Cathair dhearg, and the farms of Baile chiar and Àth shean behind them. Its right to its own tolls dates from the rivalry with the new royal seat (9 an Giblean 1300 BDE). Its scent-makers and glass-houses make it the chief seller of scent to the rest of the island, and the horses of Doire chaol go from it to three other markets.

Ros fhionn has the most towns of any market, fifty-three, from Muileann chaol and the library in the south to Caol bheag on the north coast. The salt that made the town (3 am Màrt 315 DE, 9 an Lùnastal 920 DE) left it when the harbour silted (29 an t-Ògmhios 1120 DE), but the market-court the salt-masters had set up stayed on the headland (16 an t-Ògmhios 1145 DE), and the hill towns still bring their goods to it. The forge-towns of Baile Mòr uaine and Baile Mòr dhìreach make it the first market in arms. It has no goods of its own to spare for other markets and buys scent, pottery, pearls and amber from them.

Seann Skell of the Hawk bay gathers the north-central coast from Doire ghlas and Muileann leathan to Seann Toll. The amber of its strands has been prized since the Ancient Age (8 an Gearran 6295 BDE), and it is the one good the market sends out, mostly to Ceann leathan. Whale-oil, honey and sheep are its other raw goods. The Tuathaich towns of the Doire ghlas country are in its reach and sell their cloth through it.

Ros bheag is the market of the west coast between Cuan shean and the western Seann Skell. Its harbour court was swearing trade oaths on the scorpion's sting by 854 BDE. Its clay, honey and the bog-iron of Àth naomh are worked into pottery and arms, and its surplus cattle and sheep go north to Seann Skell.

Seann Tarr is the smallest of the northern markets in people. It began as the feast-market of the ancestor shrine (26 an Dàmhair 605 DE) and is still busiest at the great feasts. Honey and wax, the dyes of Baile fhiadhaich and the hemp of Doire uaine and Achadh naomh are its goods. The hemp goes to the rope-makers chartered there in 1982 DE.

Dùn ìseal holds the market of the eastern hills under the old Hall (10 an Dùbhlachd 2443 BDE). Its reach takes in the silver town, the gold stream of Baile dhìreach, the copper-town of Àth fhiadhaich (2 an t-Ògmhios 1990 DE) and the mills of Muileann bhàn and Muileann gheal. It sends coin-blanks and copper to Baile Mòr dhìreach, Ceann leathan and Seann Skell.

Baile Mòr dhomhain is the market of the northern hills (22 an t-Samhain 1877 BDE) and the island's second exporter of livestock. When the ore trade fell away its market day drew more carts than the fair at Muileann òg (30 an t-Sultain 1987 DE). Cattle, sheep, venison, horses, the marble of its hills (29 an Dàmhair 1256 DE) and glass go from it to five other markets.

Baile Mòr dhìreach gathers the east coast from Seann Tarr's southern country to Àth bheag. Its shipyards at the two Seann Dunns build more hulls than any other market's, its glass-houses are the oldest on Rodos (8 an Lùnastal 1845 DE), and the dyers of Baile Mòr ruadh and the furriers of Àth ruadh sell through it. It buys cattle, sheep, horses and coin-blanks from the hill markets.

Baile Mòr fhionn is the chief market of the western plain. Wool was the measure of every bargain there from the Holy Age (12 am Faoilleach 1300 BDE) until the second currency reform (31 an Dàmhair 1865 DE). Its country grows grain, wine and cattle and breeds the island's horses and draught oxen. The old salt-pans of Baile ghorm and Seann Warr and the flax-fields of Seann Warr are in its reach, and its scent-makers send scent to Cathair fhada and Seann Skell.

Cathair fhada is the market of the south. Its charter dates from Queen Sìleas's tally-houses (17 an t-Samhain 248 DE), and its merchants have run the fair at Muileann òg since the fair was first held in the restored kingdom (16 an Dàmhair 1950 DE). It sends the pottery of Dùn fhiadhaich north to Ros fhionn and Seann Skell. The Crown grain-store built there in 1962 DE is the reserve of the south.

Ceann mhòr is the market of the Tuathaich north-west. It was chartered when the humans' harbour officers had gone (23 an Dùbhlachd 1932 DE), and it keeps its court in the old harbour store. It has the most varied goods of any market: grain, fish, whale-oil and seal-oil (4 an t-Samhain 297 BDE), amber, dyes, the tobacco of the concession farms and the tools of Cathair gheal. It sends out more kinds of goods than any other market and buys none.

Àth fhionn is the market of the north coast from Inis mhòr's country to Caol mhin. The north coast's fish, whales and sheep come to it, and the whale-boats that go out from it learned their trade from the humans (9 an Dùbhlachd 1834 DE). Its own market dates from the Age of Sundering (19 an Gearran 796 DE).

Muileann fhionn began as a fort and mill of the human administration and became a Tuathaich market town after the Severance (12 an Giblean 1938 DE). It is the island's greatest cattle market. Its droves of cattle and sheep go south to Ceann leathan, Cnoc bhàn, Seann Tarr and Caol ruadh, and it buys arms from Ceann mhòr.

Cnoc bhàn is the market of the south-eastern farms above the long mill-race of Muileann fhada (28 an Giblean 1012 DE). It sells pearls, clay and amber to the other markets. Its forge-towns make tools and field-guns, and its towns are the only ones on Rodos that brew ale for sale.

Caol ruadh is the youngest and smallest market. It was chartered after An Cogadh Fada to victual the garrisons and the second fleet at the southern Seann Skell (26 am Faoilleach 2022 DE). The glass of Seann Skell and the venison of the strait's woods are its goods.

The Fèill Muileann òg is not one of the sixteen. It is a yearly fair with a court of its own (14 an t-Samhain 1950 DE), held on the old ford-ground where salt was first traded for wool (10 an Cèitean 6426 BDE). Traders from every shire come to it, and the northern day set aside in 1984 DE is the only place where Tuathaich goods are sold under their makers' own marks.

IV. The Roads of Trade

In the last roll the market-courts recorded 8,058 dealings. In 6,235 of them a market sold goods to one of its towns. In 1,759 a town sold its goods into its market. Only 64 were sales from one market to another. Almost all trade on Rodos is local. The dealings between markets are few, but they carry the goods one country has and another lacks, and six roads stand out.

  1. Livestock south from the northern hills. The largest trade between markets is in cattle, sheep, horses and venison. It runs from Muileann fhionn, Baile Mòr dhomhain and the capital shore south and east to Ceann leathan, Baile Mòr dhìreach, Seann Tarr, Cnoc bhàn and Cathair fhada. Its drove roads are the ones the drovers of Àth chiar first marked with cairns (29 am Faoilleach 445 DE). The dubhan lorries have now replaced the droves on most of them (22 am Màrt 2008 DE).
  2. Scent from the capital shore and the western plain. Scent is the costliest good that goes between markets. It goes from Cathair dhomhain and Baile Mòr fhionn to Ceann leathan, Ros fhionn, Seann Skell and Cathair fhada.
  3. Amber, pearls and whale-oil to the gulf. The luxuries of the coasts go to the dearest market. Amber goes from the Hawk bay and Ceann mhòr, pearls from Cnoc bhàn and Baile Mòr dhìreach, and seal-oil and whale-oil from the north-west, and Ceann leathan takes most of all of them.
  4. Coin-blanks and copper from the eastern hills. Dùn ìseal sends the blanks of the silver and gold refiners, and the copper of Àth fhiadhaich, to Baile Mòr dhìreach, Ceann leathan and Seann Skell.
  5. Pottery and clay. Cathair fhada's pottery goes north to Ros fhionn and Seann Skell, and the clay of Cnoc bhàn and Baile Mòr dhìreach goes to the kilns of the north.
  6. Arms from the north-west to the north-western interior. Ceann mhòr's smiths sell arms to Muileann fhionn, the only road of the arms trade that crosses between markets.

Two things are sold everywhere and seldom carried far: hemp, the cheapest good in every market, and grain. Grain is dearest at Ceann leathan and cheapest at Caol ruadh; hemp is cheapest at Cnoc bhàn.

V. Taxes and the Treasury

The Crown takes two dues, both set by the council in the first weeks of the kingdom (21 am Faoilleach 1933 DE) and collected by the maoir of the shires (Appendix H). The Treasury reckons them in purses of the realm-coin.

The market-due. Seventeen in every hundred of the price is taken on every sale a town makes into its market and on every sale between markets. Sales from a market back to its own towns are not charged. The Treasury fixed the due at that rate after An Cogadh Fada and set a clerk in each of the sixteen market towns to take it and keep the market roll (22 an Cèitean 2023 DE). It is kept apart from the wartime tithe on every sale of dubhan (21 an Giblean 2020 DE), which is still taken at the pumps (29 an Giblean 2020 DE) and which the Treasury carried forward after the war as a line of its own under the regiments' pay (27 an Giblean 2023 DE). In the last roll the towns' sales into their markets were worth about 18,580 purses, the markets' sales back to their towns about 9,700 and the sales between markets about 1,200, and the market-due brought the Treasury 3,193 purses.

The head-due. Each household pays the head-due for every head in it. It was first collected on the count of 1936 DE (27 an t-Sultain 1936 DE) and stands at eighteen purses on every hundred thousand heads. It brought in 6,375 purses in the last roll, two parts in three of the Crown's money.

The Treasury's roll for the present year comes to 9,568 purses (29 an t-Iuchar 2026 DE). The towns' own chests hold about 12,660 purses together, and the towns' yearly product is about 11,460.

Earlier taxes and currencies. The first toll on Rodos was Goraidh Mòr's road-toll of one fish in twenty (22 an t-Sultain 2280 BDE). The silver weights of Muileann chiar gave the carriers' roads a common measure (30 an Dùbhlachd 2457 BDE), and the Hall's clerks first paid in stamped silver rings (20 an Cèitean 1345 BDE). In the Age of Sundering Queen Sìleas fixed the firlot of Cathair dhearg as the measure of grain (11 an Dàmhair 222 DE) and set up the tally-houses, the first account of trade kept across the whole island (22 an t-Sultain 245 DE). Ros fhionn salt was the measure of value in the north-east (3 am Màrt 315 DE), and wool was the measure on the western plain. The humans' mark and its hundred pence were struck at Ros dhomhain (10 an Lùnastal 1796 DE), and three currency reforms pushed barter out (13 an Gearran 1796 DE, 2 an Dàmhair 1865 DE, 7 an Giblean 1908 DE). The Company's tithe on ore rose without any matching return (16 an Gearran 1836 DE) and was extended to grain (4 an Lùnastal 1837 DE). The rebels burned the tithe ledgers (9 an t-Iuchar 1929 DE). The restored kingdom struck its own realm-coin (30 an Giblean 1934 DE) and pegged it to dubhan in 2014 DE.

Appendix H — The Shires of Rodos

This appendix sets out how Rìoghachd Ròdais is divided and governed: the shires, their seats and how they came to be; the Crown's dues and the Treasury; the windy coast of the far north-west, which no shire holds; and the extent of the island's peoples in the present year. It is drawn from the council's minute-books, the Treasury's rolls, the shire record-chests called in to Leabharlann Muileann chaol (7 am Màrt 1995 DE), and the humans' district surveys the kingdom inherited.

I. The Kingdom

The state styled itself Rìoghachd Ròdais, the Kingdom of Rodos, on 27 an t-Iuchar 1931 DE, and Niall was crowned at Cathair dhearg on 19 an t-Ògmhios 1932 DE. It is a monarchy in form. The crown, a royal council of twelve (23 an t-Sultain 1931 DE) and the Treasury sit at Cathair dhearg, and Cathal reigns in the present year. The kingdom counts its years in the Diosal Era, and the present year is 2026 DE (Appendix D).

The kingdom holds every coast of Rodos and every island off it but one stretch of windswept shore in the far north-west (§ V). It has no neighbour but that shore and the sea. Since the crossing closed there has been no other state within reach of its ships (11 an t-Ògmhios 1932 DE), and it keeps no envoys and makes no treaties. Its one war has been fought on its own ground, against its own people: An Cogadh Fada, the Long War of 2020 and 2021 (Appendix C). The regiments raised for it were not stood down (13 am Faoilleach 2022 DE).

The kingdom grew along the island's waters, as the island's people always had. Three shire seats in five stand on the sea or on a river, and so do nearly half of all the burgs.

II. How the Shires Came to Be

The provinces of the Holy Age. The first divisions of the island were the rìghrean's, and they were made for grain and roads. The census-takers of Beathag Mhòr worked from the waypoint houses, since every household on the island was within a day of one (9 an Gearran 1264 BDE). Lachlann Bàn built a granary in every province seat that would take one (16 am Faoilleach 593 BDE), and under Coinneach Bàn the clerks of the red hall copied the rolls for the provinces, so that every seat had its own copy of the laws (27 an Giblean 167 BDE). The Library holds several of those provincial rolls where the originals are lost (24 an t-Ògmhios 121 BDE). Most of the shire seats of the present day were already towns in the Holy Age, and many of them were seats then.

The shires of the Sundering. The word siorrachd first appears in the sail-cloth levy, when the weaving households of Siorrachd Baile àrsaidh were asked for cloth for the fleet, reckoned on tally-sticks at the shire seat (9 an t-Samhain 31 BDE). Through that age the shire was the unit in which the crown's measures were kept. The coppice law of Doire fhionn spread shire by shire (14 an t-Iuchar 70 DE); Queen Sìleas fixed the firlot of Cathair dhearg so that the shires need not quarrel over baskets (11 an Dàmhair 222 DE); Iain Ciar ordered a year's grain in store at every shire seat (20 an Giblean 1260 DE). Two rulers, Sìleas Òg and Gormshuil nic Thormoid, went round every shire seat in person (9 an t-Iuchar 1490 DE, 12 an Giblean 1732 DE). Doire shean became a shire seat on the wealth of its oyster beds (5 an Lùnastal 595 DE), the only raising of a seat in that age that the annals record.

The districts of the humans. The Administration did not use the shires. It governed by districts drawn for the pits, the customs and the Levy, counted the people by district for the first time (19 an Cèitean 1901 DE), and set district seats where its clerks found it convenient: at Cnoc bhàn and at Baile Mòr ruadh on the eastern road, among others. It kept one district that was not land at all. The outer coasts, the islands and the southern edge of the windy coast in the far north-west, where its revenue cutters chased the raiders, were governed from the harbour office at Seann Vell on Eilean ruadh (20 an Giblean 1902 DE). Its surveyors went no farther north-west than the edge of the great moss. Beyond that the district map is blank.

The drawing. On 12 an Dùbhlachd 1932 DE the council divided the kingdom into shires, each named for its seat, and kept most of the human district lines under the new names. The humans' surveys were the only complete ones on the island. Where the council did not keep a district seat it chose the old shire seat instead; so in the shire of Seann Tarr the seat went back from Baile Mòr ruadh, the humans' district town, to the old harbour. A maor was appointed to each shire to collect the Crown's dues and keep its peace (4 am Faoilleach 1933 DE). In the Tuathaich shires the maoir were Ròdaich, lodged in the seat towns. Circuit justices were set to ride among the shires a few years later (23 an Lùnastal 1936 DE).

The drawing made one hundred and twenty-two shires. One more was cut later: Doire chaol, the village of the royal household south of the capital, was taken out of the shire of Baile chiar once it had grown large enough to need its own maor (18 an Dàmhair 1967 DE). Rìoghachd Ròdais has had one hundred and twenty-three shires since then, and the number has not changed.

III. The Shape of the Shires

Names. A shire takes the name of its seat, and the island's names repeat, so the shires' names repeat too. Eleven names belong to more than one shire. There are three shires of Seann Skell, three of Seann Vell and three of Ceann mhin, and two each of Caol bheag, Àth shean, Baile ghorm, Achadh naomh, Muileann dhearg, Muileann dhomhain, Doire fhionn and Muileann naomh. The rolls tell them apart by where they lie, as the table in § VII does. Thirteen shires are named from the Old Ones' harbours (Appendix F).

The island shires. Two shires have no town at all. Eilean dhìreach, a rock off the Tuathaich coast, and Eilean ìseal, off the east coast, each kept a customs station of the Administration and was a district of its own. The council kept both as shires, having no rule for folding a district into its neighbour, and since neither has a town to name it, each is named for its island (20 an Dùbhlachd 1932 DE). They are the only shires on Rodos not named for a seat.

Scattered shires. The shire of Seann Vell of the west is the Administration's district of the outer coasts, kept whole. Its seat is a small harbour on Eilean ruadh off the west coast. Its towns, Cuan dhearg and Cnoc chaol, stand on Eilean bhàn, hard by the southern coast, where the Great Wave struck (3 an t-Ògmhios 1933 DE). Its largest land is the southern edge of the windy coast in the far north-west, where no town stands and the maor goes by boat. With it goes Eilean ghorm. The shire of Seann Vell of the south-east holds Eilean dhearg, the old island of the dead (Appendix F), with Eilean gheal and Eilean mhin, except for a corner of Eilean dhearg that belongs to Àth fhionn. Caol bheag of the north-east lies on Eilean fhada with Eilean bheag, and Caol mhin on Eilean chrom with Eilean dhubh. On the main island, one town of the shire of Tobar ghorm, Baile gheal, lies apart from the rest.

Seats that are not the largest town. In five shires the seat is smaller than another town in the same shire. Caol leathan, the strait town, is the seat and not Baile Mòr fhionn, the lords' city of the western plain. Baile àrsaidh is the seat and not Seann Bhral of the west coast. Cnoc dhubh of the charcoal-burners is the seat and not Doire fhiadhaich, the citadel village of the same hills. Baile Mòr dhomhain is the seat and not Cuan bheag. Seann Vell of the west is the seat and not Cuan dhearg. In each case the council kept the seat the humans' district had, or the older shire had, and did not follow the growth of the towns.

The Tuathaich shires. Eleven shires lie wholly or mostly in the Tuathaich north and north-west: Caol mhòr, Ceann mhòr, Doire ghlas, Baile chrom, Cnoc ghorm, Cnoc thais, Àth àrsaidh, Muileann leathan, Muileann àrsaidh, Baile ìseal and the island shire of Eilean dhìreach. Two of them keep one Ròdaich town each: Baile dhubh in Cnoc ghorm, and Achadh fhiadhaich in Muileann àrsaidh. Three Ròdaich shires have one Tuathaich town: Seann Skell of the west has Àth leathan, Muileann naomh of the west has Àth chrom, and Inis mhin on the northern shore has one town of each people. The windy coast in Seann Vell of the west is Tuathaich country too, though the shire's towns are Ròdaich. The boundary stones on the roads north (31 an t-Iuchar 1930 DE) mark where the Tuathaich country begins, not where any shire ends. The Moot at Caol mhòr has no standing in any shire court (25 an Lùnastal 1931 DE).

One kind of shire. Every shire is a siorrachd, and the kingdom knows no other kind of division. The capital's shire, the Tuathaich shires, the island shires and the scattered shires have the same standing, the same officer and the same dues. The humans' distinctions of district, concession and Residency ground were dropped at the drawing.

IV. The Crown's Dues and the Treasury

The maor of each shire collects two dues for the Crown, set by the council in the first weeks of the kingdom (21 am Faoilleach 1933 DE). The head-due, cìs-cinn, is laid on every household by the number of its heads, and so falls on the whole people of the kingdom, in town and country alike. The market-due, cìs-margaidh, is taken on every sale made by a seller of the kingdom, in a market or out of one. The humans' tariff, which the harbour-masters of Ros dhomhain kept in force for want of another (8 an t-Ògmhios 1932 DE), was folded into the market-due when the kingdom's own coin replaced the humans' mark (30 an Giblean 1934 DE).

Beside the two dues the Treasury carries the wartime tithe on every sale of dubhan, laid "for the war" in 2020 DE and never repealed (27 an Giblean 2023 DE), which pays the regiments. The shires keep what the council allows them for their own works: Cnoc leathan paid for a school in every parish from the shire's dues (21 an Giblean 1979 DE), and the shire of Baile ruadh fenced the open shafts at its own cost (3 an Lùnastal 1981 DE). The first relief the kingdom ever granted came from the Treasury: seed for the survivors of Achadh mhin when their fields lay under salt (6 an Dùbhlachd 1933 DE).

The Treasury reckons in purses, sporain, of the realm's coin. Its roll for the present year (29 an t-Iuchar 2026 DE) stands as follows:

DueRateYield in the present year
Head-due (cìs-cinn)eighteen purses on every hundred thousand heads6,375 purses
Market-due (cìs-margaidh)seventeen in the hundred of the price3,193 purses
The roll9,568 purses

Two parts in three of the Crown's money come from heads and one from trade. The kingdom counted 35,415,000 heads for the head-due in the present year. The head-due has stood at its rate since it was first collected (27 an t-Sultain 1936 DE), and the market-due at seventeen in the hundred since the Treasury fixed it after the Long War (22 an Cèitean 2023 DE). The windy coast pays neither due, and the roll carries no line for it.

V. The Windy Coast

In the far north-west, beyond the Tuathaich shires and past the northern edge of Seann Vell's lands, lies a low shore of heather moor, blanket bog and bare rock, open to the gales off the north-western sea, that no shire holds. The Ròdaich call it an Oirthir Ghaothach, the windy coast. It is a little under two parts in a hundred of the island's land, some 190 square miles, in two pieces: a long stretch of shore, and a small cape to the east of it. Its bays open on the waters where the raiders have sheltered since the Age of Strangers (10 an Giblean 1795 DE, 4 an t-Sultain 1941 DE), and the sea-beast of the north-west cape is reported off it (12 am Màrt 1834 DE, 9 an Gearran 1949 DE).

Why no one holds it. The humans' surveyors stopped at the edge of the great moss, which no chain can cross (20 an Giblean 1902 DE), and when the council drew the shires on the humans' lines it drew nothing where there were no lines. Its minute says only that the windy coast "is not in the survey" (15 an Dùbhlachd 1932 DE). No council since has taken it in. There is no ore there, no field and no harbour the kingdom would use. A shire there would need a maor, and a maor there would need the fleet to keep the raiders' bays, and when the raiders came to Cathair gheal the council, asked twice, sent no help (8 an Giblean 1949 DE). The Moot claims no land of its own and has never asked for this.

Who lives there. Tuathaich families keep the windy coast: sealers, fowlers, and herders on the moor's edge, in no town. The kingdom has never counted them. The Moot's tallies put them near nine thousand, a figure the royal clerks do not accept. No maor, justice or census clerk has gone there, and they pay no due.

In the Long War. When Cnoc thais fell, some of its holdouts went on past the hills and out onto the windy coast, and the regiments did not follow them beyond the shire line (10 an Lùnastal 2020 DE). The open record of the war names the kingdom's enemy only as those "of no shire". The holdouts who came down to the seventh regiment's posts after Muileann ghlas (10 an Dùbhlachd 2021 DE) came from the hills, and the record does not say whether any came back from the coast.

VI. The Peoples on the Land

The land of Rodos, with its islands, is some 10,900 square miles, of which the shires hold some 10,720. The two living peoples divide it between them roughly as the burgs divide it. The Old Ones hold none of it. Their names remain on thirty burgs and thirteen shires, and no household of theirs is counted anywhere (Appendix F).

PeopleBurgsShare of the island's landIn the burgsIn the country
Ròdaich441some eighty-five parts in a hundred (about 9,220 square miles)4,411,00027,224,000
Tuathaich64some fifteen parts in a hundred (about 1,680 square miles), of which the windy coast is nearly two543,0003,237,000 within the shires; the windy coast uncounted
Seann-Dhaoinenonenone——

The figures are the kingdom's count for the present year, on which the head-due is laid. The Ròdaich country is the capital's shire and every shire of the south, the east and the centre. The Tuathaich country is the north and north-west, and its middle lies in the shire of Cnoc ghorm. Together the two peoples number some 35,415,000 within the shires, one in seven of them in a burg.

Appendix I — The Land and Waters of Rodos

This appendix describes the ground the history happened on: the size and shape of the island, its countries and what covers them, the central mountains and the lesser hills, the rivers and their courses, Loch chrom, the offshore islands, the climate, and the sea and its mist. The measurements are those of the humans' surveys, which the council kept when it drew the shires, and the heights are the surveyors' heights above the sea. Where the annals record a change in the land, the date is given.

The island

Rodos is a little over two hundred miles from the capes of the far north-west to the eastern cape, and nowhere much more than a hundred miles from the north coast to the south. The main island covers about eleven thousand square miles. Twelve small islands lie off its coasts, and the largest of them is under seventeen square miles. One sea surrounds all of it, and the Ròdaich call it by one name on every coast, north and south: Muir Mhanannain, Manannan's sea, for the lord of the sea whose mist lay on it and hid the island from every ship beyond until the humans came out of the west (13 am Faoilleach 1780 DE, 5 an Gearran 1780 DE).

The coasts differ from one another. The north coast is long and broken, cut by straits and sounds into headlands and near-islands, and most of the places named Caol (strait), Ros (headland) and Ceann (point) lie along it. Its one wide bay is the Hawk bay, shared by Ros gheal, Ros leathan and Seann Skell. The south coast is shorter and more sheltered. Its great inlet is the gulf, which the Abhainn uaine reaches at Cathair mhòr and whose mouth Ros bhàn guards from its white headland. On the west coast the Abhainn gheal comes down to the sea at Inis thais and Caol leathan, and every boat bound for the capital's waters passes between them. The east coast runs from the eastern narrows round the eastern cape, where the light of Baile ìseal stands (Taigh-solais Baile ìseal).

The sea has taken land more than once. In the Ancient Age it rose over the low neck that joined Eilean dhubh to the main island (13 an t-Iuchar 12,418 BDE). A storm drove it over the harbour of Seann Chwen (18 an Dùbhlachd 2120 BDE), and in the first years of the new kingdom the Great Wave came in over the southern coast in a single night (3 an t-Ògmhios 1933 DE).

The countries and what covers them

About two parts in five of Rodos is open moor, heather, bog and short grass with no trees on it except in the valleys. Three parts in ten are birch and pine. A fifth is wet woodland of oak, alder and hazel. Something under a tenth is the drier oak woods of the east and the capital's country. The fens, the grass plateau of Dùn dhearg and the rough grazing at the north-western end of the shire of Seann Vell make up the rest.

The northern moors. The whole northern third of the island, from the Tuathaich country in the north-west to the harbours of the north-east, is low moor, most of it under a hundred and fifty feet. The winters there are long, wet and windy, snow lies on the moor for days at a time and on the higher ground for weeks, and the summers are short and dry. Trees grow only in the sheltered valleys. The groves that give so many northern villages their Doire names are some of these: oak, birch and hazel in the hollows, with bog and heather between them. The pollen in the bog under Doire ghlas shows that the oak came to these lowlands after the cold years (11 an Lùnastal 12,546 BDE), and that it fell back again when the winters lengthened (19 an t-Sultain 4013 BDE). The groves have stood in the valleys ever since. The moor is sheep country. It keeps the wool fairs of Tobar ghorm and Baile gharbh, the peat banks of Achadh gharbh and Cnoc dhubh, and barley and oats in every hollow that will take them. The north's largest towns are all on the coast or close to it: Caol mhòr, Doire ghlas, Baile Mòr mhòr on its northern plain (13 an t-Sultain 4985 BDE), and the harbours of the Hawk bay.

The windy coast. At the far north-western horn of the island the moor gives out onto an Oirthir Ghaothach, the windy coast, about a hundred and ninety square miles that no shire holds, and onto the rough grazing at the northern end of Seann Vell's shire beside it. It is the barest ground on Rodos: low heather moor and blanket bog with no tree on it, open to the gales off the north-western sea, which have kept it bare since the oak came to the rest of the island (22 an Lùnastal 12,473 BDE). Behind the shore lies the great moss, bog that no cart and no surveyor's chain can cross. The shore itself has seal-rocks, skerries and fowling cliffs, and sea mist lies on it for days together in summer. The windy coast keeps about nine thousand people, sealers, fowlers and herders, in no town, and the northern end of Seann Vell's shire about twice as many.

The birch and pine country. South of the moors a broad belt of birch and pine crosses the island from the western plain to the eastern hills, rising from under two hundred feet in the west to the skirts of the central mountains. It is the largest single stretch of woodland on Rodos, with hill pasture in its clearings. The Abhainn ìseal runs through the middle of it, past Inis bhàn and Cnoc bheag, and the western hills rise at its south-western edge.

The central mountains. East of the middle of the island the ground rises into the central mountains, a single massif about seventy miles from west to east and thirty-five from north to south, from the hills behind the capital's country to the eastern foothills. The Doire uaine hills are its heart. The highest ground stands a little under three thousand six hundred feet, above Muileann gheal. Dùn ìseal, where the flame was kept, stands at about two thousand six hundred feet under the summit ridge (28 an t-Ògmhios 2995 BDE), and the silver town of Muileann chiar at nearly three thousand. The vein lies under this massif. The crack at Tobar dhìreach is at about two thousand six hundred feet, and the high valleys round it, where the first hearths lie under the turf at Achadh dhìreach, are the oldest settled ground in the record (16 an Cèitean 12,621 BDE). The high ground is birch and pine below and bare moor above. Snowfields lay on the summits in the cold years (14 an t-Ògmhios 12,697 BDE), and snow still lies late on the high passes in a hard spring (13 an Giblean 527 BDE). The warm springs below Muileann ruadh (Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh) come up on the south-eastern side of the massif. On the eastern shoulder, round Dùn dhearg and Cnoc ghlas, is the only open grassland on the island, a dry plateau between fifteen hundred and two thousand feet in the lee of the mountains. It is the eastern plain of the annals (7 an Lùnastal 3830 BDE), and its granaries fed the mountain districts in hard years (19 am Màrt 2565 BDE, 15 an Dùbhlachd 526 BDE). The ground in the massif has moved in every age, most of all in the hills round Cill ghlas east of the capital.

The lesser hills. The hills east of the capital, the country of Muileann chrom and Cill ghlas, are the western foothills of the massif. The towns there stand between a thousand and thirteen hundred feet, with higher ground behind them. The western hills are low: round Àth leathan, where the road from the south enters them, and north to Muileann àrsaidh and Cnoc thais, they rarely rise above four hundred feet, but they are broken, wooded and easy to hide in, as the holdouts found (11 an Giblean 2020 DE).

The capital's country. Around Cathair dhearg and Loch chrom the land is low and fertile, under wet oak woods to the west and south and drier oak woods to the east. The capital itself stands on a low rise above the water (23 am Màrt 1300 BDE).

The wet west. West of the lake and along the west coast the woods are wet oak, alder and hazel, and the island's largest fens lie behind the coast from Muileann naomh north to Baile fhiadhaich and Muileann àrsaidh. The heath of the west is wet heath on thin soil, good for goats and not worth ploughing (31 am Màrt 2400 BDE). With the south, this coast has the most rain on the island.

The south. The south coast from Inis chrom to Seann Bhral is the warmest and wettest part of Rodos, almost all of it wet woodland. Behind Baile ghorm lie the fens of the south-west, whose marsh plants gave the dyers of Baile ghorm their blue, and whose salt-pans the Stone Kings fought over (9 am Faoilleach 6929 BDE).

The eastern oak country. From the eastern foothills of the massif to the east coast the woods are broad-leaved and the ground is drier: oak and hazel with pasture between, and the best cattle ground on the island. The Black Wind came in on this coast (1 an Gearran 5184 BDE).

The rivers

A hundred and fifty-seven rivers and streams are named on Rodos. A hundred and fifteen are rivers in their own right. The rest are forks and branches that join a larger river, and creeks, brooks and streams too short to carry a boat. The larger rivers are all called Abhainn with a describing word after it, and the small ones take the endings -as and -eas. The describing words are few, so the names repeat: there are three rivers called Abhainn ìseal and three called Abhainn naomh, and the record names each by the towns on it. Most of the rivers are short. They rise in the central mountains or the moors and reach the sea within a day or two's walk.

Abhainn ìseal, the longest river on Rodos, about fifty-three miles. It rises in the northern foothills of the massif near Àth ghlas, at about seven hundred and forty feet, and runs north-west through the birch and pine country past Cuan bheag, Inis bhàn, the river-island of Inis ìseal, Cnoc bheag and Ceann òg, to the north coast below Ros gheal. It settled into its present wide bed in the Ancient Age (2 an t-Ògmhios 12,233 BDE), the dawn-burning of the Hawk went up it from the coast (28 am Faoilleach 927 BDE), and it last broke its banks along its lower reach in 1963 DE.

Abhainn fhionn, about forty-five miles. It rises in the east near Baile chrom, at about nine hundred and fifty feet, and runs west past Ceann àrsaidh, Cuan chrom, Muileann mhin, Inis mhòr, Cuan uaine and Achadh àrsaidh into Loch chrom at Cathair dhomhain. It is the capital's river road to the east. Its shallows had the first made crossing of any river on the island (15 am Màrt 3973 BDE), and King Tormod Bàn's sons drowned in it in spate (18 an t-Ògmhios 495 DE).

Abhainn uaine, about forty miles. It rises in the central mountains near Doire mhòr and runs south past Ceann fhada, Baile thais, the landing of Cidhe Beag (Cidhe Beag), Seann Toll, Cuan dhearg and Ros bhàn to the gulf at Cathair mhòr. Meltwater off the mountains cut its bed (14 an t-Ògmhios 12,697 BDE), and the washing of the Company's ore upstream silted it black (27 am Faoilleach 1812 DE).

Abhainn chaol, about thirty-four miles. It rises high in the massif near Baile dhìreach, at nearly three thousand feet, and runs east to the sea below Seann Dunn. Its fork, the eastern Abhainn ìseal, joins it below Caol shean. The river towns of Ros fhionn, Ceann ghorm and the river-island of Inis uaine stand on it. It is fast and dangerous in the wet season (10 an t-Ògmhios 3921 BDE).

Abhainn gheal, the northern, about thirty-one miles. It rises in the massif near Àth gharbh and runs north to the north coast near Muileann fhada.

Abhainn dhomhain, the capital's river, about thirty miles. It rises in the low country south of the capital near Baile ìseal and runs north past Àth fhiadhaich and Doire chaol to Cathair dhearg, where Drochaid Cathair dhearg (Drochaid Cathair dhearg) crosses it. A little below the capital it joins the Abhainn gheal under Loch chrom. Its fords took the carriers in the Holy Age (3 an Gearran 2845 BDE), and the grain barges came down it to the capital (3 an Giblean 2 BDE).

Abhainn naomh, the western, about thirty miles. It rises on the low ground of the west near Achadh gheal and runs past Inis àrsaidh, Seann Skell and Àth chrom to the sea at Ros àrsaidh. After the Abhainn gheal it carries more water than any river on the island, and its deep pool at Seann Skell made that town the great river port of the west (1 an t-Iuchar 11,994 BDE).

Abhainn gheal, the lake river, about twenty-four miles. It is the outflow of Loch chrom. It leaves the lake by Seann Warr and runs short, deep and slow past Baile ghlas to the sea between Inis thais and Caol leathan. It carries more water than any other river on Rodos, and sea-going hulls can come up it into the lake (21 an t-Iuchar 1782 DE). The pilots of Caol leathan have taken a toll on it since the Holy Age.

Abhainn ghorm, the north-eastern, about twenty-seven miles. It rises in the northern massif and runs north past Inis mhòr and Caol bheag to the sea at Ros chiar, and the north-eastern grain went down it in barges (4 am Faoilleach 115 DE).

The mountain rivers of the south. The Abhainn mhòr, Abhainn dhubh, Abhainn bhàn and Abhainn chiar all rise high in the massif and fall south to the south coast in twenty miles or less. The Abhainn gheal of the east joins the Abhainn bhàn at Ceann bhàn. They rise fast after rain on the eastern hills (26 an Cèitean 124 BDE).

The rivers of the north-east. The Abhainn bheag rises below the library at Muileann chaol and runs north-east past Ros fhionn of the old bridge and Inis bheag to the sea at Caol chrom. The north-eastern Abhainn naomh runs past Ceann dhomhain to the library's landing at Ceann mhin.

Loch chrom

Loch chrom is the island's only lake of any size (24 am Faoilleach 1978 DE). It lies in the low country just north of the capital, about seventy-four square miles of fresh water. The Abhainn fhionn and the lesser Abhainn ìseal come into it from the east, the lesser Abhainn naomh from the north, and a dozen streams from the moors. Its one outflow is the Abhainn gheal.

The lake is the capital's harbour. The towns of the capital shore stand round its southern and western edge: Cathair dhomhain at the mouth of the Abhainn fhionn, Ros dhomhain, Seann Vell, Doire fhiadhaich, Doire fhada, Baile ghlas, and Seann Warr on the western shore, where brine springs rise in the reed marsh behind the town. Ceann gheal stands on the northern shore. Sea-going ships reach the lake from the west coast by the Abhainn gheal, and the lake towns have fitted, loaded and built ships for the capital since the Holy Age.

The lake rises and falls with the seasons. The keepers at Ros dhomhain began to cut its high-water line on a boulder in the harbour mouth in the Ancient Age (26 an Gearran 5893 BDE), and the rock is still called the tide-rock, though Loch chrom has no tide. By the end of that age the lake stood a hand higher on the rock than at the first cut (10 am Màrt 5854 BDE). The oldest works on the lake are the platforms on oak piles in its shallows (7 am Màrt 11,354 BDE), which burned to the waterline (24 an Cèitean 6076 BDE). Its trout were kept for the Crown's table until 1978 DE.

Sliochd Raghnaill's boats made the round of the offshore islands in a single season (27 an Giblean 223 BDE). Besides these twelve there are skerries, tidal islets and river-islands too small for the surveyors' charts. Inis mhin, Inis naomh and Inis bheag of the north coast stand on tidal islets, and Inis mhòr, Inis ìseal, Inis uaine, Inis chrom and Inis leathan on islands in their rivers.

The climate

Rodos is a mild, wet and windy island for its northern place, with cool summers and winters that are seldom hard. At sea level the year averages about forty-eight degrees of the humans' scale on every coast, a little more on the south coast than on the north, and the harbours do not freeze. The cold is in the height. The towns of the hills east of the capital, at about a thousand feet, average near forty-four; Dùn ìseal, under the summit ridge, near thirty-nine; and the summits of the massif near thirty-six. Snow lies on the high tops and the high passes through the winter and on the northern moors for days at a time, and frost is common inland from the first of an t-Samhain to the end of the spring. Winter is the long season in the north, and it is a season of gales more than of frost: a gale that drove the sea up the river before the grain fleet had sailed was remembered at Inis mhòr for generations (2 an Dàmhair 1190 DE).

The rain comes in off the western ocean. The west coast and the south get the most, and the fens lie there. The central mountains take much of what is left, so the eastern plateau and the northern moors lie in their lee and are dry. The north has springs that never fail, and the towns built round them are remembered for it (13 an t-Sultain 4985 BDE), because its summers can go without rain. Droughts come to the east: the springs of Achadh shean failed in the Ancient Age (8 an Giblean 5595 BDE), and the Long Drought lay over the island for three years in the Age of Strangers (25 an Lùnastal 1885 DE). The storm season comes at the end of the year, and the oldest law on Rodos was written for it (7 an Cèitean 5273 BDE).

The sea and the mist

Muir Mhanannain is a grey, short-tempered sea. The gales come in off it from the west and north-west, most of all between Samhain and the spring, and sea mist lies on the coasts in still weather, thickest on the north and north-west in early summer. The hunters of the north shore took seals on the skerries off Eilean fhada in the autumn gales in the Ancient Age (30 an t-Sultain 12,313 BDE), and the whale-boats of the north coast still go out in summer. The northern passage is dangerous in winter. After a Company brig was driven onto the skerries off Eilean fhada in mist and a spring gale (13 an t-Sultain 1834 DE), it was held closed from midwinter to the end of spring.

Beyond the headlands to the west lay Manannan's own mist. The Ròdaich tell that the fleet of the Sundering sailed into it (19 an Giblean 1 DE), and the order of Manannan teaches that he shut the western sea behind the fleet with it and hid the island from every ship beyond (Appendix B; 1 an t-Sultain 615 DE). The priests of Manannan recorded it thinning in the last years of the Age of Sundering (27 an Dàmhair 1774 DE), and it lifted in the winter of the Crossing, when the humans' ships came out of it (13 am Faoilleach 1780 DE). Since the Severance no ship has come from the west, and the priests say the lord of the sea has shut it again (11 an t-Ògmhios 1932 DE).

There is no lasting ice on Rodos. The snowfields that lay on the central mountains in the cold years have been seasonal since the oak came (14 an t-Ògmhios 12,697 BDE), and the snow of the high tops is gone by the summer.

Appendix J — The Arms of Rodos

This appendix sets down the arms of the kingdom, of its hundred and twenty-three shires and of its towns, as Clàr nan Suaicheantas, the roll of arms kept by the council and copied to Leabharlann Muileann chaol, records them. It gives each shire's arms in full, the arms of the capital and of the great cities, and an account of the town arms by kind. Where the record says what a charge means, or when and why it was granted, this appendix says so. Where it does not, the arms are given and nothing more is claimed.

I. How Rodos came by its arms

Signs before arms. Rodos had carved signs long before it had arms. The oldest is the hawk over a door at Àth mhòr, older than any rite (13 an Dùbhlachd 5748 BDE). The road-guards of Caol leathan swore on a white stone carved as a wolf (12 am Faoilleach 1990 BDE). At Seann Vell a scorpion was cut in yellow stone for worship (4 an t-Samhain 150 BDE), and the harbours of the order of the Stone still line their quays with wolf-head posts. These are the signs of the orders and of towns. None of them was borne on a shield, and none of them is a grant.

The custody's seal. The first arms on the island were the seal of the vein-house above Muileann dhearg: a trellis of gold on blue with a hollow lozenge, the mascle, laid over it. The custodians read the trellis as the galleries of the mountain and the mascle as the slab laid over the first break (19 am Màrt 12,773 BDE). No roll says when the seal was first cut. When the crown and the custody were joined, the king's letters were sealed with it, and the crown added only a white band across the field (1 an t-Ògmhios 826 DE). Those are the arms of the kingdom still. The seven houses of custody sealed with the custody's seal and kept no badges of their own that the record knows.

Under the humans. The Residency and the Company sealed with their own devices, and the custody's seal went out of use. The Administration's district seals were cut in the humans' manner, on a shield with a rounded foot.

The roll of arms. When the council drew the shires (12 an Dùbhlachd 1932 DE) and set a maor over each (4 am Faoilleach 1933 DE), every maor needed a seal for his court. The council's clerks made the roll of arms for them (2 an Gearran 1933 DE). The kingdom's arms were cut again from the custody's seal, and each shire was given arms of its own. The Ròdaich shires took the pointed wedge of the custody's seal. The Tuathaich shires kept the heater of the district seals they had used before, and every Tuathaich town has kept it since. Many of the charges on the roll were drawn from a book of arms left at the Residency, as the shire lines were drawn from the humans' surveys. That is why lions, parrots, dragons and crocodiles stand on the seals of shires where no one has ever seen one.

The town arms. The clerks of the first chronicle circuit copied the seal of every town they visited into the roll (2 an Giblean 1948 DE), and from then on the roll held the arms of all five hundred and five places. In the north most of the arms were copied from the humans' old town seals, because few Tuathaich would show the clerks their own.

Changes since. The roll has been changed once at an order's asking. The Hawk houses of Siorrachd Cnoc bheag, having seated their own custodian, asked for a hawk on the shire's arms, and the council granted it (29 an t-Samhain 1964 DE). The coinage seal lost its obsidian ink (3 an t-Ògmhios 2014 DE), but the arms on it were not changed, and the high custodian's protest was about the ink (31 an t-Iuchar 2014 DE).

II. How the arms are read

The arms are given here in plain heraldic English. The field is named first, then any partition, then the ordinaries (the broad bands and crosses), then the charges. The colours are:

TinctureColour
Orgold or yellow
argentsilver or white
gulesred
azureblue
sableblack
vertgreen
purpurepurple
sanguineblood-red

Trellised is the custody's trellis. A mascle is a lozenge with its middle cut away, the hollow stone. A shield is a wedge unless the entry says otherwise. Where a shire's name is shared with another shire, the entry names the part of the island it lies in.

III. The arms of the kingdom

Rìoghachd Ròdais. Azure trellised Or, a fess cotised argent, over all a mascle argent.

The trellis and the mascle are the custody's. The fess, a white band between two thin ones, is the crown's addition at the joining (1 an t-Ògmhios 826 DE). Macha's order had been the court's order for four centuries before the joining (31 an Dùbhlachd 402 DE), and no king put her horses on the seal. The house of Òrd Mhacha at Cathair dhearg keeps the regalia (26 an Gearran 1936 DE), and the seal has never been in its keeping.

Nineteen shires and a hundred and five towns bear the crown's trellis in their own arms, and sixty-seven towns bear the mascle. The roll says only that the trellis was granted where a shire asked for the crown's colours. It does not say why these asked and others did not. No Tuathaich town bears the trellis. The mascle is on the arms of one Tuathaich shire, Siorrachd Caol mhòr, and of two Tuathaich towns, Caol mhòr and Cnoc uaine.

Of the hundred and twenty-three shires, twelve bear the heater: the eleven Tuathaich shires, the island shire of Eilean dhìreach among them (Appendix H), and Inis mhin on the northern shore, which has one town of each people. Fifteen bear no charge at all, only their field, partitions and ordinaries.

V. The arms of the towns

By kind. The roll holds the arms of five hundred and five towns. Four hundred and forty-one are on the wedge and sixty-four on the heater, one heater for every Tuathaich town. A hundred and five are on the crown's trellis, and seventeen of these carry the mascle as well, so that their arms come close to the kingdom's own. Of the other fields, argent is the commonest, then azure, Or and gules, then sable, purpure and vert. Ninety-five towns bear no charge, and eighteen of those bear nothing but their field and its partition. The commonest charge is the mascle. Crosses of one kind or another are on sixty-three town arms. A hundred and five towns bear a beast, and thirty-one of those are beasts no one on Rodos has seen: lions, griffins, dragons, crocodiles, elephants, a rhinoceros. Twenty bear figures: horsemen, archers, monks, angels and two skeletons. Ships and anchors are on the harbours, and ploughs, scythes, saws and anvils on the farm and mill towns, but only twenty-eight of the hundred and thirty-three harbour towns carry anything from the sea.
