VI. The beasts of the orders on the roll

Most of the orders of the Old Faith have a beast: the Hawk order its hawk, the druid schools Flidais's stag, Macha's order the black horse and the grey, the order of the Stone the wolf of its Fianna, and Manannan's order the yellow scorpion of his Cup. The roll does not carry them as a reader of the orders might expect, and the orders have asked for them only twice.

The Hawk. Mòd, the Hawk of Acaill, is on one shield in the roll, the arms of Siorrachd Cnoc bheag, and only since the Hawk houses asked for him (29 an t-Samhain 1964 DE). No town bears a hawk. The northern Seann Skell, where the rite began, bears the crown's field, and Àth mhòr, with the oldest hawk on the island over a door, bears ploughshares. The three falcons of Siorrachd Doire shean are in the country of the Stone, and the record does not explain them.

Macha's horses. No arms on the roll bear Dubh Sainglenn as the wood-watchers told of him, the black horned beast of the wood. The order's houses show the black horse and the grey only in the black and white of their floors (14 am Màrt 1420 DE), and the capital reads its own ermine, black on white, in that way. The capital's shire bears a horseman, and Cnoc dhubh, a town of Macha's order, a horse's head; the roll does not say that either is hers. The horses on the arms of Muileann leathan and its shire are in Tuathaich church country, and nobody reads them as Macha's.

The Wolf of the Fianna. No shire of the Stone bears a wolf. Inis thais bears masonry, which its people read as the Stone itself, since its plain name Clach is the common word for stone. Caol leathan's three beasts are lions in the roll and wolves in the town. Two towns bear a wolf's head: Achadh fhada, a town of the Stone, and Ceann mhòr in the north, where the head is the old magistrate's. Baile ghorm's wolf-head posts stand on its quays and are not on its arms.

The Stag. The druid schools have never worshipped Flidais's stag (7 an Dùbhlachd 2881 BDE), and none of their chief towns bears one. The stags on the roll are at Àth shean, in shire and town, and at Cnoc òg, both towns of Macha's order, and at Doire chaol, the hunters' village of the schools that sends its oak to Caol gharbh. Stags' antlers are on the arms of four more towns.

The Scorpion. The badge of Manannan's Cup is on the arms of the western Seann Skell, at the house's asking (2 an Gearran 1933 DE). The three towns that bear a scorpion, Seann Chwen, Àth chrom and Achadh gharbh, are none of them towns of Manannan's order, and Seann Vell, which cut the first scorpion in yellow stone, bears a fleur-de-lis on the crown's field.

The others. Òrd Bhrìde has no beast. It has the mascle, the hollow stone of Crom over the vein, on the kingdom's arms and on sixty-seven towns, and it has never asked for more. Brìde's flame is on no arms. Of the other gods' signs the roll holds a harp, an Dagda's, at Cnoc dhubh, a town of the schools, and three ravens, the birds of the Morrìgan in the tellings, at Baile thais, Àth shean of the northern march and Achadh mhin; none of these towns claims the god. The Old Spirits keep no beast, and the people of the mounds are on no arms. The Church asked for no sign on the roll. The goose of the Grey Night is on no arms, and Baile chrom, the vigil's one town, bears ships.

The Houses of Rodos

Clann Fhearchair of Baile Mòr dhomhain

One of the seven houses of custody regrouped after the Sundering (4 an t-Iuchar 16 DE). Its seat at Baile Mòr dhomhain gave Rodos the first king chosen by the houses (19 an Gearran 143 DE), and the double court near the mountain lasted as long as the house held the crown. After Sìleas nic Fhearchair the crown went to her son Uisdean mac Dhùghaill and his line.

  • Lachlann mac Fhearchair b. 12 an Giblean 79 DE – d. 4 an t-Samhain 145 DE
    Father of the first king of the house; the house roll gives his name and nothing more.
    • Fearchar mac Lachlainn = Eilidh nic Dhùghaill b. 19 an Gearran 118 DE – d. 14 an Lùnastal 172 DE
      Chosen by the heads of the seven houses and crowned at Cathair dhearg 19 an Gearran 143 DE; kept part of each year's court at Baile Mòr dhomhain.
      • Fearchar Donn = Mòrag nic Iain b. 24 an t-Iuchar 149 DE – d. 12 an Cèitean 217 DE
        Crowned after his father without dispute, 21 an t-Ògmhios 172 DE.
        • Lachlann Òg mac Fhearchair b. 27 an Dàmhair 197 DE – d. 14 an Dàmhair 213 DE
          Elder brother of Sìleas; died young, before his father.
        • Sìleas nic Fhearchair = Dùghall b. 25 an t-Samhain 204 DE – d. 27 an t-Ògmhios 285 DE
          Queen after her father; fixed the firlot of Cathair dhearg, 11 an Dàmhair 222 DE; reigned more than half a century.
      • Mòr nic Fhearchair b. 9 am Faoilleach 142 DE – d. 4 an t-Ògmhios 199 DE
        Sister of Fearchar Donn; given in marriage to a man of Clann Ìomhair at Dùn dhearg.
    • Iain mac Lachlainn b. 7 an t-Ògmhios 122 DE – d. 20 an Gearran 177 DE
      The king's younger brother; kept the house's hall at Baile Mòr dhomhain in the seasons the court was away.
      • Gormshuil nic Iain b. 24 am Faoilleach 150 DE – d. 19 an Gearran 204 DE
        Named in the house roll among those who swore to Fearchar Donn.
      • Seumas mac Iain b. 24 an Gearran 162 DE – d. 11 an Gearran 224 DE
        A reeve of the house's grazing below the pass; nothing else is recorded.
        • Eilidh nic Sheumais b. 20 an t-Ògmhios 185 DE – d. 28 an Lùnastal 273 DE
          Kept the house roll at Baile Mòr dhomhain in Queen Sìleas's reign; the roll is lost and is known only from a later copy.

The custodians of Ceann àrsaidh

A custodian family of Ceann àrsaidh that gave the Council of Custodians its second high custodian under the humans (15 an Dùbhlachd 1799 DE), lost its seat on the council in the next generation, and sent the first Ròdaich child to an Tìr Thall (12 an Giblean 1830 DE).

  • Coinneach Glas = Mòrag nic Uilleim b. 17 an t-Samhain 1753 DE – d. 12 am Faoilleach 1804 DE
    High custodian after Tormod mac Ailein; had never met a human before the Crossing and dealt with little else after it.
    • Eachann Mòr = Seonag nic Dhòmhnaill b. 16 an Dàmhair 1788 DE – d. 18 an t-Iuchar 1843 DE
      A custodian of Ceann àrsaidh who lost his place on the council; sent his son west with the Mission's letter.
      • Calum mac Eachainn b. 14 am Faoilleach 1816 DE – d. 15 an t-Samhain 1853 DE
        Sailed west on a Company ship, 12 an Giblean 1830 DE, and is never recorded returning. No roll records his death, and the dates given for it are uncertain.
      • Ruairidh mac Eachainn b. 14 an Dàmhair 1819 DE – d. 12 an t-Sultain 1877 DE
        Held no seat on the council; the family's place there was not restored in the age.
        • Coinneach mac Ruairidh b. 29 an t-Samhain 1849 DE – d. 5 an Cèitean 1927 DE
          A custodian of the town's shrine of Macha; his name is on the petitions of the Levy years.
          • Tormod mac Choinnich b. 27 an t-Iuchar 1886 DE – d. 15 an t-Iuchar 1935 DE
            The last of the line the family roll records.
        • Anna nic Ruairidh b. 1 an t-Sultain 1859 DE – d. 28 an Gearran 1911 DE
          Married inland; the family roll records her going and not where.
      • Seònaid nic Eachainn b. 19 an Cèitean 1813 DE – d. 5 an Dùbhlachd 1894 DE
        Kept the family's house at Ceann àrsaidh after her brother sailed.
    • Iseabail nic Choinnich b. 9 an t-Sultain 1787 DE – d. 24 an Lùnastal 1843 DE
      Kept her father's copies of the council roll after his death.

Na Maoir of Muileann chrom

The line of the Company's overseers at Muileann chrom. The Ròdaich gave the first of them the byname Maor, steward (17 an t-Ògmhios 1815 DE), and the staff and the byname went from father to son until Mòrag nic Iain Maor broke the staff at the Company's door (24 an Cèitean 1927 DE).

  • Dòmhnall b. 5 an t-Sultain 1743 DE – d. 15 an t-Ògmhios 1801 DE
    A hewer of Muileann chrom; known only from his son's name.
    • Raghnall mac Dhòmhnaill, Raghnall Maor = Catrìona nic Ailein b. 17 an t-Ògmhios 1765 DE – d. 3 an Giblean 1841 DE

            A hewer; the staff passed over him to his sister.
          • Mòrag nic Iain Maor b. 24 an Dùbhlachd 1871 DE – d. 19 am Faoilleach 1942 DE
            The first woman to hold the staff, 12 an t-Sultain 1910 DE; fourth and last of her line to hold it.
          • Catrìona nic Iain b. 9 an Giblean 1878 DE – d. 17 an Giblean 1956 DE
            Sister of Mòrag Maor; kept the slate-roofed house after the staff was broken.
        • Ailean mac Dhòmhnaill b. 6 am Màrt 1838 DE – d. 28 an t-Ògmhios 1891 DE
          Worked the galleries under his brother's staff.

The keepers of An Taigh-seinnse Mòr

The family that has kept the carters' house at the halfway stage of the ore road (An Taigh-seinnse Mòr) since Seònaid Bhàn reopened it (1 an Lùnastal 1813 DE). Her great-grandson Aonghas kept it through the years of the fortified houses (26 an Gearran 1922 DE).

  • Seònaid Bhàn = Pàdraig mac Artair b. 29 an Dùbhlachd 1784 DE – d. 28 an Dùbhlachd 1847 DE
    Reopened the house; the only keeper on the road who took both marks and barter.
    • Murchadh mac Phàdraig b. 21 an Gearran 1816 DE – d. 12 an Giblean 1872 DE
      Kept the house after his mother.
      • Seònaid nic Mhurchaidh = Dùghall mac Iain b. 22 an t-Iuchar 1846 DE – d. 16 am Màrt 1914 DE
        Kept the house after her father, through the Levy and the Long Drought.
        • Aonghas mac Dhùghaill b. 30 an Giblean 1873 DE – d. 17 an Giblean 1965 DE
          Great-grandson of Seònaid Bhàn; kept the house in the years the constables searched it most and found least.
          • Seumas mac Aonghais b. 22 am Faoilleach 1910 DE – d. 23 am Màrt 1960 DE
            Kept the house after his father under the restored kingdom.
        • Eilidh nic Dhùghaill b. 3 an t-Ògmhios 1889 DE – d. 18 an Gearran 1956 DE
          Served in the house under her brother.
      • Ruairidh mac Mhurchaidh b. 30 an t-Sultain 1842 DE – d. 13 an t-Iuchar 1901 DE
        A carter on the ore road.
    • Peigi nic Phàdraig b. 16 an t-Samhain 1822 DE – d. 23 an t-Ògmhios 1875 DE
      Kept the byres and the carters' book.

Clann Choinnich of the silver guild

The family at the head of the refiners' guild that held the silver seam of Muileann chiar against the Company (31 am Màrt 1822 DE) and kept it under the Silver Compact until the rising. Its name is the name of the house of custody that brought the silver petitions of the Sundering age; the record does not trace the descent.

  • Coinneach mac Dhonnchaidh b. 16 an Giblean 1735 DE – d. 22 am Faoilleach 1810 DE
    A refiner of the seam; the guild ledger names him among its members at the Crossing.
    • Ùna nic Choinnich = Alasdair mac Ruairidh b. 22 an t-Sultain 1766 DE – d. 7 an Dùbhlachd 1855 DE
      Led the guild; met the Company's surveyors at the adit with the whole guild and its ledgers; refused Martha Gale's partnership when very old, 29 am Màrt 1846 DE.
      • Coinneach mac Alasdair b. 22 am Faoilleach 1795 DE – d. 6 an Lùnastal 1856 DE
        A refiner; carried the guild's bars to Seann Bhral.
        • Ùna nic Choinnich Òg b. 21 an Giblean 1828 DE – d. 29 an Dàmhair 1901 DE
          Named for her grandmother; sat on the guild's council in the years it sold bar silver for marks.
          • Ruairidh Ciar b. 30 an t-Sultain 1859 DE – d. 13 an t-Iuchar 1933 DE
            Among the guild members who opened the armoury in 1929 DE.
      • Beathag nic Alasdair b. 4 am Faoilleach 1795 DE – d. 27 an Giblean 1862 DE
        Sat on the guild's council after her mother.
    • Donnchadh mac Choinnich b. 5 an t-Samhain 1767 DE – d. 8 an Cèitean 1835 DE
      Kept the guild's weights and ledgers under his sister.
      • Iain mac Dhonnchaidh b. 3 an t-Ògmhios 1798 DE – d. 20 an Gearran 1864 DE
        Worked the new faces of the seam.
        • Dòmhnall mac Iain b. 22 an t-Iuchar 1831 DE – d. 16 am Màrt 1917 DE
          A refiner of the new town.

The Pikes

A human family descended, by its own account, from Thomas Pike, who kept the first tally-book of the trading post at Ros dhomhain (22 an t-Ògmhios 1782 DE) and held the Company alone after Harrow was lost. Its later members stayed on Rodos after the Severance and are counted among the Tuathaich of the north.

  • Thomas Pike = Anne b. 30 an Dàmhair 1754 DE – d. 11 am Màrt 1820 DE
    Trader at Ros dhomhain; partner of Harrow in the Company, and its sole holder from 1800 DE.
    • John Pike b. 22 an t-Samhain 1791 DE – d. 15 an Dàmhair 1843 DE
      Clerk of the Company's post at Ros dhomhain.
      • Daniel Pike b. 30 an t-Iuchar 1821 DE – d. 10 an Lùnastal 1887 DE
        A storekeeper on the northern concession.
        • Matthew Pike b. 14 an t-Samhain 1853 DE – d. 22 an t-Sultain 1906 DE
          A miller of the northern concession.
          • William Pike b. 26 an Dàmhair 1878 DE – d. 19 an t-Ògmhios 1947 DE
            Stayed in the north at the Severance.
            • Agnes Pike b. 22 an Gearran 1905 DE – d. 6 an Dùbhlachd 1988 DE
              A Tuathaich teacher; opened the school at Doire ghlas with Moot money and without the council's leave, 14 am Faoilleach 1944 DE.
            • Joseph Pike b. 8 an t-Iuchar 1920 DE – d. 25 an t-Ògmhios 1982 DE
              A fisherman of Caol mhòr.
      • Ann Pike b. 10 an Dùbhlachd 1818 DE – d. 18 an t-Samhain 1897 DE
        Married a farmer of the concession.
    • Sarah Pike b. 15 an t-Iuchar 1791 DE – d. 3 an Dàmhair 1856 DE
      Went home to an Tìr Thall and is not recorded returning.

The Hales

The family of the first marriage in two tongues on the record, made at Baile dhìreach (26 an Cèitean 1786 DE). The Moot's own genealogy traces its first speaker, Walter Hale, to that marriage. His great-grandson Peter Hale holds the Moot's chair in the present year (29 an Cèitean 2026 DE).

  • Samuel Hale = Eilidh nic Ruairidh, net-maker of Baile dhìreach b. 27 an Giblean 1765 DE – d. 14 am Faoilleach 1816 DE
    A human cooper; his marriage was entered in both the council's books.
    • John Hale b. 21 an Cèitean 1799 DE – d. 2 an t-Ògmhios 1853 DE
      A cooper of Baile dhìreach, like his father.
      • Thomas Hale b. 13 an Giblean 1824 DE – d. 25 am Faoilleach 1892 DE
        Claimed a customary cutting through his Ròdaich grandmother and lost it by Dunstan's rule, 4 am Màrt 1890 DE.
        • Richard Hale b. 8 an Lùnastal 1853 DE – d. 2 an Giblean 1907 DE
          A harbour hand in the north-west.
          • Walter Hale b. 31 am Faoilleach 1884 DE – d. 23 an Cèitean 1962 DE
            A former harbour clerk; first speaker of the Moot at Caol mhòr, 25 an Lùnastal 1931 DE.
            • David Hale b. 23 an t-Sultain 1914 DE – d. 1 an t-Sultain 1970 DE
              Kept the Moot's minute-books in his father's time.
              • Frank Hale b. 20 an Dùbhlachd 1943 DE – d. 25 an Giblean 2012 DE
                A fisherman of Caol mhòr; father of Peter Hale.
            • Alice Hale b. 21 am Faoilleach 1918 DE – d. 21 an Cèitean 2003 DE
              Taught in one of the Moot's schools.
    • Mary Hale b. 12 an Lùnastal 1794 DE – d. 5 an t-Iuchar 1850 DE
      A net-maker, like her mother.

The house of Mac Ùisdein of Cathair mhòr

A Ròdaich house of Cathair mhòr that held an overseer's post under the humans and the Sloc Mòr concession under the Crown (23 an Cèitean 1940 DE). It sold the concession back piece by piece, and it was the only house of the vein to move its money out before the vein failed it (4 an t-Sultain 2012 DE).

  • Ùisdean mac Ruairidh b. 20 an Giblean 1859 DE – d. 2 am Faoilleach 1932 DE
    Held the house's overseer's post under the Company; the post is the house's first entry in any roll.
    • Uisdean mac Ùisdein = Beathag nic Iain b. 18 an Dàmhair 1895 DE – d. 9 an Cèitean 1971 DE
      Given the Sloc Mòr on the humans' terms with the names changed; raised the market cross and the stone house at Cathair mhòr.
      • Ruairidh mac Uisdein b. 13 an t-Iuchar 1914 DE – d. 21 an Dàmhair 1995 DE
        Held the house's share in his father's last years.
        • Alasdair mac Ùisdein b. 3 an t-Sultain 1948 DE – d. 11 am Faoilleach 1998 DE
          Grandson of the first holder; borrowed against the house's share for the search for a second vein, 20 an Cèitean 1979 DE, and sold half the share to meet the debt.
        • Mòrag nic Ruairidh b. 6 an Dùbhlachd 1942 DE – d. 20 am Màrt 2015 DE
          Sister of Alasdair; kept the house's papers after the stone house was let to the Mine Board.
      • Dòmhnall mac Uisdein b. 28 an t-Samhain 1923 DE – d. 23 an t-Iuchar 1991 DE
        Kept the quarry at Achadh dhomhain under the house's mark.
      • Catrìona nic Uisdein b. 24 an t-Sultain 1922 DE – d. 8 an Dàmhair 2012 DE
        Married at Cathair mhòr; took no part in the concession.
    • Seonag nic Ùisdein b. 28 an t-Samhain 1895 DE – d. 5 an Giblean 1978 DE
      Kept the house's quarry accounts at Achadh dhomhain.

A Gazetteer of Rodos

Every town of the island, by shire: when and by whom it was founded, its history, and what the annals record there.

Siorrachd Achadh àrsaidh

Achadh àrsaidh

village · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 32,516

Founded 17 an t-Iuchar 791 BDE by the fishers of the capital's river. Known for the river quays that feed the capital.

An ancient field village on the Abhainn fhionn east of the capital, grown into one of the largest settlements on the island while keeping its village name. It is the seat of Siorrachd Achadh àrsaidh, and its river quays land the fish and grain that feed Cathair dhearg. It follows the order of Macha.

Cnoc dhubh

town · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 11,443

Founded 20 an Giblean 736 BDE by custodians of the capital's south. Known for black-hill citadel south of the capital.

Cnoc dhubh of Achadh àrsaidh is a black hill with a citadel, south-east of the capital, founded in the Holy Age. Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag lies to its west and the field of Muileann ghlas to its east. It keeps the capital's order, the order of Macha.

Dùn chiar

city · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 2,550

Founded 2 an Cèitean 2137 BDE by a custodian house guarding the capital's east. Known for dusky hill fort east of the capital.

Dùn chiar is a hill fort of dusky stone east of Cathair dhearg, called a city for its rank rather than its people, who are few. Its citadel and walls were rebuilt in every age, and it has served as the eastern guard of the capital since the kings of the Holy Age. It follows the capital's order, the order of Macha, and its garrison takes part in the rites of Cathair dhearg.

  • 30 am Faoilleach 1847 DE — Cloth for the camps at Dùn chiar

Siorrachd Achadh chaol

Achadh chaol

village · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 14,431

Founded 17 an Lùnastal 2815 BDE by Ròdaich barley farmers. Known for narrow barley fields.

Achadh chaol is a large village of narrow barley fields and the seat of its province. Its grain goes to the mills of Muileann dhìreach, and the two places have kept the same bargain since the Holy Age. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith.

  • 27 an Gearran 5126 BDE — Achadh chaol cleared
  • 5 an t-Sultain 2511 BDE — The shepherds of Achadh chaol
  • 16 am Màrt 1889 DE — Achadh chaol goes to the pits

Àth dhìreach

town · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 2,775

Founded 8 am Màrt 1869 DE by Ròdaich carters of the mining road. Known for the second regiment's garrison.

A straight ford with a citadel in the north-east, built as a waystation on the ore road in the Age of Strangers and fortified in the war before the Severance. Since the Long War it has been the station of An dàrna rèisimeid, the second regiment. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith.

  • 25 an Dàmhair 2020 DE — An dàrna rèisimeid raised

Baile dhearg

town · Ròdaich · Na Seann Spioradan · pop. 2,551

Founded 10 an t-Iuchar 1037 DE by farmers of Achadh chaol. Known for red town on the harbour road.

A red town in the east on the road to the harbour at Seann Toll. It keeps the Old Spirits.

Baile mhin

town · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 2,647

Founded 23 an Dàmhair 1136 DE by carters of the Achadh chaol road. Known for wheelwrights on the Achadh chaol road.

Baile mhin grew where the road from Achadh chaol to the coast levels out, a stopping place for carts. It is a small town of wheelwrights and stables. Its people send their grain to the mills at Muileann dhìreach.

Cnoc ruadh

town · Ròdaich · Na Seann Spioradan · pop. 9,725

Founded 14 am Màrt 2962 BDE by shepherds of the eastern uplands. Known for red-hill sheepwalks and Cuan ruadh wool.

Cnoc ruadh of Achadh chaol is a hill town of the eastern uplands, a sheep town since the Holy Age. Its wool goes down to Cuan ruadh for shipping. It keeps the ancestor rite of the Old Spirits.

Muileann dhìreach

town · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 10,994

Founded 17 an Lùnastal 1567 BDE by the custodian house of Achadh chaol. Known for grain mills on the straight race.

Muileann dhìreach was raised to grind the barley of Achadh chaol, and its mill-race still runs straight as a ruled line from the stream above the town. In the Age of Strangers it ground for the camps as well as for its own people, and the tithe clerks kept a counting-room beside the wheel. A reading-house of the druid schools stands on the square, and the miller's guild and the school have shared its bell since before anyone wrote the arrangement down.

Siorrachd Achadh mhòr

Achadh mhòr

village · Ròdaich · Na Seann Spioradan · pop. 42,136

Founded 13 am Màrt 1897 BDE by Ròdaich farming households of the eastern plain. Known for the great granary fields.

Achadh mhòr is still called a field village, though it is one of the largest settlements on the island and the seat of its province. It is the granary of the east, and the shared-meal custom of the Holy Age is said to have been kept here most faithfully. Travellers on the road stop at An Sligeanach Fad' às nearby.

  • 2 an t-Samhain 3601 BDE — Fields at Achadh mhòr
  • 28 am Faoilleach 1922 DE — Achadh mhòr keeps the ledgers
  • 22 am Màrt 2008 DE — Achadh mhòr's drovers

Ceann bhàn

town · Ròdaich · Na Seann Spioradan · pop. 6,325

Founded 29 an t-Samhain 1024 DE by the tavern-keepers of the white headland. Known for An Sligeanach Fad' às and dried venison.

A walled river port on a pale headland where the Abhainn gheal meets the Abhainn bhàn, with the famous tavern An Sligeanach Fad' às at its gate, where travellers eat dried venison. It grew around the tavern road, and its walls went up in the troubles, when the roadside houses became militia posts. It keeps the Old Spirits, trades with the great village of Achadh mhòr close by, and sends its goods down the Abhainn bhàn to Seann Warr on the coast.

Siorrachd Achadh naomh

Achadh naomh

village · Ròdaich · Na Seann Spioradan · pop. 26,585

Founded 5 am Faoilleach 721 BDE by keepers of the holy field. Known for holy field by Colbh Cnoc chiar.

Achadh naomh is a large village and the seat of its province in the north-central country, founded in the Holy Age on a field held sacred. Colbh Cnoc chiar stands to its east, carved 'remember the fire'. It keeps the ancestor rite of the Old Spirits.

  • 5 an t-Ògmhios 3510 BDE — Achadh naomh's spring-fields
  • 16 am Màrt 1802 DE — The hearths of Achadh naomh

Achadh naomh

village · Ròdaich · Na Seann Spioradan · pop. 24,923

Founded 28 an t-Sultain 675 BDE by Ròdaich households of the ancestor feasts. Known for the ancestor feasts on the unploughed field.

The holy field was a meeting ground for the ancestor feasts of the Old Spirits before any house stood on it, and the houses were built around its edge rather than upon it. It is now a village of twenty-five thousand and the seat of its province, yet the field at its heart is still left unploughed. The feasts are kept there as they were in the Holy Age.

Àth chaol

town · Ròdaich · Na Seann Spioradan · pop. 2,559

Founded 20 an t-Sultain 620 BDE by the ford-keepers of Achadh naomh. Known for narrow ford on the Inis mhin road.

A narrow ford in the east where the road to the harbour at Inis mhin crosses a stream. It keeps the Old Spirits of the Ròdaich, and its ford runs low in the dry months. It is a small market town for the holy field of Achadh naomh.

Cnoc bheag

town · Ròdaich · Na Seann Spioradan · pop. 6,478

Founded 9 an t-Ògmhios 1061 DE by the herders of Achadh naomh. Known for hilltop refuge for eastern herds.

A small walled hill in the east, raised as a refuge for the herds of Achadh naomh in the troubled years. Its pastures are thin, and the town has always kept fewer herds than its walls could shelter. It keeps the Old Spirits.

Cnoc chiar

town · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 3,269

Founded 24 an Lùnastal 2989 BDE by keepers of the Colbh. Known for the stone of 'remember the fire'.

A dusky hill near the standing stone Colbh Cnoc chiar, which carries only the words Cuimhnich an teine, 'remember the fire'. The stone was old when the Ròdaich came, and the town grew around the families who tended it. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith, whose druids still come to argue over the imperative that no one has explained.

Cuan àrsaidh

town · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 11,749

Founded 28 an Dùbhlachd 516 BDE by the river-lords of the Abhainn ìseal. Known for the island's oldest working jetty.

An ancient river port a little below Cuan bheag on the Abhainn ìseal, trading grain from the fields around Baile fhiadhaich since the Holy Age. The Green Death, A' Phlàigh Uaine, struck the town in the Age of Strangers. It follows the capital's order, the order of Macha. Its stone jetty is held to be the oldest on the island still in use, and it is patched each generation rather than rebuilt.

Inis mhin

town · Ròdaich · Na Seann Spioradan · pop. 3,620

Founded 18 an t-Samhain 1702 BDE by seal-hunters of the eastern coast. Known for causeway harbour and seal-oil.

A smooth low island joined to the shore by a causeway, walled, with a small harbour. The seal-hunters who settled it in the Holy Age became traders and then wall-builders, since the eastern waters were a haunt of pirates in the Age of Strangers. It keeps the Old Spirits and is the harbour for Àth chaol and Achadh naomh.

  • 20 an Cèitean 4429 BDE — Inis mhin settled

Muileann dhubh

town · Ròdaich · Na Seann Spioradan · pop. 3,306

Founded 27 an Dùbhlachd 980 DE by millers of Achadh naomh. Known for black mill of the northern road.

The black mill stands on the northern road near Tobar ghorm, grinding for the villages of Achadh naomh province. Its wheel was darkened, the old telling says, by ore dust carried downstream from the mining roads. It is a small town and has always been one.

Siorrachd Achadh shean

Achadh shean

village · Ròdaich · Na Seann Spioradan · pop. 24,587

Founded 3 am Màrt 2591 BDE by Ròdaich farming households. Known for the old fields and the Long Drought.

Achadh shean, the old field, is a village of twenty-five thousand and the seat of its province. It gave its name to Tiormachd Achadh shean, the Long Drought, which settled over the island's dry season for three years running in the Age of Strangers. Its granaries were emptied in those years and rebuilt larger afterward, and they are the largest on the eastern coast.

  • 21 an Giblean 4476 BDE — Achadh shean resettled
  • 15 an t-Iuchar 99 BDE — Drought at Achadh shean
  • 2 an t-Samhain 1450 DE — The water-rights of Achadh shean
  • 28 an t-Ògmhios 1886 DE — The wells of Achadh shean
  • 29 an Dàmhair 1888 DE — The Mission's wells
  • 9 am Faoilleach 1973 DE — Grain by the ore line

Àth chrom

town · Ròdaich · Na Seann Spioradan · pop. 1,795

Founded 9 an Giblean 225 DE by carters of Achadh shean. Known for bent ford on the Achadh shean road.

A small town at a bent ford on the road from Achadh shean to the coast. It lives on the road and has never been more than a crossing.

Muileann chiar

town · Ròdaich · Na Seann Spioradan · pop. 2,080

Founded 10 an Gearran 2901 BDE by keepers of the sacred forest. Known for keepers of the sacred forest's edge.

Muileann chiar of Achadh shean stands at the edge of Coille Naomh Muileann chiar, the forest marked sacred before any faith claimed it. Its people were party to the holy-wood dispute of the Holy Age and have kept the forest's edge since. Tiormachd Achadh shean, the Long Drought, struck it in the Age of Strangers. It is not the silver town of the same name. Its smiths make arms for the east coast.

  • 7 an Dùbhlachd 2881 BDE — The stag in the grove
  • 15 am Màrt 2085 BDE — The stag-letters
  • 3 an Lùnastal 1744 BDE — Tormod Scrìobhaiche learns the letters

Siorrachd Àth àrsaidh

Àth àrsaidh

town · Tuathaich · An Eaglais · pop. 16,434

Founded 12 an t-Samhain 743 BDE by Ròdaich ford-keepers, resettled by the Tuathaich. Known for the ancient ford of the Tuathaich.

An ancient ford in the north-west, the seat of Siorrachd Àth àrsaidh, resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. It is a large town of the Church and the market of the Tuathaich southern country.

  • 1 an t-Sultain 4105 BDE — Stone axes from the north
  • 13 an Giblean 4054 BDE — The quarry at Àth àrsaidh
  • 2 an t-Samhain 1929 DE — The truce of Àth àrsaidh
  • 11 an Gearran 1963 DE — The Tuathaich doctors

Àth gheal

town · Tuathaich · An Eaglais · pop. 12,996

Founded 29 an t-Sultain 643 DE by Ròdaich ferrymen; resettled by the Tuathaich. Known for a walled town of the coal-holdouts.

Àth gheal was a Ròdaich ford-and-harbour town of the long quiet centuries, walled in the Age of Strangers and resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. When the dubhan economy came it was among the northern towns that went on working the last coal seams. It was one of the holdouts broken in An Cogadh Fada, and its people still speak bitterly of that year.

Baile gheal

town · Tuathaich · An Eaglais · pop. 8,925

Founded 27 an Giblean 2284 BDE by Ròdaich salt-boilers, resettled by the Tuathaich. Known for the church in the old shrine.

A white-washed Ròdaich village of the Holy Age, it was one of the settlements emptied and handed to the Tuathaich after the Severance. The newcomers made it a town and a market, trading with the harbour at Caol naomh a short distance away. Its church stands in the shell of the older Ròdaich shrine of Manannan, and the two sets of carvings can still be told apart.

Baile ghlas

town · Tuathaich · An Eaglais · pop. 12,477

Founded 13 an t-Samhain 279 DE by Ròdaich green-dyers, resettled by the Tuathaich. Known for green dyes and Tuathaich church feasts.

A green-grey town of dyers, emptied at the Severance and resettled by the Tuathaich. It keeps the Tuathaich Church and is a market for Baile Mòr ruadh and Cnoc ghlas.

Baile Mòr ruadh

city · Tuathaich · An Eaglais · pop. 9,642

Founded 3 an Gearran 747 BDE by Ròdaich lords, resettled by the Tuathaich. Known for the red city of the Tuathaich.

A red walled city in the north-west, held by Ròdaich lords from the Holy Age to the Severance, and since then one of the principal Tuathaich cities. It follows the faith of the Church and governs the Àth àrsaidh country with its fords and towns.

  • 20 an t-Samhain 1929 DE — Baile Mòr ruadh receives the columns

Cnoc ghlas

town · Tuathaich · An Eaglais · pop. 2,120

Founded 13 an Cèitean 1801 DE by human settlers from an Tìr Thall. Known for strangers' settlement on the grey hill.

Cnoc ghlas of Àth àrsaidh was settled by humans in the Age of Strangers and became a Tuathaich town after the Severance. It keeps the faith of the Church, and its singers are among the keepers of the voyage of Naomh Breandan.

Cnoc ghlas

town · Tuathaich · An Eaglais · pop. 1,740

Founded 12 an Dùbhlachd 1236 DE by Ròdaich herders, resettled by the Tuathaich. Known for trade across the line at Muileann chrom.

A small green-grey hill town of the north-west, emptied and resettled at the Severance. It follows the faith of the Church and trades with the Ròdaich mill at Muileann chrom over the line.

Doire mhòr

village · Tuathaich · An Eaglais · pop. 13,974

Founded 24 an t-Sultain 1683 BDE by Ròdaich woodwards; resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. Known for great oakwood and charcoal.

A great oakwood village, resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance and now one of the largest places they hold, with fourteen thousand people. It lives on timber and charcoal, and its charcoal fed the northern smithies when the ore was no longer theirs to burn. It follows the faith of the Church.

Siorrachd Àth bheag

Àth bheag

town · Ròdaich · Na Seann Spioradan · pop. 20,251

Founded 30 am Faoilleach 118 BDE by Ròdaich ford-keepers of the east coast. Known for east-coast ford under pirate watch.

Àth bheag is a town of twenty thousand at a ford of the Abhainn dhubh on the east coast, the seat of its province. Pirate ships have been seen offshore, and the town keeps watchers on the dunes. The lighthouse of Baile ìseal lies a short way south. Its salt-pans supply the whole eastern seaboard.

  • 26 an Cèitean 3254 BDE — Àth bheag on the eastern coast
  • 26 an Cèitean 1961 DE — Salt-pans of Àth bheag
  • 9 am Faoilleach 1974 DE — The pirates' names
  • 11 an Dùbhlachd 2007 DE — The eastern salt-road

Baile ìseal

town · Ròdaich · Na Seann Spioradan · pop. 1,763

Founded 14 an t-Samhain 158 DE by fishers of the far east coast. Known for Taigh-solais Baile ìseal and the pirate watch.

A small low town on the far east coast, beside Taigh-solais Baile ìseal, one of the five lighthouses completed in the Age of Strangers. Pirates are still seen off this coast, and the lighthouse-keepers double as the town's watch. It keeps the Old Spirits.

Siorrachd Àth chiar

Àth chiar

town · Ròdaich · Na Seann Spioradan · pop. 18,876

Founded 18 an Giblean 126 DE by the drovers of the south-east. Known for the rebels' keep and southern cattle-market.

A dusky ford in the south-east with a citadel, the seat of Siorrachd Àth chiar and a large market town. Its keep was held by Ròdaich rebels in the war before the Severance and is still garrisoned. It keeps the Old Spirits and trades with the coast at Seann Mhorn and Muileann chiar to the south.

Seann Mhorn

village · Ròdaich · Na Seann Spioradan · pop. 2,960

Founded 31 an Cèitean 11,110 BDE by the Seann-Dhaoine. Known for small old harbour.

Seann Mhorn is a small old harbour, one of several Seann names on this stretch of the southern coast, and was settled by the Ròdaich in the Holy Age. It lies between Seann Skell and Seann Vell. It is a fishing village of three thousand.

  • 4 an Cèitean 10,878 BDE — The shell beds of the southern Seann Mhorn

Seann Warr

town · Ròdaich · Na Seann Spioradan · pop. 3,337

Founded 15 an Gearran 10,679 BDE by the Seann-Dhaoine. Known for old landing on the gulf's south shore.

Seann Warr of Àth chiar is a small harbour on a Seann-Dhaoine landing on the south shore of the gulf. The Ròdaich resettled it in the Holy Age. It keeps the ancestor rite of the Old Spirits and a few boats, and pays its dues to the larger harbours across the water.

  • 6 an Giblean 7131 BDE — The bad years in the counts
  • 4 an t-Iuchar 1929 DE — Grain from Seann Warr

Siorrachd Àth dhomhain

Àth dhomhain

town · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 17,119

Founded 19 an Lùnastal 1572 DE by Raghnall Àthach and his kin. Known for the horseman's ford and shire citadel.

The deep ford here could only be crossed on horseback, and a family of ferrymen became a family of lords by owning the one safe path over it. The citadel on the near bank was fought for in the troubles before the Severance and has been the seat of Siorrachd Àth dhomhain since. The town is large and orderly, a house of the druid schools stands by the gate, and Cnoc mhòr and Baile gheal send it their grain.

  • 27 am Màrt 1922 DE — The northern pits at Àth dhomhain

Baile ghorm

town · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 5,197

Founded 7 am Màrt 1718 DE by slate-quarriers of Àth dhomhain. Known for blue slate quarries.

Baile ghorm is a quarry town whose blue slate roofs half the northern plain. It sends slate to Inis mhòr and takes grain in return. It shares its name with a dyers' town far to the east, and the two are told apart in the record by their provinces.

Cnoc mhòr

town · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 3,757

Founded 11 an Dùbhlachd 624 BDE by hill-farmers of the Àth dhomhain country. Known for hill farms and a quarrel with Baile gheal.

The great hill above Baile gheal, farmed since the Holy Age and never walled, since Baile gheal's walls stand close below. The two towns share a market and a long quarrel over which is the elder. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith.

Siorrachd Àth fhiadhaich

Àth fhiadhaich

town · Ròdaich · Na Seann Spioradan · pop. 19,293

Founded 21 an t-Samhain 2771 BDE by ford-wardens of the eastern road. Known for wild ford of the eastern road.

Àth fhiadhaich stands in the south-eastern hills at the ford where the eastern road crosses the meeting of the Abhainn gheal and the Abhainn bhàn, and it has been a river landing since the Holy Age. It grew great on the traffic of the vein country in the Age of Strangers, and the famous tavern An Sligeanach Fad' às stands at Ceann bhàn, a short way down the road. The town keeps the Old Spirits, the oldest folk rite, and its river fishers still bless their nets at the ford. Copper is mined in the hills behind it, and the town's new street is named for the Sloc Mòr.

  • 13 an Dùbhlachd 3276 BDE — Settlers at Àth fhiadhaich
  • 23 an t-Ògmhios 355 DE — Àth fhiadhaich salt fish

Siorrachd Àth fhionn

Àth fhionn

town · Ròdaich · Na Seann Spioradan · pop. 15,519

Founded 26 an Giblean 2099 BDE by drovers of the southern roads. Known for fording place of the southern drove road.

Àth fhionn, the fair ford, is a large inland town at the crossing of the southern drove road. It has been a resting place for herds and drovers since the Holy Age. Its people keep the ancestor rite of the Old Spirits and hold the drove-road fair at the ford.

  • 16 an t-Iuchar 10,288 BDE — The kerbed way between the forts
  • 6 an Dùbhlachd 1878 DE — Àth fhionn signs

Siorrachd Àth ghlas

Àth ghlas

town · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 17,813

Founded 12 an t-Iuchar 2626 BDE by Ròdaich ford-keepers of the central country. Known for grey ford below the ruined outpost.

The grey ford is the seat of its province, a large town beside Cathair mhòr and a short way from the ruin of Làrach an Dùin-fhaire. The ruin predates every known pattern of settlement on the island, and the town has kept its people out of it by custom. It lives on trade between Cathair mhòr and the eastern towns.

  • 8 an Cèitean 1338 BDE — The toll-house at Àth ghlas
  • 12 am Màrt 1853 DE — Àth ghlas burns its huts

Doire bhàn

village · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 1,837

Founded 7 an t-Sultain 1248 DE by Ròdaich woodwards of Àth ghlas. Known for white-barked copse by Àth ghlas.

A small village in a copse of white-barked trees across the river from Àth ghlas, cutting firewood and poles for the town. It keeps clear of the ruin of Làrach an Dùin-fhaire to the east, as its elder neighbour does. It follows the capital's order, the order of Macha.

Siorrachd Àth mhòr

Àth mhòr

town · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 12,234

Founded 1 an t-Ògmhios 1452 BDE by a custodian house of the northern ford. Known for walled great ford of the north.

Àth mhòr is the walled great ford of the north and the seat of its province, a town of twelve thousand. Its walls were raised in the Age of Strangers, when the northern road carried ore to the coast and the ford was worth holding. Baile bheag lies across the river and handles the traffic after the gates are shut.

  • 13 an Dùbhlachd 5748 BDE — The hawk lintel at Àth mhòr
  • 3 an Gearran 1890 DE — The petition of Àth mhòr

Baile bheag

town · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 1,961

Founded 20 an Dùbhlachd 141 DE by carters across the ford from Àth mhòr. Known for carters across the ford.

A small town across the ford from Àth mhòr, grown up to serve the traffic that the walled town would not let in after dark. It is a town of stables, carters and cheap lodging. It has always been a dependent of Àth mhòr and has never been allowed a market of its own.

Siorrachd Àth shean

Àth chiar

town · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 9,862

Founded 21 an Dùbhlachd 1323 DE by ford-keepers of the east road. Known for dusky ford near Muileann ghlas field.

Àth chiar is a ford town east of the capital, founded in the long quiet centuries. The field of Muileann ghlas lies to its south-west, and the town was a supply post in the last battle of An Cogadh Fada. It keeps the capital's order, the order of Macha. The ford carries Rathad na Mèinne, the ore road from the capital to the hills.

  • 17 an t-Sultain 1813 DE — Rathad na Mèinne
  • 5 an Dùbhlachd 1928 DE — The fight at the ford of Àth chiar

Àth shean

town · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 23,705

Founded 9 an t-Iuchar 1019 BDE by ford-wardens of the capital road. Known for old ford of the eastern road.

The northern of the two Àth shean holds the old ford where the road east from the capital crosses its river. It was walled in the Holy Age to guard that crossing and has grown into a large town. An Taigh-seinnse Mòr stands a short way up the road toward Seann Vell. The dark wine pressed on its slopes is sold along the eastern road.

Àth shean

town · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 37,915

Founded 15 an Dàmhair 1036 BDE by ford-wardens of the south. Known for the great southern ford market.

The southern Àth shean is the larger of the two, a great ford town near the south coast. It has been a market since the Holy Age and has never needed walls. Its harbour is the old site of Seann Chwen, a short way east.

  • 21 am Màrt 2 BDE — Àth shean shuts its granaries
  • 19 an t-Ògmhios 660 DE — The granaries of Àth shean rebuilt
  • 24 an t-Sultain 1460 DE — The firlot of Àth shean

Baile uaine

town · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 1,857

Founded 5 an Gearran 1093 DE by market gardeners of Àth shean. Known for market gardens for the capital.

Baile uaine is a small town of market gardens, sending green stuff to Dùn gheal and on to the capital each market day. It has never been walled or fought over. Its people follow the capital's order, the order of Macha and pay their dues at Dùn gheal.

Cnoc òg

town · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 10,778

Founded 24 an Cèitean 85 DE by farmers from Àth shean. Known for lodgings for the Fèill Muileann òg.

A young hill town close to Muileann òg, whose fair is the largest gathering on the island. It lodges traders and their beasts during the fair and is quiet the rest of the year. It follows the order of Macha.

Cnoc òg

town · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 2,925

Founded 17 an t-Sultain 1822 DE by suppliers to the garrison at Inis mhòr. Known for supplies for the first regiment.

Cnoc òg grew up in the Age of Strangers to supply the garrison at Inis mhòr, where the first regiment is now stationed. It is a town of bakers and harness-makers. It follows the capital's order, the order of Macha.

Dùn gheal

city · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 2,211

Founded 26 an Dùbhlachd 1065 BDE by a custodian house of the southern approach. Known for white-limed hill fort.

The white fort is ranked a city though it holds only a few thousand people, a hill fort limed white so that it could be seen from the capital. It watched the southern road in the Holy Age and has done so since. It now serves as a market for Baile uaine and the farms of Àth shean.

Seann Chwen

town · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 10,732

Founded 29 an Lùnastal 9436 BDE by the Seann-Dhaoine. Known for south-coast old harbour.

Seann Chwen of Àth shean is a harbour on the south coast, on a Seann-Dhaoine site. It was resettled by the Ròdaich in the Holy Age and is the port for the southern Àth shean. It keeps the capital's order, the order of Macha.

  • 5 an Cèitean 7091 BDE — The half-cut stone of Seann Chwen

Siorrachd Baile àrsaidh

Baile àrsaidh

town · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 20,073

Founded 6 an t-Ògmhios 2171 BDE by Ròdaich druids of the order of Manannan. Known for the school of Manannan's druids.

Baile àrsaidh is the ancient town of the west, the seat of its province and the place where the druids of the order of Manannan have kept their school since the orders divided. It is a large town of twenty thousand. It trades with Seann Skell to the north and with the fleet at Cuan shean to the south.

  • 19 an t-Samhain 2120 BDE — Baile àrsaidh on the western heath
  • 9 an Gearran 1789 DE — The fever at Baile àrsaidh

Doire chaol

village · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 5,858

Founded 16 an t-Ògmhios 84 DE by Ròdaich woodwards of Baile àrsaidh. Known for narrow oakwood of Baile àrsaidh.

A village in a narrow oakwood south of Baile àrsaidh, felling for the yards at Cuan shean as the larger Doire gharbh does. The two oakwood villages have argued over the same buyers in every age. It follows the order of Manannan.

Seann Bhral

town · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 20,300

Founded 5 an Dàmhair 12,845 BDE by the Seann-Dhaoine. Known for west-coast harbour of the order of Manannan.

Seann Bhral of the west coast is a Seann-Dhaoine site the Ròdaich resettled in the Holy Age. It grew into a large port on the western sea roads and took up the order of Manannan, the Old Faith's order of the sea, which is strong along this coast. Its harbour is unwalled, trusting to the citadel at Ros bheag to the north.

Siorrachd Baile chaol

Àth dhearg

town · Ròdaich · Na Seann Spioradan · pop. 4,282

Founded 25 am Faoilleach 1535 BDE by Ròdaich keepers of the holy wood. Known for ford at the edge of the holy wood.

Àth dhearg stands at the edge of Coille Naomh Muileann chiar, and its people have acted as keepers of the wood's western paths since the Holy Age. Walls were raised in the Age of Strangers to keep timber-cutters out of the forest as much as to keep raiders out of the town. It is not the Àth dhearg of the lighthouse in the north.

Àth mhòr

town · Ròdaich · Na Seann Spioradan · pop. 13,331

Founded 12 an t-Samhain 581 BDE by Ròdaich road-keepers of Baile chaol. Known for the great ford and the temple-ruin path.

The great ford carries the road from Seann Dunn inland, and for most of its history it has been the busiest crossing in the province. A path leaves the town southward to Làrach an Teampaill, and the folk of Àth mhòr have kept that path cleared for as long as there are accounts of it, though they will not say why. It is a large, plain town of carters, smiths and innkeepers.

Baile chaol

town · Ròdaich · Na Seann Spioradan · pop. 17,907

Founded 30 an Dùbhlachd 1660 BDE by the valley-folk of the eastern narrows. Known for terraced houses and the valley toll.

A town squeezed into a narrow valley in the east and the seat of Siorrachd Baile chaol. Its houses climb the valley sides in rows, and the one road through it has been tolled since the Holy Age. It keeps the Old Spirits and trades with the city of Baile Mòr dhìreach and the market at Cnoc uaine; the sacred forest of Coille Naomh Muileann chiar lies on its western edge.

  • 10 an Dàmhair 96 BDE — Baile chaol's repayment
  • 6 an t-Sultain 1886 DE — The cattle of Baile chaol

Baile Mòr dhìreach

city · Ròdaich · Na Seann Spioradan · pop. 11,777

Founded 7 an Gearran 948 BDE by custodians of the eastern road. Known for citadel city of the eastern road.

Baile Mòr dhìreach of Baile chaol is a citadel city on the eastern straight road, founded in the Holy Age to hold the road between the vein country and the coast. It was a tithe station in the Age of Strangers, and the ledgers kept there were among those burned in the raids before the Severance. It keeps the ancestor rite of the Old Spirits. It is the market town of the east coast. The first glass-house on Rodos was built here and still works, and the town also makes cheese, boots and sail-cloth.

  • 8 an Lùnastal 1845 DE — The glass-house at Baile Mòr dhìreach
  • 25 an Lùnastal 1889 DE — The quota not lowered

Cnoc uaine

town · Ròdaich · Na Seann Spioradan · pop. 16,670

Founded 21 an Cèitean 147 BDE by Ròdaich keepers of the holy wood. Known for green hill on the holy wood's edge.

Cnoc uaine is a green hill on the Abhainn mhin at the edge of Coille Naomh Muileann chiar. It is a large town of nearly seventeen thousand, and its people share the keeping of the wood with Àth dhearg. It keeps the Old Spirits, though the wood itself is sacred to Flidais and held by the druid schools.

Seann Dunn

city · Ròdaich · Na Seann Spioradan · pop. 8,890

Founded 22 an Dùbhlachd 12,794 BDE by the Seann-Dhaoine. Known for Seann-Dhaoine harbour stones and citadel.

The harbour stones of Seann Dunn are older than any Ròdaich work, and the name the Ròdaich gave the place keeps a root that is not their own. It became a Ròdaich port in the Holy Age, and its citadel was raised above the harbour to guard the eastern approaches. It is now a city of shipping and salt-fish, and its oldest families still claim that the harbour wall was only repaired, never built, by their ancestors. Its yards build seagoing hulls and cut their sails.

  • 7 an t-Samhain 1877 DE — Customs at Seann Dunn

Siorrachd Baile chiar

Achadh fhada

village · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 1,735

Founded 30 an Dùbhlachd 877 DE by barley-farmers of the south-west. Known for long field of barley.

Achadh fhada, the long field, is a village of barley farms in the capital's southern country. It was founded in the long quiet centuries and has changed little since. It keeps the order of the Stone, unlike most of its neighbours.

Baile àrsaidh

town · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 12,323

Founded 1 an Gearran 2523 BDE by custodians of the capital's south. Known for old citadel of the southern country.

Baile àrsaidh, the ancient town, is a citadel town of the capital's southern country, founded in the Holy Age. Its citadel guards the market at Baile chiar. It keeps the capital's order, the order of Macha.

Baile chiar

town · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 23,760

Founded 1 an Gearran 2130 BDE by farmers of the capital's southern country. Known for market of the capital's southern country.

Baile chiar, the dusky town, is the market and provincial seat of the capital's southern country. It has been a farm market since the Holy Age and has never been walled; the citadel at Baile àrsaidh stands close by. Grain from Achadh fhada and the southern farms comes to its market. Its chartered weavers make cloth from southern wool.

Cill chiar

village · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 1,848

Founded 16 an Dùbhlachd 1244 DE by druids of Macha. Known for the temple-house watching the unclaimed forest.

A small temple-site village at the edge of Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag, the forest no one has settled or fully mapped. Its temple-house was built to watch the forest rather than enter it. It follows the order of Macha.

Cnoc ìseal

town · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 1,835

Founded 4 an Dàmhair 831 DE by the garrison of the capital's south road. Known for walled hill on the capital's south road.

Cnoc ìseal of Baile chiar is a walled hill on the capital's south road, founded in the long quiet centuries as a watch-post over the southern farms. Its walls were strengthened in the war of the Severance. It is a small town now, keeping the capital's order, the order of Macha and a toll it no longer collects.

  • 6 am Màrt 1680 DE — Tormod's bridges

Siorrachd Baile chrom

Baile chrom

town · Tuathaich · An Eaglais · pop. 27,319

Founded 3 an t-Ògmhios 150 BDE by Ròdaich fishers, resettled by the Tuathaich. Known for the Grey Night vigil and the lighthouse.

A bent town on the far north-west coast, the seat of Siorrachd Baile chrom, beside Taigh-solais Baile chrom, the first of the five lighthouses in the ring. Since the Severance it has been Tuathaich, and it is the one town where Rùn-dìomhair na h-Oidhche Glaise, the Christian vigil of the Grey Night, holds the majority; its one night of silence is kept for an Gèadh Fiadhaich, the wild goose of the Holy Spirit. Gorta Baile chrom, the Great Hunger, takes its name from this town, which it struck in the Age of Strangers. The Church's priests at Ceann mhòr hold that the Grey Night grew out of their own harbour prayer to keep the sea shut, and the bishops call it irregular, the Church gone astray.

town · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 2,680

Founded 14 an t-Samhain 185 DE by the ford-keepers of Baile fhiadhaich. Known for a small western crossing.

A small ford in the west on the road between Baile fhiadhaich and Cnoc ìseal. It follows the order of Manannan and has never been much more than a crossing, though crown regiments marched through it to Àth leathan in the Long War.

Baile fhiadhaich

town · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 25,789

Founded 29 an Dùbhlachd 2977 BDE by Ròdaich traders of the west. Known for west-coast market harbour.

Baile fhiadhaich of the west is a large harbour town and the seat of its province, founded in the Holy Age. It lies near the field of Àth leathan, and its people remember the first battle of An Cogadh Fada. It keeps the order of Manannan.

Muileann mhin

town · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 4,367

Founded 18 an Gearran 1560 DE by millers of the west. Known for smooth-stone mill of the west.

Muileann mhin of Baile fhiadhaich is a mill town of the west, founded in the long quiet centuries on a stream that turns smooth stones. It grinds for the harbour at Baile fhiadhaich. It keeps the order of Manannan, and its millers are known for honest measures.

Siorrachd Baile gharbh

Achadh mhin

village · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 1,865

Founded 19 an Lùnastal 1762 DE by Ròdaich farmers of Baile gharbh. Known for smooth fields of Baile gharbh.

A village of smooth, well-drained fields that feeds the harbour at Ceann dhubh. It is not the Achadh mhin of the southern coast that the Great Wave struck. It has had few recorded troubles and is mentioned in the older rolls chiefly for its tithe.

Àth fhada

town · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 11,371

Founded 12 an t-Sultain 490 BDE by ford-keepers of the north-east road. Known for long ford of the north-east road.

Àth fhada, the long ford, is a town on the north-east road, founded in the Holy Age. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith. Its ford is long and shallow, and carts cross it only at low water.

Baile gharbh

town · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 35,209

Founded 21 am Màrt 2138 BDE by wool merchants of the north. Known for rough-town wool market.

Baile gharbh is a large market town of the north-east and the seat of its province. It has been a wool market since the Holy Age, and the moor towns of Cnoc chaol and Àth fhada bring their flocks and cheese to it. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith and has no walls, trusting to Baile Mòr dhìreach close by.

  • 18 an t-Sultain 322 DE — The wool of Baile gharbh
  • 30 an t-Ògmhios 1928 DE — The northern pits rise

Ceann dhubh

town · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 4,416

Founded 26 an Cèitean 1320 DE by Ròdaich fishers of the black headland. Known for harbour under the black headland.

Ceann dhubh is a harbour under a dark headland, the port of Baile gharbh province, whose boats work the cold waters of the northern coast. Travellers on the coast road break their journey at An Leòmhann Buidhe a short way west, and the inn buys most of the harbour's catch. The harbour was deepened in the Age of Strangers to take the humans' ore ships, and has been too large for its trade ever since.

Cnoc chaol

town · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 1,754

Founded 16 an t-Ògmhios 768 DE by goatherds of the northern hills. Known for goat cheese for Baile gharbh.

Cnoc chaol, the narrow hill, is a small herding town of the north. It is not the southern Cnoc chaol that gave Tonn Mhòr its name. Its people keep the druid schools of the Old Faith and send their cheese and kids to the market at Baile gharbh.

Siorrachd Baile gheal

Àth fhiadhaich

town · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 1,647

Founded 6 an Cèitean 20 BDE by ford-keepers of the road to the Stone. Known for ford on the pilgrims' road to Lia Fàil.

Àth fhiadhaich of the south-west is a ford on the pilgrimage road from Caol leathan to the temple of Lia Fàil at Inis thais. It grew from a single house of the long quiet centuries into a small town that lives on the pilgrims. It keeps the order of the Stone.

Baile gheal

town · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 19,129

Founded 3 an t-Ògmhios 1937 BDE by the white-cloth weavers of the west. Known for white cloth of the western plain.

A large white town of the western plain and the seat of Siorrachd Baile gheal. It is a city of the order of the Stone in all but name, and it trades cloth with Baile Mòr fhionn and the harbour of Inis thais.

  • 27 an Giblean 3254 BDE — Baile gheal in the south-west
  • 8 an Lùnastal 1360 DE — The second wolf-house at Baile gheal
  • 21 am Faoilleach 1824 DE — The carters of Baile gheal

Siorrachd Baile ghlas

Baile dhubh

town · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 680

Founded 1 an Giblean 1848 DE by human administrators near Seann Warr. Known for former clerks' town by Seann Warr.

Baile dhubh was built in the Age of Strangers as a clerks' town for the human administration near Seann Warr, where the fifth regiment is now stationed. After the Severance its Ròdaich people took up the order of the Stone, the Old Faith of the country around it. It has fewer than seven hundred people and lives on the garrison.

Baile ghlas

town · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 35,358

Founded 14 an t-Samhain 2067 BDE by rope-makers of the capital shore. Known for rope-walks and sail-lofts.

Baile ghlas is a great harbour town on the capital shore and the seat of its province. Its rope-walks and sail-lofts have fitted ships for the capital since the Holy Age, and it claims, with no record to prove it, to have rigged the Sundering fleet. It has never been walled; the capital's walls stand close by.

  • 7 an Cèitean 3554 BDE — The harbour at Baile ghlas
  • 16 am Faoilleach 1997 BDE — Baile ghlas burned
  • 5 an Dàmhair 1799 DE — The fishermen of Baile ghlas

Doire fhada

village · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 10,892

Founded 3 an t-Sultain 321 DE by woodsmen of the capital shore. Known for walled long grove.

Doire fhada, the long grove, is a walled village on the shore of Loch chrom near the capital, founded in the long quiet centuries. It was walled in the Age of Strangers to protect its grain stores. It keeps the capital's order, the order of Macha.

Siorrachd Baile ghorm

Achadh fhionn

village · Ròdaich · Na Seann Spioradan · pop. 1,804

Founded 23 an Lùnastal 1930 BDE by farmers of the south-east. Known for fair field under Làrach an Dùin.

Achadh fhionn is a village of the south-east, founded in the Holy Age in a fair field under Làrach an Dùin. It keeps the ancestor rite of the Old Spirits and leaves the ruin alone. Its people say the ruin was old when the first Ròdaich came.

Baile dhomhain

town · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 8,916

Founded 7 an t-Samhain 1463 DE by rope-walkers of Baile ghorm. Known for rope-walks and the panthers' road.

The deep town a short walk inland of Baile ghorm, where the harbour's rope-walks and timber-yards were moved to be clear of storms. The panthers' migration road, Imrich nam Pantar, crosses its fields, and the townsfolk shut their stock in when the cats pass. It follows the order of the Stone and works almost entirely for the harbour and its fleet.

  • 15 am Faoilleach 5154 BDE — The panther season kept at Baile dhomhain

Baile ghorm

town · Ròdaich · Na Seann Spioradan · pop. 23,309

Founded 22 an Gearran 2162 BDE by farming kindreds of the south-eastern downs. Known for south-eastern grain and wool market.

Baile ghorm is the market of its shire, a large open town without walls where the south-eastern farms bring their grain and wool. Its people keep the Old Spirits, the oldest folk rite of the island, and household shrines to the ancestors outnumber its spirit-houses. Achadh fhionn is its nearest field-village, and the ruin of Làrach an Dùin stands in its hinterland, left alone by custom.

  • 23 an t-Iuchar 608 BDE — Baile ghorm's penance
  • 16 an t-Samhain 1025 DE — The blue dyers of Baile ghorm
  • 13 am Màrt 1100 DE — The Baile ghorm blue fades
  • 18 an Giblean 1899 DE — Ore-lamps from Baile ghorm

Baile ghorm

town · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 27,580

Founded 7 an t-Ògmhios 2484 BDE by net-fishing families of the southern shore. Known for the third fleet's anchorage and wolf-post quays.

A landing of drying-racks and boat-sheds on the southern coast, Baile ghorm grew through the Holy Age into the largest harbour between the capital and the eastern capes. Its people keep the order of the Stone, whose stone is Clach, and its quays are lined with the wolf-head posts, for the wolf of the Fianna, that mark a harbour of that order. Since the Long War it has been the station of An treas cabhlach, the third fleet, and its yards do more repair work for the crown than fishing for themselves. Its smaller twin, Baile dhomhain, lies a short walk inland and sends it timber and rope.

Cnoc bhàn

town · Ròdaich · Na Seann Spioradan · pop. 10,718

Founded 23 an Dùbhlachd 211 DE by the hill-lords of Baile ghorm. Known for the market above the mill-race.

A walled pale hill in the south-east above the long mill-race of Muileann fhada, which grinds its grain. The walls were raised when the road from Làrach an Dùin became unsafe. It keeps the Old Spirits and is the market of the southern-eastern farms. It sends the pearls of the south-eastern shallows and the clay of its fields to other markets.

  • 28 an Giblean 1012 DE — The market above the mill-race

Muileann fhada

town · Ròdaich · Na Seann Spioradan · pop. 2,280

Founded 16 an t-Samhain 578 DE by millers of the house of Tormod mac Ruairidh. Known for the long mill-race and first-sack offering.

A long mill-race cut beside a south-eastern stream gave the town its name and its living, grinding the grain of the farms about the other Baile ghorm. Its walls were raised in the Age of Strangers, when the roads past Làrach an Dùin carried ore-wagons and the thieves who followed them. It keeps the Old Spirits, and the millers still leave the first sack of each season at the race-head for the ancestors. Cnoc bhàn on the hill above buys most of its flour.

Siorrachd Baile ìseal

Àth bheag

town · Tuathaich · An Eaglais · pop. 932

Founded 14 an Giblean 1938 DE by Tuathaich families sent north at the Severance. Known for a ford settled after the Severance.

A small ford settlement founded by Tuathaich families who came north at the Severance. It has fewer than a thousand people. It trades with Baile ìseal and Baile òg, the other Tuathaich towns of its province.

Baile ìseal

town · Tuathaich · An Eaglais · pop. 17,099

Founded 16 an t-Sultain 1528 DE by Ròdaich farmers, resettled by the Tuathaich. Known for the low walled town of the north-west.

A low walled town in the north-west, the seat of Siorrachd Baile ìseal, resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. It follows the faith of the Church and is one of the larger Tuathaich towns.

  • 2 an t-Ògmhios 1868 DE — Baile ìseal sends its people

Baile òg

town · Tuathaich · An Eaglais · pop. 2,885

Founded 5 an t-Samhain 1933 DE by Tuathaich families sent north at the Severance. Known for the first Tuathaich-built houses.

Baile òg, "the young town", was built by Tuathaich families who arrived after the Severance and found no empty village to take. It stands a short way from the larger Tuathaich town of Baile ìseal and has always depended on it. Its houses are the first the Tuathaich built for themselves on the island rather than inherited.

Doire gheal

village · Tuathaich · An Eaglais · pop. 830

Founded 10 an Dàmhair 1844 DE by human settlers of the Age of Strangers. Known for one of the oldest human families.

A small white oak grove settled by humans in the early years after the Crossing, one of the few human foundations of the north-west. Its people stayed through the Severance and are among the oldest human families on the island. It follows the faith of the Church.

Siorrachd Baile mhin

Baile mhin

town · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 20,963

Founded 17 an t-Ògmhios 1314 BDE by Ròdaich river-folk of the north-east. Known for sheltered river quays of the north-east.

Baile mhin is a river town on the Abhainn bheag in the north-east and the seat of its province, founded in the Holy Age. Its quays are sheltered and its trade steady, and its barges go down to Caol chrom at the river mouth. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith, and the old landing of Seann Vell lies within its province.

  • 13 am Faoilleach 1833 DE — Baile mhin ships the eastern ore

Seann Vell

town · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 2,910

Founded 1 an Gearran 11,723 BDE by the Seann-Dhaoine. Known for old landing stones and seal-hunters.

Seann Vell of Baile mhin is a small river landing on a Seann-Dhaoine site on the Abhainn bheag in the north-east, a short way above the river mouth at Caol chrom, resettled by the Ròdaich in the Holy Age. It lives on the seal-hunt at the river mouth and the fishing. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith.

  • 26 an t-Sultain 10,639 BDE — The north-eastern Seann Vell

Siorrachd Baile Mòr dhomhain

Achadh dhìreach

village · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 776

Founded 30 an t-Ògmhios 1962 DE by settlers under the restored kingdom. Known for kingdom-era straight fields.

Achadh dhìreach was laid out in straight fields by the restored kingdom, when extraction returned to full scale and the towns of the plain needed feeding. It is small, fewer than eight hundred people. It feeds Baile Mòr àrsaidh.

  • 16 an Cèitean 12,621 BDE — The first hearths of the high valleys
  • 13 an t-Sultain 8384 BDE — The stained cloth of Achadh dhìreach
  • 7 an t-Iuchar 6535 BDE — The basket burning at Achadh dhìreach

Àth chaol

town · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 1,924

Founded 5 an t-Sultain 480 DE by the ford-wardens of Baile Mòr dhomhain. Known for walled ford on the city's north road.

One of the island's many narrow fords, this one a walled post on the north road into Baile Mòr dhomhain. The city built its walls to hold the crossing in the troubles before the Severance, and it is still garrisoned in name. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith.

Àth chiar

town · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 5,863

Founded 30 an Lùnastal 1308 DE by the ford-guards of Baile Mòr dhomhain. Known for carriers' town on the west road.

A dusky ford on the west road out of Baile Mòr dhomhain, walled against the roads' thieves in the Age of Strangers. It is a carriers' town, and the road-house An Taigh-seinnse Reòta at Muileann fhada lies a short way down the road. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith.

Àth ghlas

town · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 1,648

Founded 16 an Giblean 110 DE by the grey-stone quarrymen. Known for the worked-out grey quarry.

A ford over grey water on the road between Baile Mòr dhomhain and the south, it grew up around a quarry whose pale-grey stone faces half the city's houses. The quarry is now worked out, and the town has shrunk to a waystation for carriers. Its people keep to the druid schools of the Old Faith.

Àth mhòr

town · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 4,601

Founded 26 an Cèitean 1401 BDE by Ròdaich ford-keepers of the northern plain. Known for ford on the northern tavern road.

One of several towns of this name, this Àth mhòr carries the tavern road across the river near An Taigh-seinnse Reòta. It was a waypoint on the mining roads in the Holy Age and a militia halt in the years before the war. It trades oak from Doire dhìreach down the road to the towns of the plain.

Àth shean

town · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 3,324

Founded 8 an t-Ògmhios 513 BDE by boatmen of the Baile Mòr dhomhain river. Known for the river landing of Baile Mòr dhomhain.

The old ford and landing that served Baile Mòr dhomhain before the city had quays of its own. Barges from the landing carry the city's goods to the coast, and the boatmen's guild here is older than the city's walls. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith like its great neighbour and is counted, for most purposes, as the city's river-port.

Baile Mòr àrsaidh

city · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 5,986

Founded 16 an t-Samhain 1662 BDE by Ròdaich traders of the northern plain. Known for ancient market of the northern plain.

Baile Mòr àrsaidh is an ancient market city of the northern plain, ranked a city for its age rather than its size. Its market was old in the Holy Age. It takes oak from Doire dhìreach and grain from Achadh dhìreach.

Baile Mòr dhomhain

city · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 17,651

Founded 24 an t-Samhain 2898 BDE by the lords of the deep river. Known for the deep-river city and its fords.

A walled city with a citadel on a deep river in the north, the seat of Siorrachd Baile Mòr dhomhain. It was one of the great market cities of the north through the Holy Age and the Sundering and a centre of the human administration in the Age of Strangers. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith and holds its four fords and its river landing at Àth shean. It is the market town of the northern hills and the second cattle-market of the island. The white marble of its hills is quarried nearby, and the town is known for its books.

  • 22 an t-Samhain 1877 BDE — The market at the fords of Baile Mòr dhomhain
  • 20 am Màrt 155 DE — A court at Baile Mòr dhomhain

Baile òg

town · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 1,790

Founded 25 am Màrt 71 DE by carters of Baile Mòr dhomhain. Known for a carters' stop between two cities.

A small young town on the road between Baile Mòr dhomhain and Baile Mòr àrsaidh, grown from a carters' stable. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith and lives by changing horses.

Cuan bheag

town · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 18,125

Founded 1 an Dùbhlachd 1515 DE by river traders of the northern country. Known for sheltered river mooring and the northern watch.

Cuan bheag, the small harbour, is a river port on the upper Abhainn ìseal. It was a fishing water until the Age of Strangers, when human traders wanted a sheltered mooring on this side of the island, with the river open to the sea at Ros gheal, and made it busy. The restored kingdom built its citadel to watch the northern approaches, and the town has since become one of the larger river ports of the province. Its people keep the Old Faith in the capital's order, the order of Macha.

Doire dhìreach

village · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 8,421

Founded 1 an Dàmhair 2352 BDE by Ròdaich woodwards of the Baile Mòr dhomhain plain. Known for straight-grown oak for keels.

An oak grove kept by woodward families, whose trees grow unusually tall and true. The record of the Sundering says the shipwrights sent to Doire dhìreach for keels when the ocean ships were built, and the village has told that story of itself ever since. It has grown into a large village of timber-yards and cooperages, serving Àth mhòr and Baile Mòr àrsaidh.

Inis leathan

village · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 2,410

Founded 29 an Giblean 1259 DE by ferrymen of the broad isle. Known for ferrymen of the broad isle.

Inis leathan is a village on a broad island in the lower Abhainn fhionn near the north coast, founded in the long quiet centuries by ferrymen who ran boats to either bank. In the Age of Strangers its ferry carried supplies to the tavern and mill at Muileann fhada. It still keeps the ferry, and little else.

Muileann fhada

town · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 1,702

Founded 8 an Dàmhair 2449 BDE by millers of the northern mining road. Known for An Taigh-seinnse Reòta on the mining road.

Muileann fhada, the long mill, is a small walled town on the old mining road of the north. An Taigh-seinnse Reòta stands at its edge, one of the great taverns of the old circuit. Colbh Cnoc chiar stands to the west, and the town's people say the stone's two words are older than any mill.

Siorrachd Baile Mòr mhòr

Baile Mòr mhòr

city · Ròdaich · Na Seann Spioradan · pop. 35,852

Founded 26 an Lùnastal 2977 BDE by the granary-keepers of the early kings in the north. Known for the great walled city of the north.

Baile Mòr mhòr is the great city of the north, walled and crowned by a citadel, and the seat of its province. It held one of the royal granaries in the Holy Age and was a centre of the human administration in the Age of Strangers. Since the Severance it has stood close to the Tuathaich country to the west, the largest Ròdaich city on that frontier.

Caol ìseal

village · Ròdaich · Na Seann Spioradan · pop. 2,953

Founded 25 am Faoilleach 1571 BDE by the strait-watchers of the north coast. Known for the strait watch-fire.

A small harbour-village on the northern strait, with a citadel built to watch the channel. It served Baile Mòr mhòr as a signal-station and watch-post and has never outgrown that role. It keeps the Old Spirits of the Ròdaich, and the watch-fire on its citadel is still lit on the old feast nights.

Dùn thais

city · Ròdaich · Na Seann Spioradan · pop. 3,755

Founded 10 an Dàmhair 1545 BDE by custodians of the northern coast. Known for northernmost Ròdaich citadel.

Dùn thais of the north is the northernmost Ròdaich citadel, raised by the Holy Age custodians on the northern coast. Since the Severance it has watched the Tuathaich country. It keeps the ancestor rite of the Old Spirits.

Siorrachd Baile ruadh

Baile ruadh

town · Ròdaich · Na Seann Spioradan · pop. 19,896

Founded 3 an Dàmhair 2028 BDE by red-earth farmers of the east. Known for red-earth fields of the east.

A red town of the east and the seat of Siorrachd Baile ruadh. It keeps the Old Spirits and trades grain with Achadh naomh.

  • 13 an Lùnastal 90 BDE — The watch-tower at Baile ruadh
  • 3 an t-Sultain 1207 DE — Baile ruadh's quarrel with Achadh naomh
  • 20 an Dàmhair 1827 DE — Baile ruadh loses its seed
  • 3 an Lùnastal 1981 DE — The shafts at Baile ruadh left open

Cnoc fhionn

town · Ròdaich · Na Seann Spioradan · pop. 11,165

Founded 25 an t-Samhain 2811 BDE by farmers of the north-east. Known for fair-hill barley and ale.

Cnoc fhionn, the fair hill, is a large town of sheltered farms in the north-east. It has been settled since the Holy Age and keeps the ancestor rite of the Old Spirits. Its barley and ale go down to the harbour at Seann Tarr.

  • 5 an t-Iuchar 9173 BDE — The first dog graves

Siorrachd Caol bheag

Baile bhàn

town · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 6,025

Founded 21 an Giblean 1595 DE by fullers of the northern coast. Known for bleached cloth from the fulling-mills.

A town of fulling-mills and white cloth between the port-city of Ros chiar and the city of Baile Mòr dhìreach. Its fullers bleached wool for the harbours of the north coast and still do, though in smaller measure since the trade moved to Inis mhòr. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith.

Baile Mòr dhìreach

city · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 2,107

Founded 8 an Gearran 1267 BDE by custodians of the north-eastern road. Known for walled town on the straight road.

Baile Mòr dhìreach of Caol bheag is a walled town with a citadel, built by Holy Age custodians where the north-eastern road runs straight. It is small for a city, but it holds the road and the market between Inis mhòr and Baile gharbh. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith.

Caol bheag

town · Ròdaich · Na Seann Spioradan · pop. 2,189

Founded 15 am Màrt 2522 BDE by fishers of the north coast. Known for the elder Caol bheag on the strait.

A small harbour on the northern strait, older than its far larger namesake inland and the one that gave that town its name. It keeps the Old Spirits and is a quiet fishing town, though An ceathramh rèisimeid, stationed at the larger Caol bheag, sends its patrols here. It stands on Eilean fhada, the long island off the north coast, and the strait it is named for is the sound between that island and Rodos.

  • 13 an t-Sultain 1834 DE — A brig lost in the mist
  • 9 an Dàmhair 1924 DE — Caol bheag's empty quay

Caol bheag

town · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 42,649

Founded 14 an Lùnastal 2406 BDE by Ròdaich boatmen of the small narrows. Known for fourth regiment's river port.

Caol bheag is a river port of more than forty thousand on the narrows of the Abhainn ghorm, crowned by a citadel and the seat of its province; its barges run down to Ros chiar at the river mouth. The fourth regiment, raised in the Long War, is stationed here. The mills of Muileann bheag and the wool of Cnoc chiar pass through its quays.

  • 14 an Gearran 5154 BDE — Boats named for the winds
  • 2 an t-Samhain 2020 DE — An ceathramh rèisimeid raised
  • 22 an Dùbhlachd 2024 DE — The fourth regiment leaves Ceann mhòr

Siorrachd Caol fhiadhaich

Caol fhiadhaich

town · Ròdaich · An Creideamh Sean · pop. 19,115

Founded 12 an t-Iuchar 2857 BDE by the strait-pilots of the south-west. Known for strait-pilots and the harbour wolf-stone.

A harbour on a wild strait whose pilots earned their living guiding ships through the rocks. It is the seat of Siorrachd Caol fhiadhaich and a large town of the order of the Stone, trading with the great tavern-village of Doire shean on its road. The strait pilots still take no ship through without an offering to Clach, the Stone, at the harbour wolf-stone.

  • 14 an Dùbhlachd 1963 BDE — Caol fhiadhaich rebuilt
